docs.title: XRPL Playbook
docs.text:
An opinionated, decision-oriented guide for engineers and architects building real financial products on the XRP Ledger. Favors production realities over toy examples, explains the trade-offs behind each design choice, and treats security and compliance as first-class concerns.

"We wanted to build a better version of Bitcoin — faster, greener, and built specifically for payments. Everything that followed grew from that idea." — David Schwartz (JoelKatz), Chief Technology Officer, Ripple

docs.title: ⚡ Quickstart — get something running in 5 minutes
docs.text:
# 1. Clone and install
git clone https://github.com/your-org/awesome-xrpl-playbook.git
cd awesome-xrpl-playbook
npm install

# 2. Fund a fresh Testnet account and confirm it on-ledger
node examples/01-connect-and-fund/connect-fund.js
# → Account rXXX... funded with 1000 XRP on Testnet
# → Ledger sequence: 12345678  Balance: 1000000000 drops

# Python alternative
pip install xrpl-py
python examples/01-connect-and-fund/connect-fund.py

What just happened?

  • A fresh keypair was generated client-side (no server ever saw the private key).
  • The Testnet faucet funded the account with 1,000 XRP.
  • The confirmed balance was read from a validated ledger — not a mempool prediction.

Where to go next:

Goal Start here Understand why this works Mental Models Send your first real payment Payments + examples/02-reliable-submission Issue a token or stablecoin Issuing Value + examples/03-trust-line-and-issue Provide liquidity on the DEX/AMM Markets & Liquidity + examples/04-amm-deposit Harden keys and custody Security + examples/05-offline-signing

docs.title: A brief history of the XRP Ledger
docs.text: Source: xrpl.org/about/history

docs.title: 2011 — Origin: Provide a Better Alternative to Bitcoin
docs.text:
In early 2011, three developers — David Schwartz, Jed McCaleb, and Arthur Britto — were fascinated with Bitcoin but observed the waste inherent in mining. They sought to create a more sustainable system for sending value (an idea outlined in a May 2011 forum post: "Bitcoin without mining").

Their initial observations about the high energy consumption and scalability issues that would plague Bitcoin proved prescient. In 2019, estimates suggest Bitcoin mining used more energy than the entire country of Portugal. Moreover, their initial read indicated that significant problems could arise if any miner obtained — or miners colluded to obtain — greater than 50% of the mining power. That risk persists with Bitcoin today as mining power has consolidated.

docs.title: 2012 — XRPL Launches its Native Currency, XRP
docs.text:
The trio continued the work to build a distributed ledger that improved upon these fundamental limitations of Bitcoin, originally naming the code Ripple. The ledger included a digital asset that would originally be called "ripples" (XRP as the currency code) to follow the same naming convention as Bitcoin (BTC). At the time, the name Ripple stood for the open-source project, the unique consensus ledger (Ripple Consensus Ledger), the transaction protocol (RTXP), the network, and the digital asset.

By June 2012, Schwartz, McCaleb, and Britto finished code development and the Ledger was complete. Once live, 80% of the XRP was gifted to a new company — initially called NewCoin, quickly renamed OpenCoin. Chris Larsen was the CEO; Jed was co-founder and CTO; David Schwartz was Chief Cryptography Officer; and Arthur Britto an advisor.

docs.title: 2013 — OpenCoin Rebranded to Ripple Labs
docs.text:
Since the early days, OpenCoin set out to revolutionize the global financial system. Chris Larsen never thought blockchain technology should be used to overthrow the existing financial system — he believed history's most transformative innovations have always relied on the great ideas that came before them, not displacing them.

With the community starting to refer to the digital asset as XRP, company leaders decided to rebrand to Ripple Labs (shortened over time to "Ripple"). Today, Ripple has created a use case leveraging the XRP Ledger and XRP for liquidity management in its cross-border payments business, and remains a stakeholder and contributor to the broader XRPL community.

docs.title: 2020 — XRPL Foundation Launched
docs.text: Founded September 24, 2020, the XRPL Foundation is an independent, nonprofit entity with a mission to accelerate the development and adoption of the decentralized XRP Ledger. The Foundation received an initial donation of over $6.5 million from Coil, Ripple, and Gatehub to fund its work in service of the growing number of developers and global community members building on the XRP Ledger.

docs.title: The architects and core developers
docs.text: The ledger you are building on was shaped by a small group of engineers whose fingerprints are still visible in the source code today.

docs.title: What is this playbook?
docs.text:
The XRPL Playbook is an opinionated, decision-oriented guide for engineers and architects building real financial products on the XRP Ledger. It favors production realities over toy examples, explains the trade-offs behind each design choice, and treats security and compliance as first-class concerns.

The decisions those engineers made in 2011–2012 — consensus without mining, reserves as spam prevention, trust lines as programmable credit relationships, a fixed transaction type set extended only by amendments — are not arbitrary constraints. They encode deliberate trade-offs. This playbook exists to explain why those trade-offs were made and what they mean for your system so you can build with the grain of the ledger rather than against it.

docs.title: How to use this playbook
docs.text:
1. Start with Mental Models. Every other section assumes you're comfortable with reserves, trust lines, fees, and finality.
  2. Jump to your domain — payments, stablecoins, tokenization, DeFi.
  3. Apply Security as a cross-cutting layer over whatever you build.
  4. Study the Reference Architectures to see how the primitives compose into complete systems.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Section What it covers Mental Models Foundational ways to reason about the ledger: state machine, reserves, trust lines, fees, finality. Payments Direct and cross-currency payments, pathfinding, partial payments, channels, escrow, and reliable submission. Stablecoins Issuing fiat-backed tokens: issuer configuration, authorization, freeze/clawback, and reserves. Tokenization Representing real-world and digital assets with MPTs and NFTs, including lifecycle controls. DeFi The native DEX, AMM mechanics, liquidity provision, routing, and oracles. Security Key management, multi-signing, account hardening, custody, and operational security. Reference Architectures End-to-end designs combining the primitives into production systems.

docs.text: This playbook is under active development. See the ROADMAP for what exists today and what's planned next, and the living Open questions log for the hypothesis-labeled questions across the playbook that still need source verification.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: This roadmap describes the planned evolution of the XRPL Playbook. It is a living document — priorities will shift as the XRP Ledger and its ecosystem evolve. See CONTRIBUTING.md if you'd like to help.

docs.title: Guiding principles
docs.text:
• Production-first. Every chapter targets real, deployable systems — not toy examples.
  • Decisions over recipes. Explain the trade-offs so readers can make their own informed choices.
  • Safety by default. Security, compliance, and operational concerns are treated as first-class, not afterthoughts.
  • Current and accurate. Content tracks the live protocol and is revised as amendments ship.

docs.title: Phase 0 — Coming from other chains → ch00-coming-from-other-chains
docs.text:
• [x] Chapter-level README — an optional on-ramp for engineers arriving from EVM, Solana, or Bitcoin; the four mappings that matter most (no smart contracts → native primitives; failure is usually free and off-ledger; state costs a refundable reserve; fees burn), and pointers into the chapter each topic is covered in depth.
  • [x] Concept Mapping (ch00-coming-from-other-chains/concept-mapping) — side-by-side translation tables (account/execution model; tokens & value; failure, finality & programmability) with a Watch out note on every lossy analogy. XRPL-side claims source-anchored to rippled/: account-based AccountRoot/sfSequence and ltTICKET; tec-vs-EVM-revert semantics ("claim fee to use the sequence number", TER.h); trust lines (ltRIPPLE_STATE) vs ERC-20; native ltOFFER/ltAMM/ltMPTOKEN*/ ltNFTOKEN_PAGE objects vs deployed contracts; amendments vs contract upgrades. Cross-linked to ch01–ch06.
  • [x] RPC Method Mapping (ch00-coming-from-other-chains/rpc-method-mapping) — the day-one API lookup mapping EVM/Solana JSON-RPC calls to XRPL command equivalents (eth_getBalance→account_info/account_lines, eth_call→ledger_entry/ripple_path_find, eth_sendRawTransaction→submit, eth_getTransactionReceipt→tx, eth_estimateGas→fee), each pinned to the canonical command dispatch table (src/xrpld/rpc/detail/Handler.cpp) with Watch out notes.
  • [x] Indexing (History & State) (ch00-coming-from-other-chains/indexing-and-history) — the TheGraph/Etherscan/eth_getLogs replacement: account_tx pagination (ledger_index_min/max -1 sentinels, forward, binary, the opaque {ledger, seq} marker, the 10/200/400 limit envelope from Tuning.h), the Clio read-replica vs validating-node split, and state indexing via ledger_data (type filtering, hex-key marker, kBinaryPageLength = 2048 / kJsonPageLength = 256 from Tuning.h, source-anchored to LedgerData.cpp). Dual comparison tables: mental-model contrast (query unit, scope, use case) and parameter-level reference (pagination cursor type, limit, forward).
  • [x] Subscriptions & the Event Model (ch00-coming-from-other-chains/subscriptions) — the logs/topics/webhooks replacement: the subscribe streams, accounts/accounts_proposed, and books feeds, with the exact message type each publisher emits (ledgerClosed, transaction, validationReceived, …) from NetworkOPs.cpp, and the validated-gated finality + reconnect/backfill pattern.

docs.text:

docs.title: Open questions — living log
docs.text:
A single index of the hypothesis-labeled open questions scattered across the playbook, so they are easy to find, revisit, and promote to "Confirmed against source" as they get verified against the rippled/ tree.

This is a living document. When you add a new open question to a section, add a row here. When you verify a hypothesis against source, move it to Recently resolved and update the label in its section.

docs.title: How to read the status column
docs.text:
• 🔬 Hypothesis — a reasoned answer that has not been verified against rippled/ source. Highest priority to resolve.
  • 🧭 Educated guess — an operational/best-practice answer that is not directly encoded in the protocol source (so it cannot be "confirmed against source" the same way), but reflects informed judgement.
  • ❓ Unanswered — a plain question with no answer written yet.
  • ✅ Confirmed — verified against source; tracked in Recently resolved, not the open list below.

Counts as of last sync: 12 🔬 Hypothesis · 14 🧭 Educated guess · 11 ❓ Unanswered · 9 ✅ Confirmed. (Some questions carry a mixed label — e.g. a confirmed mechanism with a still-open operational half — and are listed under their primary open status; H1, G6/G8, and the ch00 API guesses G9/G11/G13 are the notable mixed cases.)

docs.title: XRPL Playbook — Runnable Examples
docs.text: Self-contained scripts demonstrating core XRPL patterns. Every script targets the XRPL Testnet by default; no Mainnet funds are needed. Each script also supports an opt-in standalone mode against a local node — see standalone/.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
JavaScript (Node 18+) 

npm install xrpl

Python (3.9+) 

pip install xrpl-py

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Required Description TESTNET_SEED Optional Pre-funded Testnet seed (e.g. sEd...). If absent the Testnet faucet is called automatically. STANDALONE Optional Set to 1 to run against a local standalone node instead of Testnet. See standalone/. STANDALONE_WS Optional Standalone admin WebSocket for the JS scripts (default ws://127.0.0.1:6006). STANDALONE_URL Optional Standalone admin JSON-RPC for the Python scripts (default http://127.0.0.1:5005).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: # Directory What it demonstrates Playbook section 01 01-connect-and-fund/ Connect to Testnet, auto-fund via faucet, inspect account info ch01 › Getting Started 02 02-reliable-submission/ Reliable submission loop — LastLedgerSequence + hash-based retry ch01 › Payments 03 03-trust-line-and-issue/ Hot/cold IOU issuance (set trust line, send issued currency) ch02 › Stablecoins 04 04-amm-deposit/ Create an AMM pool and deposit liquidity (standalone: see caveat) ch03 › DeFi 05 05-offline-signing/ Fetch server_definitions, cache codec hash, sign transaction offline ch04 › Custody

docs.title: Running an example
docs.text:
# JavaScript
cd examples/01-connect-and-fund
node connect-fund.js

# Python
cd examples/01-connect-and-fund
python connect-fund.py

Each script prints step-by-step progress and exits non-zero on error so it is CI-friendly.

docs.title: Standalone mode
docs.text:
To run against a local node with no external network, start the bundled standalone node and set STANDALONE=1:

# JavaScript
STANDALONE=1 node connect-fund.js

# Python
STANDALONE=1 python connect-fund.py

Setup, endpoints, teardown, and a known limitation for example 04 (AMM) are documented in standalone/README.md.

docs.title: The Playbook
docs.text: "We wanted to build a better version of Bitcoin — faster, greener, and built specifically for payments. Everything that followed grew from that idea." — David Schwartz (JoelKatz), Chief Technology Officer, Ripple

docs.title: A brief history of the XRP Ledger
docs.text: Source: xrpl.org/about/history

docs.title: 2011 — Origin: Provide a Better Alternative to Bitcoin
docs.text:
In early 2011, three developers — David Schwartz, Jed McCaleb, and Arthur Britto — were fascinated with Bitcoin but observed the waste inherent in mining. They sought to create a more sustainable system for sending value (an idea outlined in a May 2011 forum post: "Bitcoin without mining").

Their initial observations about the high energy consumption and scalability issues that would plague Bitcoin proved prescient. In 2019, estimates suggest Bitcoin mining used more energy than the entire country of Portugal. Moreover, their initial read indicated that significant problems could arise if any miner obtained — or miners colluded to obtain — greater than 50% of the mining power. That risk persists with Bitcoin today as mining power has consolidated.

docs.title: 2012 — XRPL Launches its Native Currency, XRP
docs.text:
The trio continued the work to build a distributed ledger that improved upon these fundamental limitations of Bitcoin, originally naming the code Ripple. The ledger included a digital asset that would originally be called "ripples" (XRP as the currency code) to follow the same naming convention as Bitcoin (BTC). At the time, the name Ripple stood for the open-source project, the unique consensus ledger (Ripple Consensus Ledger), the transaction protocol (RTXP), the network, and the digital asset.

By June 2012, Schwartz, McCaleb, and Britto finished code development and the Ledger was complete. Once live, 80% of the XRP was gifted to a new company — initially called NewCoin, quickly renamed OpenCoin. Chris Larsen was the CEO; Jed was co-founder and CTO; David Schwartz was Chief Cryptography Officer; and Arthur Britto an advisor.

docs.title: 2013 — OpenCoin Rebranded to Ripple Labs
docs.text:
Since the early days, OpenCoin set out to revolutionize the global financial system. Chris Larsen never thought blockchain technology should be used to overthrow the existing financial system — he believed history's most transformative innovations have always relied on the great ideas that came before them, not displacing them.

With the community starting to refer to the digital asset as XRP, company leaders decided to rebrand to Ripple Labs (shortened over time to "Ripple"). Today, Ripple has created a use case leveraging the XRP Ledger and XRP for liquidity management in its cross-border payments business, and remains a stakeholder and contributor to the broader XRPL community.

docs.title: 2020 — XRPL Foundation Launched
docs.text: Founded September 24, 2020, the XRPL Foundation is an independent, nonprofit entity with a mission to accelerate the development and adoption of the decentralized XRP Ledger. The Foundation received an initial donation of over $6.5 million from Coil, Ripple, and Gatehub to fund its work in service of the growing number of developers and global community members building on the XRP Ledger.

docs.title: The architects and core developers
docs.text: The ledger you are building on was shaped by a small group of engineers whose fingerprints are still visible in the source code today.

docs.title: What this playbook is
docs.text:
This directory is the core of the XRPL Playbook — a practitioner's guide to building production-grade financial applications on the XRP Ledger. Each chapter targets a specific domain of knowledge, written in order of dependency: later chapters assume mastery of earlier ones.

The decisions those engineers made in 2011–2012 — consensus without mining, reserves as spam prevention, trust lines as programmable credit relationships, a fixed transaction type set extended only by amendments — are not arbitrary constraints. They encode deliberate trade-offs. This playbook exists to explain why those trade-offs were made and what they mean for your system so you can build with the grain of the ledger rather than against it.

docs.title: Why this structure exists
docs.text:
Most XRPL documentation explains what the protocol does. This playbook explains why it is designed that way and what that means for your system.

The chapters follow a deliberate progression:

  1. Get the mental models right first. Almost every production incident on the XRPL traces back to a wrong assumption — about finality, about reserves, about what "success" means before a ledger is validated. No amount of domain-specific knowledge compensates for a broken foundation.

  2. Apply the foundation to the first real domain (payments). Payments are the simplest domain but still contain most of the traps: partial payment exploits, race conditions on sequence numbers, hard-coded fees that break under load, stuck transactions that are silently queued, not failed.

  3. Layer on value issuance. Once you can move value reliably, the next question is how to represent it. Stablecoins and tokenization share the same underlying primitives (trust lines, issued currencies, account flags) but serve different risk and compliance postures.

  4. Add liquidity and markets. The native DEX and AMM are protocol-level primitives, not smart contracts. Understanding their mechanics — how offers cross, how AMM pricing works, how pathfinding routes across both — is required for anything involving exchange rates, cross-currency flows, or treasury management.

  5. Harden the system. Security and operations are not a chapter you read after finishing — they are a layer you apply retroactively to everything else. The hardening chapter is placed here intentionally: by this point you have enough domain context to understand why each security control exists.

  6. Compose into real systems. The reference architectures chapter shows how the primitives from all prior chapters combine into production deployments: account topologies, transaction flows, failure modes, and reconciliation loops.

docs.title: Learning tracks
docs.text: You probably arrived here with a goal, not a desire to read six chapters in order. Pick the track that matches what you're building. Each one lists the minimum path through the playbook and the runnable example that cements it.

docs.text:
"I need to issue a fiat-backed or RWA token with freeze, clawback, and reserve attestation."

docs.title: 💸 Cross-border payment provider
docs.text:
"I need to send value between currencies with atomic on-ledger settlement and deterministic finality."

Step Chapter / Section Runnable example 1 Mental Models — finality, result codes, fee escalation — 2 Payments — cross-currency, reliable submission, partial payments examples/02-reliable-submission 3 DeFi — DEX + AMM routing — 4 Security examples/05-offline-signing 5 Reference Arch #1 — Cross-border payment provider —

docs.text:
"I'm fluent in EVM and need to understand how XRPL's model differs before writing a single line."

docs.text:

docs.title: ch00-coming-from-other-chains
docs.text:
Optional on-ramp for engineers arriving from another chain.

A translation layer for developers already fluent in EVM, Solana, or Bitcoin. It maps the concepts you know to their XRPL equivalents and flags exactly where the analogy breaks down — so the rest of the playbook reads as refinement, not contradiction. Skip it if the XRPL is your first ledger.

Section What you will be able to do Concept Mapping Translate the account model, tokens, fees, failure semantics, finality, and programmability from your home chain to the XRPL; predict which home-chain habits cause bugs; know which chapter covers each topic in depth. RPC Method Mapping Map the JSON-RPC / SDK calls you reach for on day one (eth_getBalance, eth_call, eth_sendRawTransaction, eth_getTransactionReceipt) to their XRPL command equivalents, each anchored to the rippled/ dispatch table. Indexing (History & State) Replace TheGraph / Etherscan / eth_getLogs with account_tx (history) and ledger_data (state) pagination; avoid the classic marker/range bugs. Subscriptions & the Event Model Replace logs / topics / webhooks with the subscribe streams and per-account feeds, keying finality off validated and owning the reconnect/backfill layer.

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: The biggest gap is not syntax — it is the location of capability. On EVM, capability lives in deployed code; on the XRPL it lives in a fixed, versioned set of transaction types and ledger objects, extended only by amendments. Almost every "false friend" (nonce, revert, token, finality) traces back to that one difference.

docs.title: ch01-foundations
docs.text:
Prerequisite for everything.

The three sections here — Mental Models, Getting Started, and Payments — establish the vocabulary and reasoning framework used throughout the rest of the playbook. They are the only sections with no prerequisites. Read them in order.

Section What you will be able to do Mental Models Reason about the ledger as a state machine; correctly calculate reserves; distinguish finality from confirmation; read transaction result codes; avoid the most common submission bugs. Includes source-anchored internals (transaction engine, STAmount, consensus/UNL). Getting Started Connect a client (xrpl.js / xrpl-py), fund a Testnet account, and run the connect → fund → autofill → sign → submit → confirm loop with reliable submission; stand up a local standalone xrpld node for deterministic testing. Payments Select the right payment primitive for any use case; implement a reliable submission loop; handle all failure modes including fee escalation, TxQ queuing, and partial payments; use CTID for cross-network transaction tracking.

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: The XRP Ledger is not a general-purpose blockchain with financial applications bolted on. It is a financial settlement network whose every primitive — reserves, trust lines, fees, finality — encodes a specific operational trade-off. Internalizing those trade-offs is the foundation that everything else builds on.

docs.title: ch02-issuing-value
docs.text:
Prerequisite: ch01.

Covers everything needed to put value on-ledger: creating and managing issued currencies as stablecoins, and representing real-world or digital assets as tokens.

Section What you will be able to do Issuer Controls Configure an issuer account correctly; understand the implications of DefaultRipple, RequireAuth, NoFreeze, and Clawback; manage object-level enforcement; navigate the tecOWNERS constraint. Stablecoins Design a regulated issuance model; structure hot/cold account topologies; handle minting and redemption flows; design a reserve attestation process. Tokenization Choose between MPTs and NFTs for a given asset type; manage token lifecycle from mint to burn; anchor metadata correctly; plan reserve capacity for MPT sets.

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: Issuing value on the XRPL is not a technical act — it is a legal and operational commitment. Every issuer flag (DefaultRipple, NoFreeze, RequireAuth) has a real-world counterpart in the trust relationship between issuer and holder. Get the flags wrong at launch and there is no clean rollback.

docs.title: ch03-markets-and-liquidity
docs.text:
Prerequisite: ch01, ch02.

Covers the native DEX and AMM — both are protocol-level objects, not smart contracts — and how pathfinding routes cross-currency payments through them.

Section What you will be able to do DeFi Place and manage orders on the native DEX; understand AMM geometric-mean pricing and the continuous auction mechanism; provide and withdraw liquidity; consume on-ledger oracles safely; build systems that route through both DEX and AMM.

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: Because liquidity exists at the protocol level rather than in application contracts, it composes atomically with payments. A cross-currency payment can route through DEX hops and AMM pools in the same transaction, with no intermediate settlement steps and no possibility of partial execution.

docs.title: ch04-hardening
docs.text:
Applies to all prior chapters.

Two complementary disciplines, kept separate because they address different failure modes: account security (key compromise → funds loss) and node operations (software lag, disk exhaustion → availability loss).

Section What you will be able to do Security Disable master keys safely; configure multi-signing with the correct quorum; use regular keys and signing layers; set DepositAuth and DisallowIncoming; write and drill an incident response runbook. Operations Monitor amendment activation before it blocks a node; configure online delete to prevent disk exhaustion; design a read-path with failover; upgrade xrpld without service disruption. Custody Design 3-tier signing stacks (builder / codec gate / offline signer); implement server_definitions codec pinning; manage the amendment lifecycle for HSMs.

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: On the XRPL, both failure modes are irreversible in their own way — a key lost behind lsfDisableMaster cannot be recovered, and an amendment that activates on an unprepared node cannot be rolled back. Hardening is not remediation; it is prevention.

docs.title: ch05-reference-architectures
docs.text:
Prerequisite: all prior chapters.

Shows how the primitives from every prior chapter compose into real production systems. Each architecture covers account topology, transaction flows, failure and recovery paths, reconciliation, and monitoring.

Section What you will be able to do Reference Architectures Design a complete cross-border payment provider, stablecoin issuer, RWA tokenization platform, exchange integration, or DeFi treasury — with documented failure modes and a production-ready checklist.

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: The hardest problems in XRPL production systems are not protocol problems — they are system boundary problems: reconciling on-ledger finality with off-ledger databases, handling partial failures across fiat rails, and keeping account topologies auditable as systems grow. The reference architectures make these boundaries explicit.

docs.title: ch06-features-and-amendments
docs.text:
Cross-cutting reference: consult before building on any feature.

Maps every XRPL amendment to the xrpld version that introduced it, its current mainnet status, and the use cases it enables — from active features already in production to upcoming features still in development.

Section What you will be able to do Feature Reference Determine whether a feature is active, open for voting, or in development; identify the minimum xrpld version; understand the practical use case; plan upgrade and monitoring workflows.

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: The XRPL feature pipeline is not a simple queue — amendments can be withdrawn, obsoleted, or replaced mid-vote (as happened with Batch and PermissionDelegation). Building on an amendment before it activates — or worse, on an obsoleted one — is a silent architectural risk. Always validate status against server_info, not documentation.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
Mental Models ──► Payments ──► Stablecoins ──► DeFi ──► Reference Architectures
                                    │                            ▲
                              Tokenization ───────────────────────
                                                    ▲
                     Security + Operations (apply throughout)
                                                    ▲
                     Feature Reference (ch06 — consult before any feature use)

If you are new to the XRPL, read sequentially from ch01. If you already build on another chain (EVM, Solana, or Bitcoin), start with ch00 — Coming from Other Chains for the concept-mapping tables, then continue into ch01. If you are building a specific product, jump to the relevant chapter — but read Mental Models first regardless. Consult the Feature Reference (ch06) any time you are planning to use a feature that may not yet be active on Mainnet.

Keep the Glossary and prefix conventions open alongside any chapter — it decodes the tes/tec/ter/tef/tem/tel result-code prefixes and the tf/asf/lsf/sf/lt/tt flag/field/type prefixes used throughout, all anchored to the rippled/ source.

For a quick lookup while coding, see the Cheat Sheet — a single-page reference for common tasks, transaction types, result codes, and reserve costs.

docs.title: Table 2: Result code families — fee and ledger behavior
docs.text:
Prefix Meaning Fee charged? Reaches validated ledger? Recovery action tes Success ✅ Yes ✅ Yes None needed tec Claim (partial failure) ✅ Yes ✅ Yes Fix the root cause; rebuild + resubmit ter Retry ❌ No ❌ No Resubmit after a moment (transient condition) tef Failure ❌ No ❌ No Fix the issue (bad sequence, bad sig); rebuild tem Malformed ❌ No ❌ No Fix the transaction structure; rebuild tel Local ❌ No ❌ No Transient node load issue; retry or use different node

Critical tec codes every payment flow must handle:

Code Value Meaning tecNO_DST 124 Destination account does not exist tecNO_DST_INSUF_XRP 125 Destination exists but balance below reserve tecUNFUNDED_PAYMENT 104 Sender has insufficient XRP/IOU balance tecPATH_DRY 128 No path with sufficient liquidity tecPATH_PARTIAL 101 Partial fill only; tfPartialPayment not set tecDST_TAG_NEEDED 143 Destination requires a destination tag

Critical tef codes (sequence management):

Code Value Meaning tefPAST_SEQ -168 Sequence already consumed; fetch and update tefALREADY -198 Exact same tx already in the ledger

docs.title: Table 3: Reserve cost reference
docs.text:
Reserves are denominated in XRP drops. Fetch live values via: 

{ "command": "server_info" }
→ result.info.validated_ledger.reserve_base_xrp   (base reserve)
→ result.info.validated_ledger.reserve_inc_xrp    (per-object increment)

Or via fee command: 

{ "command": "fee" }
→ result.drops.base_fee
→ result.drops.minimum_fee

Current values (subject to fee voting):

Reserve type Current value Formula Base account reserve 2 XRP Fixed per account Owner reserve (per object) 0.2 XRP reserve_inc × owner_count

Common object costs:

Object type Owner reserve Trust line (RippleState) 0.2 XRP DEX offer (Offer) 0.2 XRP Escrow (Escrow) 0.2 XRP Payment channel (PayChannel) 0.2 XRP Signer list (SignerList) 0.2 XRP × (N+1) where N = number of signers NFT page (NFTokenPage) 0.2 XRP per page (up to 32 NFTs per page) MPT holder entry (MPToken) 0.2 XRP Price oracle (PriceOracle) 0.2 XRP Check (Check) 0.2 XRP Ticket (Ticket) 0.2 XRP each

Reserve calculation example: 

Account with: 3-of-5 SignerList + 10 trust lines + 5 open offers + 2 escrows
= 2 XRP (base)
+ (5+1) × 0.2 XRP (signer list)
+ 10 × 0.2 XRP (trust lines)
+ 5 × 0.2 XRP (offers)
+ 2 × 0.2 XRP (escrows)
= 2 + 1.2 + 2.0 + 1.0 + 0.4 = 6.6 XRP locked

The account needs 6.6 XRP + safety_buffer to remain able to submit transactions. Spendable XRP = balance − 6.6 XRP. If spendable drops to 0, the account cannot pay fees.

See Glossary for full definitions. See ch01 › Payments for submission gotchas.

docs.title: Glossary and prefix conventions
docs.text:
A single reference for the terminology and the naming prefixes used throughout this playbook. The XRPL source uses terse, systematic prefixes for result codes, flags, fields, ledger objects, and transaction types. Once you can decode a prefix, an unfamiliar identifier becomes largely self-documenting.

Every prefix meaning here is anchored to the vendored rippled/ source.

docs.title: Result-code prefixes (TER family)
docs.text:
Every transaction returns a result code. The two-and-a-bit-letter prefix tells you what class of outcome it is — and, critically, whether it reaches a validated ledger and whether a fee is charged. Source of truth: rippled/include/xrpl/protocol/TER.h (the code ranges and their comments).

Prefix Class Code range Reaches a validated ledger? Fee charged? Meaning tes Success 0 (tesSUCCESS) Yes Yes The transaction succeeded. tec Claimed cost ≥ 100 Yes Yes Failed to achieve its effect, but was well-formed, so it claims the fee and consumes the sequence. "Claim fee to use the sequence number." ter Retry -99 .. -1 No No Could succeed in a later ledger (e.g. terQUEUED, terPRE_SEQ). May be held/forwarded. tef Failure -199 .. -100 No No Cannot succeed now (e.g. sequence already used, tefPAST_SEQ) but could in an imagined ledger. tem Malformed -299 .. -200 No No The transaction is invalid in any ledger (bad signature, bad amount). Never applies. tel Local error -399 .. -300 No No Rejected by this node's local policy (fee below load, telINSUF_FEE_P). Another node might accept it.

Non-obvious insight (the line that matters most): only tes and tec ever appear in a validated ledger, and both charge a fee. Everything with a negative code (tel/tem/tef/ter) is rejected before it lands, so it costs nothing and does not consume the sequence number. This is the single most important thing a developer coming from a gas-metered chain must internalize: a malformed or premature transaction is free, and only a transaction that made it far enough to claim a sequence slot (tec) costs you the fee on failure. See ch01 transaction engine internals for why the pipeline enforces this.

The helper predicates isTesSuccess, isTecClaim, isTerRetry, isTefFailure, isTemMalformed, and isTelLocal in TER.h implement exactly these range checks.

docs.title: Flag and field prefixes
docs.text:
XRPL uses distinct prefixes for the different kinds of flags and identifiers. Confusing them is a common source of bugs — an asf* value is not interchangeable with a tf* value even when they concern the same setting.

Prefix Kind Where set / stored Source tf Transaction flags — per-submission bits in the Flags field (e.g. tfPartialPayment, tfFullyCanonicalSig). Set on the transaction you submit. TxFlags.h asf AccountSet flags — enable/disable persistent account settings via AccountSet SetFlag/ClearFlag (e.g. asfRequireDest, asfDisableMaster, asfDefaultRipple). Passed as an integer to AccountSet. TxFlags.h lsf Ledger state flags — the stored bits that an asf* setting toggles, read back on the on-ledger object (e.g. lsfRequireAuth, lsfDisableMaster, lsfDefaultRipple). Read from AccountRoot / RippleState. LedgerFormats.h sf Serialized fields — the canonical named fields of every object/transaction (e.g. sfAccount, sfSequence, sfAmount). The serialization/type layer. SField / sfields.macro lt Ledger entry types — the kinds of on-ledger objects (e.g. ltACCOUNT_ROOT, ltRIPPLE_STATE, ltOFFER, ltAMM). Ledger object type tags. ledger_entries.macro tt Transaction types — the enumerated transaction kinds (e.g. ttPAYMENT, ttOFFER_CREATE, ttAMENDMENT). The TransactionType field. transactions.macro

Watch out: asf* (the verb you send) and lsf* (the noun you read back) frequently describe the same setting under different names. For example, sending asfDefaultRipple sets the stored lsfDefaultRipple bit; sending asfDisableMaster sets lsfDisableMaster. When you submit, use asf*; when you inspect account state, expect lsf*.

docs.title: Core terms
docs.text: Term Definition Account An entry (ltACCOUNT_ROOT) identified by an r-address, holding the XRP balance, Sequence, flags, and owner count. Must be funded above the base reserve to exist. Amendment An on-ledger, vote-activated protocol change. Requires ~80% validator support sustained for two weeks. Permanent once activated. See ch06. Autofill SDK step that populates Fee, Sequence, and LastLedgerSequence before signing. See Getting Started. Base reserve The minimum XRP an account must hold to exist. A protocol-level, adjustable amount. Drops The integer unit of XRP; 1 XRP = 1,000,000 drops. XRP amounts are always integers of drops. Flag ledger A ledger (index divisible by 256) on which amendment/fee voting is tallied. IOU / issued currency A balance denominated in a non-XRP currency, represented as a RippleState (trust line) with mantissa/exponent precision. Keylet A typed, hashed key locating an object in the state tree (sha512Half of a type prefix + identifiers). LastLedgerSequence The last ledger index at which a transaction may apply; the expiry that makes reliable retry safe. Owner reserve Additional XRP locked (not spent) per owned ledger object (trust line, offer, etc.). Released when the object is deleted. Reserve Collective term for base + owner reserve: XRP held, not burned, to back ledger state. Sequence A per-account, monotonically increasing counter; a transaction is valid at exactly one sequence. Replay prevention. Standalone mode A private, peerless xrpld instance (-a) where you advance ledgers manually via ledger_accept. See Getting Started. server_definitions RPC method returning the full serialization codec (field metadata, transaction formats, ledger entry formats, flags, result codes) plus a SHA512Half hash of the entire payload. The hash is the canonical codec version identifier for custody and offline-signing systems — if the hash matches a cached copy, the codec is byte-identical and offline transaction construction is safe. See ch04 Custody. STAmount The value type holding either XRP drops (integer) or an IOU mantissa/exponent. See ch01 internals. Trust line A bilateral RippleState object encoding a credit limit and balance between two accounts for one currency. UNL / nUNL Unique Node List (the validators a node trusts) and the Negative UNL (validators temporarily excluded to preserve liveness). See ch01 consensus internals. Validated The only authoritative transaction state: included in a ledger agreed by consensus. Not the same as the preliminary engine result. xrpld The XRP Ledger server daemon (the software historically named rippled; the vendored source tree here retains the rippled/ directory name).

docs.title: Chapter 0 — Coming from Other Chains
docs.text:
If you already build on Ethereum (or another EVM chain), Solana, or Bitcoin, you arrive with a set of instincts. Most of them are useful. A few of them are actively dangerous on the XRP Ledger, because the XRPL made different design choices at the protocol level — and those choices are not configurable.

This chapter is a translation layer. It maps the concepts you already know to their XRPL equivalents, flags the places where the mapping is lossy (where your instinct will mislead you), and points you to the chapter that covers each topic in depth.

Read this chapter if you are already fluent in another chain. If the XRPL is your first ledger, skip it and start at Chapter 1 — Foundations; the concept-mapping tables assume you already hold the source-side mental models.

docs.title: Why this chapter comes before Chapter 1
docs.text:
The single most expensive category of mistake for an experienced blockchain engineer on the XRPL is false familiarity — assuming a word means what it means on your home chain:

  • "Token" does not mean a deployed contract. There is no contract.
  • "Nonce" is close to XRPL's account Sequence, but the failure modes differ.
  • "Revert" is not the same as a failed XRPL transaction — most XRPL failures never touch the ledger at all, and cost nothing.
  • "Finality" is deterministic here, not probabilistic. There is no confirmation count to wait for and no reorg to defend against.

Getting these right up front means the rest of the playbook reads as refinement rather than contradiction.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Section Scope Concept Mapping Side-by-side translation tables (EVM / Solana / BTC → XRPL) for the account model, tokens, fees, failure semantics, finality, and programmability — each with the XRPL claim anchored to rippled/ source. RPC Method Mapping The day-one API lookup: which XRPL command replaces eth_getBalance, eth_call, eth_sendRawTransaction, eth_getTransactionReceipt, etc. — every method pinned to the rippled/ dispatch table. Indexing (History & State) Where TheGraph/Etherscan/eth_getLogs go: account_tx (history) and ledger_data (state) pagination; avoid the classic marker/range bugs. Subscriptions & the Event Model The replacement for logs/topics/webhooks: the subscribe streams (ledger, transactions, per-account, order books) and the exact message type each emits.

docs.title: The four mappings that matter most
docs.text:
If you internalize nothing else from this chapter, internalize these four, because each one inverts a load-bearing assumption from your home chain:

  1. No smart contracts — native primitives instead. Payments, escrow, the DEX, the AMM, tokens (IOUs, MPTs, NFTs), and account controls are all built-in transaction types and ledger objects, not user-deployed code. New capabilities arrive through amendments (on-ledger governance), not deployments. See ch06.

  2. Failure is usually free and off-ledger. On EVM a failed call still costs gas and lands in a block. On the XRPL, only two outcomes reach a validated ledger: success (tes) and a claimed failure (tec, which costs the fee and consumes the sequence). Everything else (tem, tef, tel, ter) is rejected before consensus and costs nothing. See the result-code taxonomy in ch01 mental models and the transaction engine internals that explain why only tes/tec reach a validated ledger.

  3. State costs a reserve, refundable. Like Solana rent, every account and every object it owns locks up XRP (base + owner reserve). Unlike gas, the reserve is not spent — it is held, and released when the object is deleted. See ch01 mental models.

  4. Fees burn. Transaction fees are destroyed, not paid to validators or miners. There is no block reward and no MEV auction to a proposer, because there is no proposer being paid. See ch01 mental models.

docs.title: What you should be able to do after this chapter
docs.text:
• Translate any core concept from EVM/Solana/BTC into its nearest XRPL equivalent, and state precisely where the analogy breaks down.
  • Predict which of your home-chain habits will cause bugs on the XRPL (nonce gaps, waiting for confirmations, treating IOUs like ERC-20 balances, expecting reverts to be on-chain).
  • Know which chapter to open for the full treatment of each topic.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Once the mappings click, read Chapter 1 — Foundations in full — it is written for a blank slate, so treat the parts you already understand as confirmation and slow down on the parts this chapter flagged as lossy.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text:
Every experienced blockchain engineer carries a mental dictionary. When you read "token," "nonce," or "gas," you reach for the definition from your home chain. On the XRPL some of those definitions translate cleanly and some are traps. This section is the dictionary — with the traps marked.

Each row states the concept as you know it, its nearest XRPL equivalent, and a Watch out note wherever the analogy is lossy. Every XRPL-side claim is anchored to the vendored rippled/ source (see References), so you can verify rather than trust.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text: Hold one framing above all others: the XRPL is not a world computer with finance built on top; it is a settlement network whose finance primitives are the protocol. On EVM chains, capability lives in deployed code. On the XRPL, capability lives in a fixed, versioned set of transaction types and ledger objects, extended only through amendments. This single difference is the root cause of most of the mapping mismatches below.

docs.title: The account & execution model
docs.text: You know (EVM / Solana / BTC) XRPL equivalent Watch out Account/UTXO model. EVM & Solana are account-based; Bitcoin is UTXO. Account-based. Each account is an AccountRoot ledger object holding balance, Sequence, flags, and owner count. Coming from Bitcoin: there are no UTXOs, no coin selection, no change outputs. State is a mutable per-account record. Nonce (EVM) — per-account counter, must be strictly sequential. Sequence — a per-account counter; a transaction is valid only at the account's current sequence. Closer to EVM nonce than Solana. But a gap does not "queue forever" the same way — and you can escape strict ordering with Tickets (ltTICKET / sfTicketSequence) for pre-authorized, out-of-order submission. Solana recent blockhash — dedup/expiry via a recent blockhash. LastLedgerSequence — sets a hard expiry ledger; the transaction cannot apply after it. Always set it. A transaction with no LastLedgerSequence can be applied long after you signed it. Rent (Solana) — lamports locked to keep an account alive. Reserves — base reserve per account + owner reserve per owned object (trust line, offer, escrow…). The reserve is held, not spent. Delete the object and the owner reserve is freed. There is no "rent collection" that drains you to zero. Gas (EVM) / compute units (Solana) — metered execution paid to the block producer. Transaction fee — a flat-ish cost that scales under load and is burned. No per-opcode metering (there is no VM). No producer is paid — the fee is destroyed. No priority tip to a proposer; congestion is handled by fee escalation + a transaction queue.

docs.title: Tokens & value
docs.text: You know XRPL equivalent Watch out ERC-20 — a deployed contract holding a balances mapping. Issued currency (IOU) held in a trust line (ltRIPPLE_STATE) — a bilateral ledger object between holder and issuer. There is no per-token contract. The "token" is a 160-bit/3-char currency code plus an issuer account. The holder must first establish a trust line; balances are a signed number relative to the issuer. ERC-20 approve/allowance. No allowance concept for IOUs. Authorization is at the trust-line / account level (RequireAuth, DepositAuth, NoRipple). Do not look for approve. Model authorization with issuer flags and trust-line authorization instead. See ch02. ERC-721 / ERC-1155 NFTs — deployed contract. Native NFTs (ltNFTOKEN_PAGE, NFTokenMint) — a first-class ledger object type. Minting is a transaction, not a deploy. No custom transfer logic; behavior is fixed by the protocol + flags. Fungible token with rich controls / "programmable token." Multi-Purpose Token (MPT) (ltMPTOKEN_ISSUANCE / ltMPTOKEN). Controls (transfer fee, max amount, lock, clawback) are fields and flags, not code. See ch02 tokenization. Native coin (ETH, SOL, BTC). XRP — native, no issuer, no counterparty risk, cannot be frozen or clawed back. Sharpest distinction on the ledger: XRP ≠ IOU. An IOU is an obligation of its issuer; XRP is not. Never equate their risk.

docs.title: Failure, finality & programmability
docs.text: You know XRPL equivalent Watch out Revert (EVM) — failed call still consumes gas and lands in a block. Result-code taxonomy. Only tes (success) and tec (claimed failure) reach a validated ledger. tec costs the fee and consumes the sequence but the operation has no effect. This inverts the EVM instinct. tem (malformed), tef (would fail against ledger), tel (local/fee), and ter (retry) are rejected before consensus and cost nothing. Most failures are free and never on-chain. Probabilistic finality — wait for N confirmations; defend against reorgs. Deterministic finality — a transaction in a validated ledger is final. There is no confirmation count and no reorg. "Validated" is binary, not a probability that grows over time. Stop writing confirmation-counting logic. Smart contract / VM (EVM, SVM). No general VM. Capability = fixed transaction types + ledger objects, extended via amendments. You do not deploy code. You compose native primitives (Payment, OfferCreate, EscrowCreate, AMM*, tokens…). New behavior ships as an amendment the whole network votes on. See ch06. On-chain DEX / AMM = a deployed contract (Uniswap, Serum). Native DEX (ltOFFER) and native AMM (ltAMM) are protocol ledger objects. Liquidity composes atomically with payments at the protocol level — a cross-currency payment can route through order books and AMM pools in one transaction. See ch03. Governance via token vote / multisig upgrade of a proxy contract. Amendments — validators vote on-ledger; ≥80% sustained for two weeks activates, irreversibly. No admin key can upgrade the protocol. No proxy pattern. Activation is one-way — plan node upgrades ahead of it (see ch04 operations).

docs.title: Example flow
docs.text:
"I want to issue a token and let users trade it" — how the instinct maps.

On EVM you would: write an ERC-20, deploy it, verify it, then deploy or list on a DEX. On the XRPL there is nothing to deploy:

  1. Configure the issuer account (an AccountSet) with the right flags — DefaultRipple to let balances ripple, optionally RequireAuth for a permissioned token. This is your "token contract," expressed as account flags. (See ch02 issuer-controls.)
  2. Holders create a trust line to the issuer for your currency code (TrustSet). This is the on-ramp equivalent of a user's wallet "adding" the token — except it is the holder's own ledger object, costing them an owner reserve.
  3. Issue by paying — a Payment from the issuer delivers the IOU into the holder's trust line. No mint() call; issuance is a payment from the issuer.
  4. Trade natively — holders place offers (OfferCreate) or swap against an AMM. No DEX contract to list on; the order book keyed by the currency/issuer pair already exists.

The lesson: every step is a built-in transaction against built-in objects. The design work is choosing flags and topology, not writing and auditing code.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Do not port approve/allowance mental models. There is no allowance; over-authorizing here means wrong trust-line or issuer flag configuration, which is often irreversible (e.g. NoFreeze). See ch02.
  • Do not treat tec as "safe like a revert." A tec did consume the sequence and the fee. Retrying blindly with the same sequence will fail; you must advance correctly. See ch01 payments.
  • Do not wait for "confirmations." Reading un-validated (open-ledger) state as if final is the deterministic-finality equivalent of acting on an unconfirmed Bitcoin transaction.
  • Reserves are a liveness dependency, not just a fee. An account that dips below its required reserve cannot create new objects; sweeping XRP off a hot account can strand it. See ch01 mental models.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Nonce/Sequence conflation. Assuming XRPL sequencing behaves exactly like EVM nonces — it is close, but Tickets and the transaction queue change the operational picture.
  • Looking for a token contract address. Identifying an IOU by a "contract" instead of by (currency code, issuer account).
  • Confirmation counting. Building reorg-defense or N-confirmation logic that the XRPL neither needs nor supports.
  • Assuming failures are on-chain. Logging/monitoring built around the assumption that every failed transaction is retrievable from the ledger; most are not.
  • Expecting to deploy logic. Trying to express custom transfer rules or hooks as if the base ledger were programmable, rather than composing native primitives + amendments.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Team has mapped each home-chain primitive it relies on to a concrete XRPL primitive (and identified the ones with no equivalent).
  • [ ] Submission code uses LastLedgerSequence and correct Sequence/Ticket handling — not ported nonce logic.
  • [ ] Finality logic keys off validated ledgers, with no confirmation-count or reorg handling carried over.
  • [ ] Failure handling distinguishes on-ledger tec (fee + sequence consumed) from off-ledger rejections (tem/tef/tel/ter).
  • [ ] Token model uses trust lines / MPTs / NFTs and issuer flags — no attempt to emulate an ERC-20 contract or an allowance.
  • [ ] Reserve requirements are budgeted per account and per owned object.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• XRPL for Ethereum developers
  • Transaction results
  • Accounts
  • Trust lines and issued currencies

xrpld source referenced in this section (paths relative to the vendored rippled/ tree — the on-disk directory retains the historical name):

  • Account-based model, AccountRoot with required sfSequence; ltTICKET with sfTicketSequence (out-of-order sequencing) — include/xrpl/protocol/detail/ledger_entries.macro.
  • Result-code taxonomy: tel/tem/tef/ter reject before consensus; tec is "claim fee only… claim fee to use the sequence number" and is stored in metadata for historic transactions (i.e. on-ledger) — include/xrpl/protocol/TER.h.
  • Genesis supply (kInitialXrp = 100e9 XRP), amendment activation threshold (kAmendmentMajorityCalcThreshold = 80/100) and two-week hold (kDefaultAmendmentMajorityTime = weeks{2}) — include/xrpl/protocol/SystemParameters.h.
  • Native token/market/asset ledger objects — ltRIPPLE_STATE (trust line), ltOFFER, ltAMM, ltMPTOKEN_ISSUANCE / ltMPTOKEN, ltNFTOKEN_PAGE — include/xrpl/protocol/detail/ledger_entries.macro.
  • Native transaction types (e.g. ttPAYMENT, ttESCROW_CREATE, ttACCOUNT_SET) and the ttAMENDMENT pseudo-transaction — include/xrpl/protocol/detail/transactions.macro.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• The biggest gap is not syntax — it is the location of capability. On EVM, capability lives in deployed code; on the XRPL it lives in a fixed, versioned set of transaction types and ledger objects. Every mapping mismatch below traces back to that one fact.
  • tec is the only "revert" that costs anything, and it is the exception. Because tel/tem/tef/ter are filtered before consensus, the XRPL's economic model for failure is the inverse of EVM's: failing is normally free and invisible, and paying-to-fail (tec) is the rare, deliberate case.
  • Reserves are held, not consumed. The Solana-rent analogy is useful for intuition but wrong on the crucial point — deleting the object returns the owner reserve. This makes account/object lifecycle a balance-management problem, not a cost problem.
  • Deterministic finality removes an entire category of code. No reorg handling, no confirmation thresholds. Engineers coming from Nakamoto chains often over-build here; the correct amount of finality code is nearly none.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Is there any way to run custom logic on the XRP Ledger like an EVM contract?

Confirmed against source (base ledger): the core rippled/ transaction set is fixed and enumerated in transactions.macro; there is no general-purpose VM or user-deployed bytecode in the base protocol. New behavior is added by amendment, not deployment. Educated guess (ecosystem, not verified in this vendored tree): programmability initiatives such as Hooks and the EVM-compatible sidechain exist in the broader XRPL ecosystem, but they are separate from the L1 transaction set documented here; treat them as out of scope for the base-ledger mental model until you have confirmed their availability on the specific network you target.

How do I identify a token uniquely if there is no contract address?

Confirmed against source: an issued currency is identified by its currency code plus the issuer account; the holding itself is a ltRIPPLE_STATE trust-line object between the two accounts. MPTs carry an sfMPTokenIssuanceID. There is no contract address because there is no contract — the (currency, issuer) pair (or the MPT issuance ID) is the canonical identifier.

← Back to Chapter 0 — Coming from Other Chains

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text:
The first non-trivial thing a migrant builds is usually a dashboard or a reconciliation job: "show me every transaction this account has ever made" or "show me every current holder of this token."

On EVM the reflex is TheGraph, Etherscan, or a block-range eth_getLogs scan. None of those map directly. The XRPL distinguishes between History (what happened) and State (what is true now), and provides different tools for each:

  1. History is a per-account, cursor-paginated query (account_tx).
  2. State is a global ledger snapshot you can scan by type (ledger_data).
  3. Analytics should run against Clio, a purpose-built read replica.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Two framings replace the EVM ones:

  1. There is no global event log to scan. EVM events are a global stream. XRPL history is the transactions that affected a given account, retrieved via account_tx. To index "all payments for my token," you must index the issuer's account history.
  2. The ledger is a KV store you can walk. If you need a snapshot (e.g., "current balances of all 10,000 holders"), you don't replay history. You walk the ledger_data stream for ltRIPPLE_STATE objects.

docs.title: The EVM habit → XRPL equivalent
docs.text: You know (EVM / Solana) XRPL equivalent Watch out TheGraph subgraph (History). Clio + account_tx. No mapping to deploy; query the JSON-RPC/WS API. No custom schema. You post-process account_tx results yourself. TheGraph subgraph (State). ledger_data — walk the entire ledger state by object type. Iterating 100M+ objects is slow; use for snapshots or specialized indexing. Etherscan API — txlist by address. account_tx — transactions by account, paginated by a marker. Range is by ledger index, not block number; cursor is a {ledger, seq} object. eth_getLogs over a range. No global log scan. Iterate account_tx per account, or subscribe live. Design around per-account history.

docs.title: account_tx vs. ledger_data — Mental model comparison
docs.text: Feature account_tx (History) ledger_data (State) Query unit Single account Global ledger snapshot Pagination marker: {ledger, seq} marker: <hex_key> Order forward: true/false (chronological) Hexadecimal key order Scope All txs affecting the account All objects in the ledger Use case Reconciliation, dashboards Holder lists, state snapshots

docs.title: State indexing: "Who holds my token?"
docs.text: To get a snapshot of all holders of an issued currency: 1. Call ledger_data with type: "state" (or ripple_state). 2. Filter results where the issuer/currency match your token. 3. Paginate using the returned marker until exhausted. 4. Optimization: hosted indexers (like Bithomp or XRPScan) maintain their own SQL/NoSQL indexes of these relations so you don't have to scan the whole ledger state for a single token's holders.

docs.title: account_tx vs. ledger_data — Parameter reference
docs.text:
Parameter account_tx (History) ledger_data (State) Watch out ledger_index_min / max Inclusive range to search. N/A (single ledger) Use -1 for widest range on account_tx. ledger_index / hash Single ledger (API v2). The ledger to snapshot. Mutually exclusive with min/max. forward true/false (chronological). N/A (hex order) Keep constant across pagination. limit Min 10, max 400. Max 256 (JSON) or 2048 (binary). Page sizes are server-enforced; you must paginate. marker Object {ledger, seq}. String (hex key). Treat as opaque; pass back verbatim.

Pagination loop: issue the first call with your range + limit; if the response contains a marker, call again with that same marker (and identical range/order/filters) until no marker is returned. Changing the range or forward direction between calls invalidates the cursor's meaning.

docs.title: Example flow
docs.text:
"Reconcile every payment an account received last month" — the migrant job.

On EVM you would scan a block range for Transfer logs to the address. On the XRPL:

  1. Point at Clio, not a validator. Choose a Clio endpoint (self-hosted or a provider) so deep history is actually retained and the query load is served by the read replica.
  2. Bound the range. Set ledger_index_min/ledger_index_max to the ledger indices spanning the month (or -1/-1 for everything available), fix forward to one direction, and set limit (≤ 400).
  3. Paginate to exhaustion. Loop account_tx, passing back each returned marker unchanged, until no marker comes back.
  4. Filter client-side. For each transaction, inspect the meta for delivered_amount and the transaction type — the ledger does not pre-filter "received payments" for you the way an event topic would.
  5. Cross-check finality. Every returned transaction is already validated; there is no reorg to reconcile against later.

The lesson: history is a cursor walk per account against a read replica, and the semantic filtering you expressed as an event topic on EVM now happens in your own code over the returned metadata.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Do not run analytical history load against a validator. It competes with consensus work and the node may not even retain the ledgers you need. Use Clio (or a provider) for history and indexing.
  • Treat the marker as opaque. Never parse, mutate, or persist it as a reconstructable offset; store and replay it verbatim. Synthesizing markers is a source of silent gaps.
  • Verify the data window. A "complete" answer depends on the server's retained ledger range; confirm the endpoint actually covers the range you are querying (server_info → complete_ledgers) before trusting a result set.
  • Do not assume a provider's non-standard indexes exist everywhere. Hosted indexers may add convenience endpoints beyond account_tx; code to the standard API so you can fail over.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting a global log scan. There is no eth_getLogs equivalent; iterate per account or subscribe live.
  • Using limit as if it were unbounded. Values above 400 are capped; you still must paginate.
  • Flipping forward or changing the range mid-pagination. This invalidates the cursor and produces gaps or duplicates.
  • Querying a validator for deep history. It may have deleted old ledgers via online deletion; point historical reads at Clio.
  • Confusing ledger index with block number. Ranges are ledger indices; there is no "block."

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Historical/analytical reads target Clio (or a provider running one), not a validating node.
  • [ ] account_tx pagination passes the returned marker back verbatim and loops until no marker remains.
  • [ ] Range (ledger_index_min/max), forward, and filters are held constant across a pagination run.
  • [ ] limit respects the 10/200/400 min/default/max envelope.
  • [ ] The queried endpoint's complete_ledgers window is verified to cover the requested range.
  • [ ] Semantic filtering (payment vs. other types, delivered_amount) is done client-side over meta.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Clio server
  • account_tx
  • Ledger history & online deletion
  • Pagination with markers

xrpld source referenced in this section (paths relative to the vendored rippled/ tree — the on-disk directory retains the historical name):

  • account_tx request parsing — ledger_index_min/ledger_index_max with the -1 "widest available" sentinel, forward, binary, and the marker continuation object {ledger, seq} — src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/account/AccountTx.cpp.
  • ledger_data state scanning — type filtering, binary output, and the hex-key marker continuation — src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/ledger/LedgerData.cpp.
  • Server-enforced page-size envelope for account_tx and ledger_data (kAccountTx, kPageLengthBinary) — src/xrpld/rpc/detail/Tuning.h.
  • Recent-window retention / online deletion that motivates a separate history server — src/xrpld/app/misc/SHAMapStoreImp.cpp and the [node_db] online_delete config (see ch04 operations).

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• History is account-shaped, not log-shaped. The single most important reframing: you cannot filter the whole chain by a topic; you walk each account's transactions. Dashboards are built by choosing which accounts to index, not which events to subscribe to globally.
  • Clio is the archive/subgraph analogue, and it is a first-class concept. Sending history load to a validator is the equivalent of pointing your indexer at a consensus-critical node — technically possible, operationally wrong.
  • The marker is the whole pagination contract. Because it is an opaque {ledger, seq} cursor rather than an offset, correct pagination is entirely about replaying it faithfully and holding every other parameter constant.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Does Clio serve the exact same command set as xrpld, or a subset/superset?

Confirmed against source (API surface): the public command vocabulary is the rippled/ dispatch table in src/xrpld/rpc/detail/Handler.cpp; Clio is designed to answer the same public API for reads. Educated guess (not verified in this vendored tree, which does not include Clio): Clio focuses on read/history methods and delegates or omits some admin/submission commands, and may retain deeper history than a default node. Confirm the specific method coverage and retention window against the Clio server you actually target before depending on it.

What is the cheapest way to get a full historical sync of one account?

Educated guess (operational, not protocol-encoded): use account_tx with binary: true and limit: 400, paginating by marker, against a Clio endpoint with a complete_ledgers window covering the account's whole life; decode client-side. The trade-off between binary bulk sync and JSON convenience is an application decision, not a protocol rule.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text:
On day one of a port, you are not thinking about consensus philosophy — you are thinking "which call replaces eth_getBalance?" This section is that lookup. It maps the JSON-RPC / SDK calls you reach for reflexively on EVM (and, where it differs, Solana) to their XRPL equivalents, with a Watch out on every call whose shape or semantics differ enough to bite you.

Every XRPL method here is a real command string registered in the rippled/ dispatch table (src/xrpld/rpc/detail/Handler.cpp), so the spelling is canonical — you can send it over both JSON-RPC (HTTP POST) and WebSocket.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Three framing differences drive every row below:

  1. One endpoint, method + params, not a fixed method namespace. EVM exposes a closed eth_* / net_* namespace. The XRPL exposes a single command dispatcher: you send {"method": "account_info", "params": [...]}. The same command works over HTTP and WebSocket.
  2. Read the ledger directly, not "call a view function." There is no eth_call because there is no contract to call. State reads are typed queries against ledger objects (account_info, account_lines, ledger_entry) — you ask for the object, not for the result of running code.
  3. account (r-address), not from/to topics. Almost every read is keyed by an XRPL account address, and history/subscription filters are by account, not by contract address or event signature.

docs.title: Reads — balances & account state
docs.text: You call (EVM / Solana) XRPL equivalent Watch out eth_getBalance / getBalance (SOL) account_info — returns the AccountRoot (XRP balance in drops, Sequence, flags, OwnerCount). Returns XRP only. IOU balances live in trust lines, not the account — you need account_lines. Balance is in drops (1 XRP = 1,000,000 drops). ERC-20 balanceOf (an eth_call) account_lines — lists trust lines (per-issuer, per-currency IOU balances). There is no per-token contract to call. One call returns all the holder's IOU balances as signed amounts relative to each issuer. Paginated via marker. Reading a token's total supply / config gateway_balances (issuer's obligations) / account_objects (owned ledger objects). "Total supply" is the sum of the issuer's outstanding obligations, not a contract field. eth_getTransactionCount (nonce) account_info → account_data.Sequence. The account Sequence is the nonce equivalent; there is no separate call.

docs.title: Reads — contract calls & simulation
docs.text: You call XRPL equivalent Watch out eth_call (view function) ledger_entry — fetch a specific ledger object by key/type (offer, escrow, AMM, trust line, MPT issuance…). No code executes. You are reading typed state directly. Pick the object type you actually want rather than calling a getter. eth_call for a quote / route ripple_path_find (interactive) or path_find (WebSocket subscription that streams updated paths). Pathfinding is the XRPL's "quote": it finds routes across order books + AMM for a cross-currency payment. ripple_path_find is one-shot; path_find streams. eth_estimateGas fee — current base fee, load factor, and queue state; plus server_info. Cost is not "gas for this call." It is a network-load fee (see ch01 payments). You do not estimate per-operation compute. Reading a DEX order book (contract call / subgraph) book_offers — the live order book for a (taker_pays, taker_gets) pair. The book is a native ledger structure keyed by the currency/issuer pair; it always exists without anyone "deploying" it.

docs.title: Writes — submitting transactions
docs.text: You call XRPL equivalent Watch out eth_sendRawTransaction (pre-signed) submit with a signed tx_blob. You sign client-side (SDK) and submit the blob. This is the production path. Sign-then-send in one call (dev convenience) submit with tx_json + secret (admin/local only). Never send a seed to a remote server. Use client-side signing + tx_blob in production. Multisig submission submit_multisigned — a tx_json carrying a Signers array. Collect signatures out-of-band (sign_for), then submit the assembled multisigned transaction. See ch04 security. eth_getTransactionReceipt tx — look up a transaction by hash; check validated: true and the meta result. A missing/validated:false result is not failure — it may simply not be in a validated ledger yet. Poll until validated or LastLedgerSequence passes (see ch01 getting-started).

docs.title: Reads — history (see the dedicated section)
docs.text: You call XRPL equivalent Watch out eth_getLogs / block-range scans / subgraph account_tx — paginated transaction history for one account. Keyed by account, not by contract/event topic. Pagination and range semantics are non-obvious — see Indexing & Historical Queries.

docs.title: Example flow
docs.text:
"Check a balance, quote a swap, submit it, confirm it" — the EVM reflex vs the XRPL calls.

On EVM you might: eth_getBalance → eth_call a router's getAmountsOut → eth_estimateGas → eth_sendRawTransaction → poll eth_getTransactionReceipt. On the XRPL the same job is:

  1. Balance: account_info for XRP, or account_lines for the IOU you hold.
  2. Quote: ripple_path_find with your source_currencies and the destination amount — it returns concrete paths across the DEX and AMM.
  3. Fee: fee (or read server_info) for the current base fee and load factor; autofill it into the transaction rather than estimating per-op gas.
  4. Submit: sign client-side, then submit the tx_blob.
  5. Confirm: tx by hash, waiting for validated: true — or watch the transactions subscription instead of polling.

The lesson: the read side is direct typed queries, and the "quote" is pathfinding — there is no view function to call because there is no code to run.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Never send a secret/seed to a remote server. The submit-with-secret and sign conveniences are for local/admin nodes only. Production signs client-side and submits a tx_blob. See ch04 security.
  • Do not treat a missing tx result as failure. Absence means "not in a validated ledger yet," not "rejected." Key retry/finality logic off validated + LastLedgerSequence, not off a 404-style absence.
  • Admin-only methods are a footgun on public endpoints. Commands like sign, wallet_propose, ledger_accept, and stop are gated by role; never expose an admin-configured port publicly.
  • Read amounts in the right units. account_info returns XRP in drops; IOU amounts are objects ({currency, issuer, value}), not integers. Mixing the two is a classic port bug.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Calling account_info and expecting IOU balances. It returns XRP only; reach for account_lines.
  • Looking for eth_call. There is no contract to call — use ledger_entry for state and ripple_path_find for quotes.
  • Estimating "gas" per operation. The fee is network-load-based, not per-opcode; use fee/server_info.
  • Scanning "blocks" for events. History is per-account via account_tx, not a global log scan; event streams come from subscribe.
  • Submitting tx_json + secret to a public server. Sign locally; submit a tx_blob.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] All state reads mapped to concrete commands (account_info, account_lines, account_objects, ledger_entry, book_offers).
  • [ ] Quotes/routes use ripple_path_find/path_find, not a "view call."
  • [ ] Signing is client-side; only tx_blob (or submit_multisigned) is sent to the server.
  • [ ] Confirmation logic uses tx + validated + LastLedgerSequence, not receipt-absence.
  • [ ] Fee handling reads fee/server_info; no per-operation gas estimation carried over.
  • [ ] No admin-only method (sign, wallet_propose, ledger_accept, stop) is reachable on a public endpoint.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• API methods (public)
  • account_info
  • account_lines
  • ripple_path_find
  • submit

xrpld source referenced in this section (paths relative to the vendored rippled/ tree — the on-disk directory retains the historical name):

  • Canonical command dispatch table (every command string a client can send, e.g. account_info, account_tx, ledger_entry, ripple_path_find, book_offers, submit, submit_multisigned, tx, fee, server_info) — src/xrpld/rpc/detail/Handler.cpp.
  • Balance/account reads — src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/account/AccountInfo.cpp, AccountLines.cpp, AccountObjects.cpp, GatewayBalances.cpp.
  • State read by object — src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/ledger/LedgerEntry.cpp.
  • Quotes/routing — src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/orderbook/RipplePathFind.cpp, PathFind.cpp, BookOffers.cpp.
  • Writes — src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/transaction/Submit.cpp, SubmitMultiSigned.cpp, Tx.cpp.
  • Fee/server state — src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/server_info/Fee.cpp, ServerInfo.cpp.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• The read side is the biggest reflex to unlearn. There is no eth_call because there is no code path to invoke — every read is a typed query against a named ledger object. Once that clicks, the whole read namespace maps cleanly.
  • "Quote" is pathfinding, not a view function. ripple_path_find is the closest thing to getAmountsOut, and it is a first-class protocol capability, not a helper contract someone deployed.
  • One dispatcher, two transports. The same method string works over HTTP and WebSocket, which is why the subscription model (next section) reuses the exact command vocabulary rather than introducing a parallel one.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Is there a single call that returns everything about an account (XRP + all IOUs + all owned objects) in one round trip?

Confirmed against source (per-command): the reads are split by object type — account_info (the AccountRoot), account_lines (trust lines), account_objects (owned objects), each a distinct handler in src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/account/. Educated guess (composition): a full account snapshot is assembled client-side by combining these calls (each paginated by marker); there is no single "get account state" super-command in the base handler set. Verify the exact object coverage you need against account_objects before assuming one call suffices.

When should a migrant use path_find (streaming) instead of ripple_path_find (one-shot)?

Educated guess (operational, not protocol-encoded): ripple_path_find returns paths once, suited to a request/response quote; path_find is a WebSocket subscription that keeps re-computing paths as the ledger changes, suited to a live trading UI. The trade-off (freshness vs. connection cost) is an application decision, not a protocol rule.
