  • Transaction engine pipeline (preflight/preclaim/doApply, the Transactor base class, and stage dispatch) — include/xrpl/tx/Transactor.h (PreflightContext, PreclaimContext), include/xrpl/tx/ApplyContext.h (ApplyContext), src/libxrpl/tx/applySteps.cpp, src/libxrpl/tx/Transactor.cpp.
  • View hierarchy (ReadView → OpenView → ApplyView) — include/xrpl/ledger/ReadView.h, include/xrpl/ledger/OpenView.h, include/xrpl/ledger/ApplyView.h.
  • Fixed-precision amounts (kDropsPerXrp, kMinValue/kMaxValue, kMinOffset/kMaxOffset, kMaxNativeN, canonicalize, mulRound/divRound) — include/xrpl/protocol/STAmount.h, src/libxrpl/protocol/STAmount.cpp, include/xrpl/protocol/IOUAmount.h, include/xrpl/protocol/XRPAmount.h.
  • Validator trust and Validator Lists — src/xrpld/app/misc/ValidatorList.h (quorum via calculateQuorum), src/xrpld/app/misc/detail/ValidatorList.cpp.
  • Negative UNL (water marks, max-listed, voting, flag-ledger application) — src/xrpld/app/misc/NegativeUNLVote.h (kNegativeUnlLowWaterMark/HighWaterMark, kNegativeUnlMaxListed, kNewValidatorDisableSkip), src/xrpld/app/misc/NegativeUNLVote.cpp, ltNEGATIVE_UNL and ttUNL_MODIFY in include/xrpl/protocol/detail/ledger_entries.macro / include/xrpl/protocol/detail/transactions.macro.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Finality is a design choice, not a spectrum. Most chains offer probabilistic finality and force you to pick a confirmation depth. XRPL's deterministic finality changes the entire error-handling architecture — once a ledger is validated, there is nothing to wait for.
  • Reserves encode state cost directly. The owner reserve is not just spam protection; it is a direct signal that you are consuming persistent ledger state. Modeling reserve consumption is a capacity-planning concern, not an afterthought.
  • tesSUCCESS from submission is a prediction. It reflects how the node would apply the transaction to its current open ledger. The actual result can differ. The validated ledger is the only authoritative source.
  • Trust lines are bilateral objects, not unilateral balances. Both the issuer and the holder can set limits and flags independently. The issuer's flags (freeze, require auth) have direct operational consequences for holders.
  • Sequence numbers are a replay-prevention primitive. Each account has a monotonically increasing sequence number. A transaction is only valid at exactly the current sequence — this is what makes idempotent resubmission tractable.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
How does the consensus protocol handle validator set changes and UNL divergence at scale?

Confirmed against source — see Consensus internals for the full mechanism. Validator trust is configured through signed Validator Lists from trusted publishers (ValidatorList / ValidatorSite), so a node's UNL updates automatically as new lists are issued; keys are never hard-coded. Consensus is measured against that UNL with the 80% minConsensusPct floor and the avalanche escalation (50% → 65% → 70% → 95%). When validators become unreliable, the Negative UNL shrinks the effective UNL so the network stays live, while a hard floor keeps the quorum at ≥ 60% of the original UNL (quorum = max(ceil(0.8 × effectiveUnlSize), ceil(0.6 × originalUnlSize)), calculateQuorum in ValidatorList.cpp) — the network halts rather than forks if too many are down. Application-level implication: a node running a stale or divergent VL can compute a different UNL — and therefore potentially a different validated ledger — than its peers, so monitor VL expiry and update promptly.

What are the performance characteristics of the SHAMap state tree under very high object counts (e.g., accounts with thousands of trust lines or offers)?

Hypothesis: SHAMap is a 16-way radix (Merkle prefix) tree — not a binary trie. Each inner node fans out to exactly 16 children (kBranchFactor = 16, indexed by nibbles of the 256-bit key). Lookup depth is bounded by the key length (up to 64 nibble levels), making it effectively O(1) in the number of stored objects once the tree is populated. For accounts with thousands of owned objects, raw lookup performance degrades slowly — the practical bottleneck is not computational but economic: each object consumes 0.2 XRP in owner reserve, so the cost of holding 1,000 trust lines is 200 XRP locked indefinitely. At the network level, high object counts on popular accounts increase the cost of ledger serialization and snapshot delivery. Application-side, fetching all owned objects for an account with thousands of entries via account_objects requires pagination (the limit and marker fields); fetching all at once will time out on a public node. Design around this by pruning stale objects (closing zero-balance trust lines, canceling unfilled offers) to keep owner counts manageable.

Confirmed against source — see Storage model: the 16-way fan-out (kBranchFactor = 16) and nibble-indexed depth bound are verified in SHAMap.h / SHAMapInnerNode.h.

How do reserve value changes (via fee votes) propagate, and what is the minimum notice a well-operated application should plan for?

Hypothesis: Reserve values are changed by a fee voting mechanism: each validator can express a preferred BaseFee, ReserveBase, and ReserveIncrement in its validation messages. When a majority of validators vote for a new value over a voting window (~256 ledgers ≈ 15–20 minutes), the new values take effect in the following ledger. There is no advance warning period beyond observing the vote in progress via the fee command. Existing objects are grandfathered — accounts that already owned objects below the new minimum will not become invalid, but they may lose the ability to send new transactions if their available XRP falls below the updated minimum. Best practice: monitor fee.reserve_base and fee.reserve_inc each ledger close, alert when they change, and maintain a buffer of at least 2–5 XRP above the current minimum to absorb a reserve increase without triggering an operational incident.

How should a multi-account application reason about aggregate reserve consumption and XRP liquidity across all its accounts?

Hypothesis: Reserves are per-account and cannot be pooled — an account can only spend XRP it holds above its own minimum. The right model is a per-account reserve ledger: for each operational account, track base_reserve + (owned_objects × owner_reserve) as locked XRP, and actual_balance − locked_xrp as spendable XRP. Aggregate these across all accounts to understand total locked vs. liquid XRP at the system level. High-frequency accounts that open many offers or escrows should be provisioned with a reserve buffer sized to their maximum expected concurrent object count. New account creation (funding a previously unfunded address) requires at least base_reserve XRP in the funding transaction — this should be modeled as a capital expense in account provisioning budgets.

What are the operational implications of the lsfDisableMaster flag if a regular key is lost — and how should key rotation be designed to avoid lockout?

Hypothesis: If lsfDisableMaster is set and the regular key is lost with no SignerList configured, the account is permanently inaccessible — there is no recovery mechanism, no admin override, and no fork to revert the state. This is a funds-at-risk scenario with no remedy. The safe pattern is: (1) configure a SignerList with a threshold ≥ 2 before disabling the master key — multi-sig can still submit AccountSet to re-enable the master or set a new regular key even after lsfDisableMaster is set; (2) store master key material offline in cold storage even after disabling it — it is the last-resort recovery tool if the signer list is also lost; (3) write a rotation runbook that covers setting a new RegularKey, verifying it on Testnet, and only then disabling the master on mainnet; (4) schedule and test key rotation before credentials approach their shelf life.

← Back to Chapter 1 — Foundations

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: Payments are the XRPL's foundational use case. The ledger provides 3–5 second deterministic finality, atomic cross-currency settlement, and native pathfinding — capabilities that typically require multiple intermediaries and days of settlement in traditional finance. Getting payment logic right means understanding not just the happy path but every failure mode and how to recover from it safely.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
A payment is an atomic state transition: the sender's balance decreases, the receiver's increases, and any intermediate currency conversion and liquidity routing happen in the same transaction — or none of it does.

There is no "pending" state in a validated payment. Either the full delivery occurred, or it did not.

Key distinctions:

  • Delivered amount vs. send amount. For cross-currency and partial payments, the amount delivered may differ from the amount sent. Always read delivered_amount from the transaction metadata — never the Amount field alone.
  • Direct vs. rippled payments. Direct XRP payments require no trust line. Issued currency payments require trust lines and may traverse multiple hops through the order book or AMM.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Direct payments — XRP or same-currency IOU; single hop, minimal complexity. For XRP, no trust line required. For IOUs, both parties need a trust line to the same issuer (or the payment ripples through one).
  • Cross-currency payments — pathfinding (ripple_path_find for streaming, find_path for one-shot) discovers routes through the DEX order book and/or AMM pools. Settlement is fully atomic — the entire conversion and delivery succeed or nothing moves. The liquidity these payments consume — order-book offers, AMM pools, and how pathfinding composes them — is documented in Markets and Liquidity → DeFi.
  • Partial payments (tfPartialPayment) — delivers as much as possible up to the specified maximum Amount. Used legitimately for return payments (to avoid dust left by fees) but a common accounting exploit vector. Use tfLimitQuality to reject paths below a minimum exchange rate.
  • Payment channels — off-ledger signing of incremental signed claims; the channel is funded on-ledger and settled on-ledger. Full lifecycle:
  • PaymentChannelCreate — open and fund the channel.
  • Sender issues signed off-ledger claims (no transaction per claim).
  • Receiver submits PaymentChannelClaim to redeem the latest claim.
  • Either party closes with PaymentChannelClaim (with tfClose) or the sender reclaims after expiry with PaymentChannelClaim (with tfRenew). Suited for high-frequency micropayment streams where per-claim latency must be sub-second.
  • Escrow — conditional or time-locked XRP delivery.
  • Time-based: funds release after FinishAfter and before CancelAfter.
  • Condition-based: funds release when the submitter provides a PREIMAGE-SHA-256 crypto-condition fulfillment.
  • Escrows lock the full XRP amount plus owner reserve for the duration.
  • Checks — a deferred pull-payment primitive (analogous to a paper check). The sender creates a Check authorizing the receiver to pull up to a specified amount. The receiver cashes it with CheckCash; either party can cancel it. Useful for authorized payment flows where the receiver initiates settlement.

docs.title: Fee escalation and the transaction queue
docs.text:
The required fee is not a single "base × load" number. Two distinct mechanisms interact, and a robust submitter must account for both:

  • Load-based fee. The server-wide load multiplier. Read load_factor from server_info and multiply by base_fee_xrp. This is the classic base_fee × load_factor.
  • Open-ledger fee escalation. Independent of load. There is a base fee level of 256 and an adaptive limit on how many transactions fit in the open ledger at that base level (at least 5, growing ~20% per healthy ledger up to 50, then tracking recent large ledgers; clamping down 50% when consensus is unhealthy). Once the open ledger exceeds the limit, the required fee level jumps quadratically: lastLedgerMedianFeeLevel × TxInOpenLedger² / limit². Read load_factor_fee_escalation (the openLedgerFeeLevel) from server_info; a burst can push this far above the load-based fee. Pay the max of the two to guarantee immediate inclusion.
  • Transaction queue (TxQ). A transaction that clears the base fee level and the load minimum but not the escalated open-ledger fee is queued and broadcast, not rejected. When the next ledger opens, queued transactions apply highest-fee-level first. A queued transaction is not a failure — it may still be applied in a later ledger. It leaves the queue only when it applies, fails, retries 10 times, its LastLedgerSequence expires, it is replaced by a same-sequence transaction paying ≥25% more, or it is dropped when the queue fills. Per account, at most 10 sequential transactions may be queued.

Operational implication: a "pending" transaction is often queued, not lost. Distinguish "queued" from "expired/failed" before rebuilding and resubmitting.

docs.title: Direct XRP payment — the baseline
docs.text:
Before tackling cross-currency, internalize this simpler case. Everything here maps directly to the transaction lifecycle in the mental models section.

{
  "TransactionType": "Payment",
  "Account": "rAlice...",
  "Destination": "rBob...",
  "DestinationTag": 12345,
  "Amount": "10000000",        // 10 XRP in drops (1 XRP = 1,000,000 drops)
  "Fee": "12",                 // fetched from server_info, not hard-coded
  "Sequence": 47,
  "LastLedgerSequence": 91234  // current validated ledger + ~4
}

Key points: - Amount for XRP is always a string integer in drops. Never use decimals. - DestinationTag is required if rBob's account has RequireDestTag set; omitting it returns tecDST_TAG_NEEDED and the fee is charged. - Fee must be fetched dynamically from server_info.load_factor × server_info.base_fee_xrp.

Validated success metadata: 

{
  "TransactionResult": "tesSUCCESS",
  "delivered_amount": "10000000"
}

Validated failure metadata (e.g. insufficient XRP): 

{
  "TransactionResult": "tecUNFUNDED_PAYMENT",
  "delivered_amount": "unavailable"
}
The fee is charged even on tec failures. State did not change, but the sequence number advanced and the fee burned.

docs.title: Cross-currency payment: USD → EUR, atomic on-ledger settlement
docs.text:
Scenario: Alice holds RLUSD (USD stablecoin) and wants to pay Bob, who expects EUR-denominated IOUs. Both currencies are live on the XRPL DEX.

Step 1 — Pathfinding

// Request: find routes from Alice's RLUSD to Bob's EUR trust line
{
  "command": "ripple_path_find",
  "source_account": "Alice",
  "destination_account": "Bob",
  "destination_amount": { "currency": "EUR", "issuer": "rEURIssuer", "value": "100" }
}
// Response includes candidate paths through DEX order books and/or AMM pools

Step 2 — Build the transaction

{
  "TransactionType": "Payment",
  "Account": "Alice",
  "Destination": "Bob",
  "Amount": {
    "currency": "EUR",
    "issuer": "rEURIssuer",
    "value": "100"
  },
  "SendMax": {
    "currency": "USD",
    "issuer": "rUSDIssuer",
    "value": "112"              // Alice is willing to spend up to 112 USD
  },
  "Paths": [ /* paths from ripple_path_find */ ],
  "Fee": "12",
  "Sequence": 47,
  "LastLedgerSequence": 91234   // current ledger + ~4
}

Step 3 — Submit and wait for validation

Alice signs → submits → node broadcasts → consensus → ledger validated

Step 4 — Inspect metadata

// From the validated tx metadata:
{
  "TransactionResult": "tesSUCCESS",
  "delivered_amount": {
    "currency": "EUR",
    "issuer": "rEURIssuer",
    "value": "100"             // exactly 100 EUR delivered
  }
}
// AffectedNodes shows: Alice's USD balance decreased, Bob's EUR balance
// increased, and intermediate offer/AMM objects consumed — all atomically.

If liquidity was insufficient for the full 100 EUR, the transaction returns tecPATH_DRY (no path) or tecPATH_PARTIAL (partial fill not allowed without tfPartialPayment). Nothing moves in either case.

docs.title: Reliable submission loop
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Build : start
    Build --> Sign : autofill sequence + fee
    Sign --> Submit : sign offline

    Submit --> PollValidated : preliminary response (any code)

    PollValidated --> Done : tx found in validated ledger\nread meta.TransactionResult\n+ meta.delivered_amount
    PollValidated --> Expired : not found AND\ncurrent_ledger > LastLedgerSequence

    Expired --> Build : increment sequence\nrebuild + re-sign

    Done --> [*]

    note right of PollValidated
        Poll every ~1 s.
        Never resubmit before
        checking the validated ledger.
    end note

Never resubmit without verifying the original tx is absent from the validated ledger. Resubmitting a transaction that already succeeded is wasteful; with a different Amount it is dangerous.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Using the Testnet faucet at https://xrpl.org/resources/dev-tools/xrp-faucets:

  1. Run examples/02-reliable-submission/ — observe the polling loop. Kill the process mid-poll and restart; does it correctly detect the already-validated transaction or resubmit?
  2. Submit a cross-currency payment (USD→EUR) without any AMM pool or DEX offers in the path. What result code do you get? Is the fee charged?
  3. Submit a payment with tfPartialPayment and insufficient liquidity. Check meta.delivered_amount — is it the full Amount or less?
  4. Deliberately use a past LastLedgerSequence (e.g., current − 10). What happens? Does the node reject it immediately or after submission?
  5. Open a payment channel with a 100 XRP capacity. Issue three off-ledger claims for 10 XRP each. Submit the highest claim via PaymentChannelClaim — what balance does the receiver actually get?

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Always set LastLedgerSequence. Without it, a transaction can remain pending indefinitely — safe retry logic is impossible.
  • Never trust tesSUCCESS from the submission response. It is a prediction. Only the validated ledger is authoritative.
  • Validate delivered_amount in every ingestion pipeline. Partial payments exploit systems that credit Amount rather than the actual delivered amount. This is a documented attack vector.
  • Enforce RequireDestTag on all custodial accounts. Any account that uses destination tags for user attribution must set this flag. Without it, a payment with no tag will succeed and land in a limbo state in your reconciliation system.
  • Manage sequence numbers carefully under concurrent load. If two threads submit transactions for the same account simultaneously, both may use the same sequence number. Only one will succeed; the other returns tefPAST_SEQ or terPRE_SEQ. Use a sequence-number dispenser with a mutex or queue.
  • Payment channel settlement risk. If a receiver stops cooperating, the sender can reclaim channel funds only after the Expiration or CancelAfter time. Design channels with appropriate expiry windows and a tested reclaim runbook.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading Amount instead of delivered_amount. For cross-currency and partial payments this causes significant accounting errors.
  • Omitting LastLedgerSequence. Transactions without an expiry can be applied to the ledger arbitrarily far in the future.
  • Floating-point amounts. XRPL amounts are exact. Use string or integer representations throughout.
  • Not handling tecPATH_DRY and tecPATH_PARTIAL. Liquidity is not guaranteed; applications must handle and retry or surface these errors.
  • Ignoring destination tags. Exchanges and custodians rely on destination tags for attribution; silently dropping them breaks reconciliation.
  • Hard-coding fees. The required fee scales under load and under open-ledger congestion. A hard-coded "12" drop fee will be queued or dropped during a spike. Compute the fee as the max of the load-based fee (base_fee_xrp × load_factor) and the escalated open-ledger fee (load_factor_fee_escalation), both from server_info.
  • Treating a queued transaction as failed. A transaction that lands in the TxQ is still live — resubmitting a fresh one with a new sequence can create duplicates or a tefPAST_SEQ cascade. Poll for the queued transaction (or replace it with a ≥25% higher fee at the same sequence) instead of blindly rebuilding.
  • Misunderstanding SendMax. SendMax is the maximum the sender is willing to spend — not the exact amount. If liquidity allows a better rate, the sender spends less than SendMax. Applications that treat it as an exact debit will overstate costs.
  • Using ripple_path_find when find_path is sufficient. ripple_path_find opens a streaming subscription that sends path updates every ledger close. For one-shot payment construction, use find_path to avoid holding an open subscription and leaking connections.
  • Race condition on account sequence under concurrent submissions. Two goroutines/threads submitting transactions for the same account will collide on the sequence number. One will succeed; the other must detect tefPAST_SEQ and retry with the correct sequence fetched from the validated ledger.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Every transaction has a valid LastLedgerSequence.
  • [ ] All payment results are verified against the validated ledger.
  • [ ] delivered_amount is read from metadata — not Amount.
  • [ ] Partial payment flag (tfPartialPayment) detected and handled in all ingestion pipelines.
  • [ ] Submission loop is safe to retry without double-spending (hash-based idempotency check before resubmit).
  • [ ] Destination tag policy defined and enforced; RequireDestTag flag set on all custodial accounts.
  • [ ] Path errors (tecPATH_DRY, tecPATH_PARTIAL) trigger alerting and a human-readable error surface for the end user.
  • [ ] Fee calculated dynamically as max(base_fee_xrp × load_factor, load_factor_fee_escalation) from server_info — no hard-coded fee constants in transaction construction code.
  • [ ] Submission logic distinguishes queued from expired/failed before resubmitting; replacement uses ≥25% higher fee at the same sequence.
  • [ ] Account sequence number dispenser is concurrency-safe (mutex, queue, or atomic counter) under concurrent transaction submission.
  • [ ] Stuck transaction monitoring in place: alert if any account's in-flight transaction is not confirmed within N ledger closes.
  • [ ] Payment channel settlement runbook written and tested: how to reclaim funds if the counterparty goes offline or becomes uncooperative.
  • [ ] Escrow expiry windows and cancel-after times tested on Testnet before any mainnet deployment.

This checklist covers the payment path. Before production, also complete the account-security checklist in ch04-hardening/security and the node-operations checklist in ch04-hardening/operations.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• delivered_amount is the only number that matters. The Amount field is what the sender requested. For cross-currency and partial payments, the actual settlement amount can be lower. Ingestion pipelines that read Amount will silently misbook balances.
  • LastLedgerSequence is your expiry valve. It turns an open-ended "maybe it lands eventually" problem into a deterministic "the transaction is dead after ledger N" guarantee. Without it, safe retry logic is impossible.
  • Pathfinding is advisory, not guaranteed. Routes returned by ripple_path_find are a snapshot of current liquidity. By the time your transaction is applied, offers may have moved. Design for tecPATH_DRY and tecPATH_PARTIAL as normal operating conditions, not exceptional ones.
  • x402 inverts the payment flow. Traditional payment APIs pull funds server-side. x402 embeds a signed payment authorization in an HTTP 402 challenge/response cycle — the client proves payment before the server serves the resource. This is composable with any XRPL payment primitive.
  • RLUSD is the preferred bridge currency. For corridors with thin native asset liquidity, RLUSD provides a USD-denominated settlement path without requiring a direct trust line between sender and receiver. It reduces pathfinding complexity and slippage in cross-currency flows.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Why is the XRPL uniquely suited for high-throughput payment systems compared to traditional rails and other L1 networks?

Hypothesis: Three properties compound to make XRPL structurally superior for payments. First, deterministic 3–5 second finality — SWIFT takes 1–5 business days; Bitcoin requires 60+ minutes for probabilistic confidence; XRPL settles once and permanently. Second, native atomic cross-currency settlement — no correspondent banking, no nostro/vostro pre-funding, no multi-leg settlement risk; the full conversion happens in a single transaction. Third, sub-cent fees that burn — at ~0.00001 XRP per transaction, fees are economically irrelevant for most payment sizes, and they don't accumulate to a validator rent-seeking problem. Compared to Ethereum (~15–30 TPS, probabilistic finality, gas fees that spike under load) and Solana (higher TPS but validator-concentrated and prone to outages), XRPL's consensus mechanism is specifically optimized for financial settlement: low latency, low variance, high availability.

How does atomic cross-currency settlement actually work at the ledger level — what prevents partial fills from leaving state inconsistent?

Confirmed against source (rippled/include/xrpl/ledger/PaymentSandbox.h, rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/payment/Payment.cpp): When a Payment with Paths is applied, the XRPL transaction engine executes the entire path as a single atomic state transition using a PaymentSandbox — a transactional view that records tentative balance changes without committing them. At each hop, the engine identifies the best available liquidity, computes the exchange, and records tentative changes in the sandbox. Only if every hop succeeds end-to-end are all changes committed to the ledger simultaneously via PaymentSandbox::apply(). If any hop fails — insufficient liquidity, trust line limit hit, quality below tfLimitQuality threshold — the engine returns tecPATH_DRY or tecPATH_PARTIAL and the sandbox is discarded. The fee is charged and the sequence advances, but no balances move. It is impossible for a cross-currency payment to leave the ledger in a half-converted state.

For how the engine models each hop — order-book offers and AMM pools competing as interchangeable liquidity via synthetic AMM offers — see Markets and Liquidity → DeFi.

What are all the failure modes for payments and the correct recovery path for each?

Confirmed against source (rippled/include/xrpl/protocol/TER.h): Failure modes fall into three categories:

Liquidity failures (tec — fee charged, sequence advances): - tecPATH_DRY — no path with sufficient liquidity; retry later or with a higher SendMax. - tecPATH_PARTIAL — partial fill possible but tfPartialPayment not set; add the flag or wait for liquidity to improve. - tecUNFUNDED_PAYMENT — sender balance insufficient; top up and retry.

Destination failures (tec): - tecNO_DST — destination account does not exist; fund it with at least base_reserve XRP first. - tecDST_TAG_NEEDED — destination requires a tag; always include it. - tecNO_LINE_INSUF_RESERVE — no trust line and recipient can't create one (reserve exhausted); recipient must free reserve or top up.

Submission / sequence failures (ter / tef — fee NOT charged, sequence unchanged): - terPRE_SEQ — sequence too high (gap exists); fill the gap or fetch current sequence and rebuild. - tefPAST_SEQ — sequence already consumed; fetch current sequence and retry. - terINSUF_FEE_B — account balance cannot cover the fee (the account's XRP balance is literally too low to pay even the base fee); top up the account. Note: telINSUF_FEE_P is the distinct local-node error when the offered fee is below the node's current load threshold — the fix for that case is to fetch server_info and recalculate the fee amount.

Expiry: - Transaction not found after LastLedgerSequence closes → permanently expired; safe to rebuild with fresh sequence and LastLedgerSequence.

Network partition: - Node unreachable during submission → cannot confirm broadcast; poll a different node for the transaction hash before deciding to resubmit.

What is the x402 protocol, and how does embedding payment authorization in HTTP headers change the architecture of monetized APIs?

External ecosystem pattern — not protocol-encoded in rippled. Source: x402.org. No rippled source verification possible or needed. x402 is an extension of the HTTP 402 Payment Required status code into a machine-to-machine payment flow. The server responds to a request with a 402 containing a payment payload (amount, destination address, network, expiry). The client constructs and signs an XRPL payment, then retries the request with a X-Payment header containing the signed transaction. The server verifies on-chain inclusion before serving the resource. The architectural implication is a fundamental inversion of the traditional pull-payment model: instead of the server initiating a charge against stored credentials (card, ACH), the client proves payment inline in the HTTP request. This eliminates the need for API keys, subscriptions, and billing infrastructure for the common case of pay-per-use access. It also makes payment composable with any client — an AI agent, a CLI tool, or a browser — without requiring account registration. The main constraint is that it requires the client to hold an XRPL account and manage keys, which limits applicability to machine-to-machine and developer-facing APIs today.

What specific role does RLUSD play in the payment ecosystem — as a bridge currency, a settlement asset, and a liquidity anchor for cross-corridor flows?

Confirmed (ecosystem-level, not protocol-encoded). The pathfinding engine treats RLUSD as any other IOU; its bridge/settlement/anchor roles are operational advantages, not enforced by xrpld. RLUSD plays three compounding roles. As a bridge currency, it reduces the trust-line combinatorics of cross-currency payments: instead of needing a direct IOU trust line between every sender-currency/receiver- currency pair, corridors converge on RLUSD as a common intermediate, so N currencies need only N RLUSD pairs rather than N×(N−1)/2 bilateral pairs. As a settlement asset, it provides USD-denominated atomic finality in 3–5 seconds — replacing the pre-funded nostro/vostro accounts that correspondent banks require to provide same-day settlement. As a liquidity anchor, RLUSD/XRP and RLUSD/IOU AMM pools provide reliable, deep routing for the pathfinding engine; thin corridors that would otherwise return tecPATH_DRY become viable when RLUSD is an intermediate hop. The compliance dimension also matters: Ripple maintains KYC/AML controls on RLUSD issuance, making it acceptable for regulated payment corridors that cannot use unattested issued currencies.

How do payment channels change the throughput and latency profile for high-frequency micropayment use cases, and what are their settlement risks?

Confirmed against source (rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/payment/ PaymentChannelCreate.cpp, PaymentChannelClaim.cpp): Payment channels decouple the per-payment cost and latency from on-ledger transaction fees. Once a channel is open and funded (one on-ledger transaction), the sender issues signed off-ledger claims for each micropayment — no consensus, no fee per claim, latency limited only by network round-trip between the two parties (sub-100 ms). Throughput is theoretically unlimited within the funded capacity. The trade-offs are settlement risk on both sides: the receiver holds signed claims that have not yet been cashed, so the sender's on-ledger balance is the backstop — if the sender drains their account before the receiver cashes, the claim may fail. Conversely, if the receiver stops cooperating, the sender must wait for the channel's Expiration or CancelAfter time to reclaim funds. The mitigations are: (1) receiver should cash claims periodically — not just at channel close — to bound exposure; (2) sender should not set excessively long expiry windows; (3) both parties should test the reclaim path on Testnet before going live. Channels are best suited for streaming payments between known, trusted counterparties (e.g., API metering, content streaming) rather than one-shot payments to unknown recipients.

← Back to Chapter 1 — Foundations

docs.title: Chapter 2 — Issuing Value
docs.text: This chapter covers how to design, deploy, and manage assets on the XRPL, from regulated stablecoins to high-performance Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs).

docs.title: Architect's Intent
docs.text:
"The original insight behind Ripple was that money is already credit. Your bank balance is not money — it's the bank's promise to pay you money. We just made that relationship explicit and put it on a shared ledger." — Ryan Fugger, designer of RipplePay (2004)

Ryan Fugger's 2004 RipplePay system was built on a single observation: in the real world, value already flows through networks of trust. When you pay a friend with a check, you are not transferring physical value — you are transferring a credit relationship through a banking system. Fugger asked: why not encode the trust relationship itself on a shared ledger and let value flow along chains of mutual credit?

That insight became the trust line — the RippleState ledger object at the heart of every issued-currency flow on the XRPL. When Jed McCaleb and David Schwartz integrated Fugger's concept into the 2012 genesis design, they made a choice that distinguishes the XRPL from every subsequent chain: value issuance is not a contract; it is a declared credit relationship with protocol- enforced controls.

This has two practical consequences that every issuer must understand from day one:

  1. Issuance is a legal commitment, not just a technical act. Every flag you set on an issuer account (RequireAuth, DefaultRipple, NoFreeze, Clawback) encodes a real-world promise to your holders — and many of those flags cannot be reversed once set.
  2. The protocol enforces the relationship. You do not need an audited smart contract to implement freeze, clawback, or authorization controls. They are native primitives because the original architects built them in, not because a later team bolted them on.

MPTs (Multi-Purpose Tokens) extend this lineage — they are a more efficient encoding of the same credit relationship, designed by the rippled team for high-throughput issuance without the per-holder ledger-object cost of trust lines. The concept is the same; the implementation is optimized.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: The XRPL was the first blockchain designed specifically for asset issuance (IOUs). Understanding the nuances of trust lines, rippling, and issuer controls is the difference between a secure, compliant financial product and a chaotic, unmanaged pool of liquidity.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text: Issuing value on the XRPL is not about "minting" in the Ethereum sense; it's about establishing trust relationships. - Trust Lines (IOUs): Bidirectional ledger entries that track debt between an issuer and a holder. - MPTs: Native, optimized fungible tokens that don't require trust line ledger objects for every holder.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
This chapter is divided into three core domains:

  1. Issuer Controls: The protocol-level enforcement mechanisms (Freeze, Clawback, Auth).
  2. Stablecoins: Designing for deep liquidity, fiat redundancy, and regulatory compliance.
  3. Tokenization: Mapping real-world assets (RWA) and specialized fungible tokens to the ledger.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
1. Start with Issuer Controls to understand what you cannot change once you start.
  2. Move to Stablecoins to see these controls in a production architecture.
  3. Explore Tokenization for advanced asset designs.

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: Issuing value on the XRPL is not a technical act — it is a legal and operational commitment. Every issuer flag (DefaultRipple, NoFreeze, RequireAuth) has a real-world counterpart in the trust relationship between issuer and holder. Get the flags wrong at launch and there is no clean rollback.

docs.title: What you should be able to do after this chapter
docs.text:
• Explain why RequireAuth must be set on an empty account before the first trust line is authorized.
  • Differentiate between a Trust Line (bilateral RippleState) and an MPT (native, holder-side MPToken object), and choose between them for a given use case.
  • Predict how DefaultRipple affects cross-issuer pathfinding and what routing side effects it creates.
  • Design a disaster recovery flow using Clawback that is compliant with irreversible flag constraints.

docs.title: Issuer Controls
docs.text: Mechanisms for enforcing regulatory compliance, managing risk, and maintaining token integrity through protocol-level account and object flags.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: On a public, decentralized ledger, issuers are often legally or operationally responsible for the tokens they issue. Without protocol-level controls, an issuer cannot: - Block sanctioned actors from holding their tokens. - Recover funds sent to a lost or compromised account (Clawback). - Halt trading during a security incident (Global Freeze). - Signal immutability to users to build trust (NoFreeze).

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Issuer controls exist at two distinct layers:

  1. Account-level flags (The Policy): Set once on the issuer's account root to define the rules for all tokens issued by that account.
  2. Object-level flags (The Enforcement): Set on specific trust lines (IOUs) or token issuances (MPTs) to enforce policies on a per-holder basis.
Control Type Account Flag (Policy) Object Flag (Enforcement) Authorization asfRequireAuth tfSetfAuth (TrustSet) / MPTokenAuthorize Freezing asfGlobalFreeze tfSetFreeze (TrustSet) / tfMPTLock Clawback asfAllowTrustLineClawback Clawback transaction Immutability asfNoFreeze n/a (Account-wide permanent lock)

docs.title: The tecOWNERS Gate
docs.text:
The most critical architectural constraint in the XRPL is that fundamental policy flags (RequireAuth and AllowTrustLineClawback) can only be enabled when the issuer account's owner directory is empty.

Consequence: You must configure your issuer account before issuing a single token, creating an offer, or setting up a signer list. Retroactive enforcement is impossible without migrating to a new issuer account.

docs.title: Trust Line (IOU) vs. MPT Controls
docs.text:
• Trust Lines: Use AccountSet for policy and TrustSet for per-holder enforcement.
  • MPTs: Use MPTokenIssuanceCreate to define capabilities (sfMutableFlags) and MPTokenIssuanceSet to toggle them. MPTs do not use AccountSet for most controls.

docs.title: Example flow: Clawing back funds
docs.text:
The Clawback transaction was introduced via amendment to allow issuers to repossess tokens (e.g., for legal compliance or fraud recovery).

  1. Setup: Issuer sets asfAllowTrustLineClawback via AccountSet (while owner count is 0).
  2. Issuance: Issuer sends tokens to a holder.
  3. Trigger: A recovery event occurs.
  4. Transaction: Issuer submits a Clawback transaction.
    • Trust Line: sfAmount's issuer is the holder's account.
    • MPT: sfHolder specifies the account to claw back from.
  5. Result: Balance is deducted from the holder and credited back to (or burned by) the issuer.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Using the Testnet faucet at https://xrpl.org/resources/dev-tools/xrp-faucets:

  1. Set asfNoFreeze on a test issuer account, then attempt to set asfGlobalFreeze. What result code do you get? Is the fee charged?
  2. Enable asfRequireAuth on the issuer, then have a second account attempt to create a trust line and receive tokens without authorization. What happens?
  3. Attempt asfAllowTrustLineClawback without first enabling it. What happens if the flag is not set and you submit a Clawback transaction?
  4. Set a TransferRate of 1,005,000,000 (0.5% fee). Send 100 USD between two non-issuer accounts. How much does the recipient receive? How much goes to the issuer?
  5. Set asfGlobalFreeze, verify the state via account_info Flags field, then attempt a peer-to-peer transfer. What result code is returned?

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• asfNoFreeze is permanent. Once enabled, the issuer can never freeze tokens again. This is used to signal "permissionless" status to the market but is a massive liability if the token is regulated.
  • Master Key requirement. Setting asfNoFreeze requires signing with the Master Key (if not disabled). This prevents a secondary "regular key" from accidentally or maliciously revoking the issuer's control.
  • Clawback is a "trust me" feature. Exchanges and DeFi protocols often flag tokens with clawback enabled as higher risk, as the issuer can unilaterally remove liquidity.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Enabling DefaultRipple before RequireAuth. On a regulated token, this creates a window where anyone can create a trust line and receive tokens via rippling before you can authorize them.
  • Forgetting tecOWNERS. Trying to enable Clawback or RequireAuth after the account is already operational. This usually results in a failed deployment.
  • Misunderstanding NoFreeze. Thinking it only applies to new trust lines. It actually prevents the issuer from clearing an existing GlobalFreeze as well.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Issuer account configured with RequireAuth before any tokens issued.
  • [ ] AllowTrustLineClawback set if regulatory recovery is required.
  • [ ] DefaultRipple enabled ONLY if cross-issuer rippling is intended.
  • [ ] Cold wallet master key used to set NoFreeze (if applicable).
  • [ ] Holder authorization workflow (KYC -> tfSetfAuth) automated.

This checklist covers issuer controls. Before production, also complete the account-security checklist in ch04-hardening/security and the node-operations checklist in ch04-hardening/operations.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• rippled: AccountSet.cpp
  • rippled: TrustSet.cpp
  • rippled: Clawback.cpp
  • XLS-39: Clawback

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text: The tecOWNERS constraint is the "Original Sin" of XRPL issuance. It enforces a strict "Config-then-Operate" lifecycle. If you forget to set RequireAuth at T-0, your token is effectively permissionless forever on that account.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• DeepFreeze (active since v2.4.0, 2025-05-04): how does it interact with AMMs — can a deep-frozen balance be used as liquidity?
  • MPT Global Freeze: Is there a single-transaction equivalent to GlobalFreeze for an MPT issuance, or must every holder be locked individually?

← Back to Chapter 2 — Issuing Value

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: A stablecoin issuer bears asymmetric risk: any misconfiguration of the issuer account — DefaultRipple, RequireAuth, TransferRate, freeze — has immediate, on-ledger consequences for every holder. Getting issuance right is not just a technical exercise; it directly governs the legal and operational relationship between the issuer and every counterparty.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
An issued currency on the XRPL is a bilateral credit relationship encoded in a trust line. The issuer is not a smart contract — it is an account whose configuration flags determine the rights and restrictions of every holder. Issuance is fundamentally about managing those relationships at scale.

Key issuer flags (see Issuer Controls for full technical details):

  • DefaultRipple — allows balances to ripple across trust lines.
  • RequireAuth — restricts trust line creation to authorized counterparties.
  • GlobalFreeze / Individual Freeze — emergency controls to halt movement.
  • NoFreeze — permanently revokes the freeze capability to build holder trust.
  • Clawback — enables the recovery of tokens from a holder's account.
  • TransferRate — an on-ledger fee charged on peer-to-peer transfers.

docs.title: Hot/cold account topology
docs.text:
graph TD
    BANK["Bank / Reserve Custodian<br/>(off-ledger)"]
    COLD["COLD Account (issuer)<br/>asfDisableMaster<br/>asfRequireAuth<br/>asfDefaultRipple<br/>never online"]
    HOT["HOT Account (operator)<br/>regular key or multi-sig<br/>day-to-day customer sends"]
    CUST["CUSTOMER Accounts<br/>trust line authorized by cold"]

    BANK -->|"fiat in → mint signal"| COLD
    COLD -->|"IOU issuance"| HOT
    HOT -->|"IOU delivery"| CUST
    CUST -->|"IOU redemption"| HOT
    HOT -->|"IOU return"| COLD
    COLD -->|"redeem signal"| BANK

docs.title: Reserve math for a typical issuer setup
docs.text:
A fresh issuer account needs:

Object XRP cost Count Base account reserve 2 XRP 1 Signer list (3 signers) 0.2 XRP × (N+1) = 0.8 XRP 1 Hot account trust line 0.2 XRP 1 Additional authorized trust lines 0.2 XRP each N

Example: cold account with 3-of-5 multi-sig + 1 hot account trust line = 2 + (5+1)×0.2 + 0.2 = 3.4 XRP minimum. Add a buffer of 2–5 XRP for fee capacity and future object growth.

docs.title: TransferRate encoding
docs.text:
TransferRate is a UINT32 stored as a ratio with 1,000,000,000 as the denominator (1.0 = no fee):

Desired fee TransferRate value Formula 0% (no fee) 1,000,000,000 1.000 × 10^9 0.1% 1,001,000,000 1.001 × 10^9 0.5% 1,005,000,000 1.005 × 10^9 1.0% 1,010,000,000 1.010 × 10^9

The fee is charged to the sender on peer-to-peer transfers between non-issuer accounts. Transfers directly to/from the issuer do not incur the fee. Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/payment/Payment.cpp.

docs.title: Trust line authorization workflow (when RequireAuth is set)
docs.text:
1. Customer submits TrustSet → trust line created in lsfNoRipple + pending auth state.
  2. Issuer (or hot account via delegation) submits TrustSet with tfSetfAuth flag.
  3. Trust line moves to lsfAuth state → customer may now hold the token.
  4. To revoke: issuer submits TrustSet with zero limit; line auto-deleted when balance = 0.

Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/TrustSet.cpp.

docs.title: Regulated stablecoin minting
docs.text:
1. Issuer setup
  2. Create cold account; fund to at least base reserve + signer-list + buffer.
  3. Set asfRequireAuth and asfDefaultRipple in a single AccountSet.
  4. Configure a multi-sig SignerList (e.g., 3-of-5).
  5. Disable master key (asfDisableMaster) — irreversible without multi-sig available.

  6. Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/account/AccountSet.cpp

  7. Customer onboarding

  8. Customer completes off-ledger KYC/AML; their XRPL address is recorded.
  9. Customer submits TrustSet with a limit ≥ expected maximum holding.

  10. Trust line is created in "pending auth" state (lsfLowAuth/lsfHighAuth unset).

  11. Trust line authorization

  12. Hot account (authorized by cold via delegation or multi-sig) submits TrustSet with tfSetfAuth targeting the customer's trust line.

  13. Trust line transitions to authorized state; customer may now receive tokens.

  14. Minting

  15. Off-ledger: fiat received into reserve custodian account.
  16. Cold account (multi-sig quorum) sends Payment of issued currency to hot account.
  17. Hot account sends Payment to customer — no additional on-ledger supply created (supply exists between cold and hot; hot redistributes).

  18. On-ledger total supply = sum of all balances held by non-issuer accounts.

  19. Redemption

  20. Customer sends currency back to issuer (cold or hot) via Payment.
  21. Balance returns to the issuer — supply is destroyed.
  22. Off-ledger: operator releases fiat to customer's bank account.
  23. Reconcile: on-ledger total supply must equal attested off-ledger reserves.

docs.title: Reserve attestation workflow
docs.text:
Periodically (e.g., daily) verify total on-ledger supply against off-ledger reserves:

1. Fetch all trust lines via account_lines (cold account)
   → sum all non-zero balances (from cold's perspective: negative = issued)

2. Compare sum to off-chain reserve custodian balance

3. If |on_chain_supply − off_chain_reserve| > threshold → alert

4. Publish attestation hash (hash of (timestamp, supply, reserve_balance))

Using account_lines with pagination: 

{ "command": "account_lines", "account": "<cold_address>", "limit": 400,
  "marker": "<opaque_marker_from_previous_response>" }

Repeat until no marker is returned. Source: rippled account_lines handler.

docs.title: Emergency freeze sequence
docs.text:
When a regulatory freeze is required:

  1. Cold account (multi-sig) submits AccountSet with asfGlobalFreeze.
  2. All trust lines on the cold account are immediately frozen — no peer-to-peer transfers possible for the token, regardless of individual line state.
  3. Verify freeze: account_info on cold account; Flags field has lsfGlobalFreeze set.
  4. Notify holders per legal requirement.
  5. To selectively unfreeze specific counterparties: TrustSet with tfClearFreeze on individual lines (only possible if NoFreeze was not set).
  6. Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/account/AccountSet.cpp

Non-obvious insight: GlobalFreeze freezes all trust lines on the issuer account atomically, but individual line freezes can coexist. Setting asfNoFreeze permanently removes freeze capability — useful for building holder trust in permissionless tokens, but it also removes the issuer's regulatory lever. Choose at design time.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Using the Testnet faucet at https://xrpl.org/resources/dev-tools/xrp-faucets:

  1. Run examples/03-trust-line-and-issue/ — observe the DefaultRipple flag and trust line authorization in action. What does the trust line state look like before the issuer authorizes it? Query account_lines on the hot account to find out.
  2. Attempt to set TransferRate to 999999999 (below minimum). What result code is returned? Look up the code in the Glossary.
  3. Enable asfGlobalFreeze on the cold account, then try to send the issued currency peer-to-peer between two non-issuer accounts. What result code do you get?
  4. Compute the reserve cost for a cold account with 5 signers and 1000 authorized trust lines. Is it economically feasible for a retail stablecoin issuer?

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• The issuing account's master key must be disabled after configuration; use multi-signing for any subsequent administrative changes.
  • RequireAuth should be set before enabling DefaultRipple on a regulated token to avoid unauthorized holders.
  • Freeze capability is a double-edged sword: holders may discount the token's value. Decide between NoFreeze (permissionless) and freeze (regulated) as part of the initial design — not reactively.
  • AllowTrustLineClawback is irrevocable once set. Set it intentionally as part of the issuance design.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Enabling DefaultRipple without RequireAuth on regulated tokens. Without it, anyone can create a trust line and hold the token.
  • Misconfiguring TransferRate. A TransferRate of 1000000000 means no fee; values must be ≥ 1000000000. Off-by-one errors cause systematic fee miscalculation across every transfer.
  • Burning supply without reconciling off-ledger. On-ledger supply and off-ledger reserves must be kept in sync and regularly attested.
  • Operating the issuer as a hot account. The issuing key should only be used for configuration and bulk operations — never for day-to-day transfers.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Issuer account uses multi-signing; master key disabled.
  • [ ] RequireAuth is set if the token has a restricted holder list.
  • [ ] DefaultRipple is set correctly and its routing implications are understood.
  • [ ] TransferRate is validated against expected fee behavior.
  • [ ] Freeze and clawback posture is documented and communicated to holders.
  • [ ] Minting and redemption flows are auditable end-to-end.
  • [ ] On-ledger supply is reconciled against off-ledger reserves on a defined schedule.
  • [ ] Reserve attestation process is defined, documented, and scheduled.

This checklist covers stablecoin issuance. Before production, also complete the account-security checklist in ch04-hardening/security and the node-operations checklist in ch04-hardening/operations.
