docs.text:
XRPL.org documentation - Issued Currencies - Freezing Tokens - Authorized Trust Lines - Transfer Fees

rippled source references - rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/account/AccountSet.cpp — asfRequireAuth, asfDefaultRipple, asfGlobalFreeze, asfDisableMaster - rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/TrustSet.cpp — trust line creation, tfSetfAuth, individual freeze - rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/Clawback.cpp — AllowTrustLineClawback enforcement - rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/payment/Payment.cpp — TransferRate application

Runnable examples - examples/03-trust-line-and-issue/ — hot/cold IOU issuance end-to-end

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Configuration is irreversible (mostly). Flags like asfNoFreeze and asfAllowTrustLineClawback are permanent. You must design your issuance model before the first transaction.
  • Cold wallets should stay cold. Moving funds from a cold issuer directly to customers is standard, but the key that signs those transactions should be managed via secure, multi-party signing (like a vault or specialized custody service).
  • Rippling is a feature, not a bug. Enabling DefaultRipple allows your token to be used in cross-currency pathfinding, increasing its utility and liquidity.
  • Trust is bilateral. A trust line isn't just "holding" a token; it's an agreement that the issuer owes you value. The lsfNoRipple flag on the customer side is just as important as the issuer flags.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• What are the strategic advantages of issuing a stablecoin on the XRPL?
  • How should treasury operations be structured for hot/cold wallet security?
  • What are the best practices for on-ledger reserve management and attestation?
  • How are compliance requirements (KYC/AML) enforced via trust lines and authorization flags?

← Back to Chapter 2 — Issuing Value

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: Tokenizing a real-world asset is not just minting a token — it is encoding an asset's legal rights, transfer restrictions, and lifecycle events into a programmable ledger object. The choice of primitive (issued currency, MPT, or NFT) has permanent consequences for the asset's behavior, compliance posture, and secondary market liquidity. Choose wrong and you'll be redeeming and re-issuing under pressure.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Choose the smallest primitive that fully satisfies the asset's requirements:

  • Issued currencies — fungible, highly liquid, deep DEX/AMM integration. Best for high-volume homogeneous assets (stablecoins, commodities).
  • Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs) — fungible tokens with richer on-ledger metadata and lifecycle controls; lower reserve overhead than trust lines at scale. Best for regulated securities and structured products.
  • NFTs (XLS-20) — non-fungible; each token is unique. Best for assets where individual provenance matters (real estate, art, loans).

The key question is fungibility: are all units of this asset economically interchangeable? If yes, use MPT or issued currency. If no, use NFT.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Asset onboarding — off-ledger legal wrapper, on-ledger token configuration, metadata anchoring.
  • Holder management — authorized trust lines (issued currency / MPT) or transfer restrictions (NFT) tied to KYC/AML verification.
  • Lifecycle events — corporate actions (dividends, splits), maturity, redemption, and burning.
  • Metadata — on-ledger URI plus off-ledger verifiable document; integrity anchored via content hash in the token URI field.

docs.title: Issuing a permissioned, transferable MPT
docs.text:
This traces a regulated (allowlisted) Multi-Purpose Token from configuration through holder onboarding to a restricted secondary transfer. On a classic (pre-DynamicMPT) issuance the capability flags are fixed at creation — you cannot add Clawback, Transfer, or RequireAuth to an existing issuance (contrast the account-level flags in Issuer Controls), so the design decision is made once, up front. The DynamicMPT amendment relaxes this only for capabilities you explicitly pre-declare mutable at creation via MutableFlags (see the note at the end of this flow).

  1. Create the issuance. The issuer submits MPTokenIssuanceCreate with the capability flags baked in:
  2. tfMPTRequireAuth — every holder must be explicitly authorized before they can receive units (the allowlist gate).
  3. tfMPTCanTransfer — permits holder-to-holder (secondary) transfers. Without it, units can only move to and from the issuer.
  4. tfMPTCanClawback / tfMPTCanLock — reserve the right to repossess or freeze balances for compliance.

Optional configuration set here: MaximumAmount (hard supply cap, ≤ kMaxMpTokenAmount = 2⁶³−1), AssetScale (decimal places), TransferFee (≤ kMaxTransferFee = 50000, i.e. 50%, and only valid when tfMPTCanTransfer is set), and MPTokenMetadata (≤ kMaxMpTokenMetadataLength = 1024 bytes). MaximumAmount and AssetScale are permanently immutable; TransferFee and MPTokenMetadata are immutable too unless you opt into mutability at creation with the matching MutableFlags bit (DynamicMPT). The transaction returns a deterministic MPTokenIssuanceID derived from the issuer account and sequence — the stable handle every later step references.

  1. Holder opts in. The prospective holder submits MPTokenAuthorize naming the MPTokenIssuanceID (and no Holder field). This creates the holder's MPToken object with a zero balance. The issuer cannot create this object on the holder's behalf — the holder must opt in first (preclaim in MPTokenAuthorize.cpp requires the MPToken to exist before the issuer can authorize it). An issuer also cannot authorize itself: holding your own issuance returns tecNO_PERMISSION.

  2. Issuer authorizes the holder. Because lsfMPTRequireAuth is set, the issuer submits MPTokenAuthorize with the Holder field to flip the holder's lsfMPTAuthorized flag. Skipping the on-ledger RequireAuth flag makes this step a no-op — the transaction returns tecNO_AUTH, so an allowlist you never enabled provides no enforcement.

  3. Primary issuance. The issuer sends units to the authorized holder via Payment. This raises sfOutstandingAmount on the issuance (the MPT analogue of total supply), capped by MaximumAmount if one was set.

  4. Restricted secondary transfer. Holder A pays Holder B. This succeeds only because tfMPTCanTransfer was set at creation and Holder B is already authorized. If a TransferFee was configured, it is deducted here — analogous to TransferRate on an issued currency, but encoded on the issuance object rather than the account.

  5. Compliance action (optional). To halt a specific holder, the issuer submits MPTokenIssuanceSet with tfMPTLock (requires lsfMPTCanLock), setting lsfMPTLocked on that holder's MPToken; tfMPTUnlock reverses it. To repossess, the issuer submits a Clawback naming the Holder (requires lsfMPTCanClawback), reducing the holder's balance and sfOutstandingAmount together.

The through-line: on an MPT, policy is decided at creation and enforced per-holder thereafter. There is no AccountSet-style free retrofit: a capability is available later only if it (or the right to enable it) was declared at creation. Concretely, with DynamicMPT an issuer may pre-authorize future changes by setting MutableFlags bits (tmfMPTCanEnableCanTransfer, tmfMPTCanMutateTransferFee, tmfMPTCanMutateMetadata, etc.); a later MPTokenIssuanceSet can then flip only those pre-blessed capabilities. Anything not pre-declared mutable — and MaximumAmount/AssetScale in all cases — is permanently fixed.

docs.title: DynamicMPT lifecycle — deferring policy decisions
docs.text:
The DynamicMPT amendment (voting as of xrpld 3.4; Supported::Yes, DefaultNo in features.macro) enables issuers to defer specific policy decisions by pre-declaring capabilities as mutable at creation time. This is controlled, opt-in evolution — not a free-form retrofit.

Amendment gate: requires featureDynamicMPT active on the network; any MPTokenIssuanceCreate with sfMutableFlags returns temDISABLED without it.

Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/MPTokenIssuanceCreate.cpp (line 38)

docs.title: Phase 1: Creation with mutability pre-declarations
docs.text:
Submit MPTokenIssuanceCreate with sfMutableFlags encoding which capabilities the issuer reserves the right to enable later:

sfMutableFlags bit Allows future enable of Ledger flag enabled tmfMPTCanEnableCanLock lsfMPTCanLock Per-holder lock capability tmfMPTCanEnableRequireAuth lsfMPTRequireAuth Holder authorization requirement tmfMPTCanEnableCanEscrow lsfMPTCanEscrow Escrow support tmfMPTCanEnableCanTrade lsfMPTCanTrade DEX trading tmfMPTCanEnableCanTransfer lsfMPTCanTransfer Holder-to-holder transfers tmfMPTCanEnableCanClawback lsfMPTCanClawback Issuer clawback tmfMPTCanMutateMetadata — Allows MPTokenMetadata updates tmfMPTCanMutateTransferFee — Allows TransferFee changes

Source: rippled/include/xrpl/protocol/TxFlags.h (lines 359–390), rippled/include/xrpl/protocol/LedgerFormats.h (lines 183–207).

Example: an issuer launching a bond token may want to defer the transfer capability decision pending regulatory approval: 

{
  "TransactionType": "MPTokenIssuanceCreate",
  "Account": "<issuer>",
  "MaximumAmount": "1000000000",
  "AssetScale": 2,
  "Flags": 0,
  "MutableFlags": 32
}
MutableFlags=32 is tmfMPTCanEnableCanTransfer — the issuer does not enable transfers now but reserves the right to do so later.

docs.title: Phase 2: Enabling a pre-declared capability
docs.text:
Once the regulatory green-light arrives, the issuer submits MPTokenIssuanceSet with the corresponding sfMutableFlags bit:

{
  "TransactionType": "MPTokenIssuanceSet",
  "Account": "<issuer>",
  "MPTokenIssuanceID": "<issuance_id>",
  "MutableFlags": 16
}
MutableFlags=16 is tmfMPTSetCanTransfer — this flips lsfMPTCanTransfer to enabled. Holders can now transfer among themselves.

Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/MPTokenIssuanceSet.cpp (lines 51–69, kMptMutabilityFlags mapping table).

docs.title: Key constraints (source-verified)
docs.text:
1. One-way enablement. Once a capability is enabled via MPTokenIssuanceSet, it cannot be disabled. The MPTokenIssuanceSet has no "remove capability" path — only tfMPTLock/tfMPTUnlock for per-holder operations.

  2. Permanently immutable fields.

  3. MaximumAmount — hard cap, set once, never changed.

  4. AssetScale — decimal precision, set once, never changed. These are not subject to DynamicMPT mutability regardless of what sfMutableFlags bits are set.

  5. Pre-declaration required. If tmfMPTCanEnableCanTransfer was NOT set in sfMutableFlags at creation, a later MPTokenIssuanceSet with tmfMPTSetCanTransfer returns tecNO_PERMISSION.

  6. Confidential balance exclusivity. If lsfMPTCanHoldConfidentialBalance is enabled, TransferFee > 0 cannot coexist (encrypted amounts make fee computation impossible). Source: MPTokenIssuanceSet.cpp line 88.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Clawback and freeze posture (see Issuer Controls) must match the asset's legal offering documents.
  • MPT MaximumAmount is set at creation and cannot be changed.
  • Authorized minter accounts for NFTs should use multi-signing.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing NFTs for fungible assets. Non-fungible tokens cannot be aggregated or routed through the DEX; fungible assets need fungible primitives.
  • Mutable metadata. Using a centrally-controlled URL as the token URI allows silent modification of the asset record after issuance.
  • Missing transfer restrictions. Regulated assets require on-ledger enforcement — RequireAuth and authorized trust lines — not just off-ledger policy.
  • Not modeling MPT reserve costs. MPT holder entries still consume ledger objects; plan reserve requirements for large holder sets.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Token primitive chosen based on fungibility and compliance needs.
  • [ ] Metadata points to content-addressed or hash-verified storage.
  • [ ] Transfer restrictions are enforced on-ledger, not just in policy.
  • [ ] Authorized minter accounts use multi-signing.
  • [ ] MaximumAmount is capacity-planned before MPT deployment.
  • [ ] Lifecycle events (maturity, redemption, clawback) are scripted and tested before issuance.
  • [ ] On-ledger token state is reconciled with the off-ledger asset register on a defined schedule.

This checklist covers tokenization. Before production, also complete the account-security checklist in ch04-hardening/security and the node-operations checklist in ch04-hardening/operations.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Non-Fungible Tokens
  • Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs)
  • Authorized Trust Lines

xrpld source referenced in this section (paths relative to the vendored rippled/ tree — the on-disk directory retains the historical name):

  • MPT capability flags (tfMPTRequireAuth, tfMPTCanTransfer, tfMPTCanLock, tfMPTCanClawback, tfMPTCanEscrow, tfMPTCanTrade) — include/xrpl/protocol/TxFlags.h; ledger-side lsfMPT* counterparts in include/xrpl/protocol/LedgerFormats.h.
  • Issuance creation + immutable-at-creation validation (TransferFee requires tfMPTCanTransfer, sfOutstandingAmount init) — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/MPTokenIssuanceCreate.cpp.
  • Holder-opts-in-before-issuer-authorizes flow, tecNO_AUTH / tecNO_PERMISSION paths — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/MPTokenAuthorize.cpp.
  • Per-holder lock / mutable-flag mechanics — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/MPTokenIssuanceSet.cpp.
  • Bounds kMaxMpTokenAmount (2⁶³−1), kMaxTransferFee (50000), kMaxMpTokenMetadataLength (1024) — include/xrpl/protocol/Protocol.h.
  • Identity / compliance objects — DID (ltDID; fields DIDDocument, URI, Data), Credential (ltCREDENTIAL; Subject, Issuer, CredentialType, optional Expiration/URI), PermissionedDomain (ltPERMISSIONED_DOMAIN; AcceptedCredentials array) — include/xrpl/protocol_autogen/ledger_entries/{DID,Credential,PermissionedDomain}.h.
  • MPT-to-domain binding (DomainID requires tfMPTRequireAuth) — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/MPTokenIssuanceCreate.cpp.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• MPT capabilities are decided at creation. Unlike issued currencies, where account flags (RequireAuth, freeze, clawback) can be toggled on the issuer over its lifetime, an MPT's Transfer/Clawback/Lock/RequireAuth capabilities are set in MPTokenIssuanceCreate. On a classic issuance they are frozen for good; with DynamicMPT an issuer can change only the specific capabilities it pre-declared mutable (via MutableFlags) at creation. MaximumAmount and AssetScale are immutable in every case. The design decision is effectively permanent — plan it before the first transaction.
  • Authorization is a two-party handshake. With RequireAuth, the holder must create their MPToken object first (opt in), and only then can the issuer authorize it. The issuer can never conjure a balance on an account that has not opted in — a meaningful contrast to some allowlist models.
  • A capability flag you forgot to set fails silent-ish. Authorizing a holder on an issuance without RequireAuth returns tecNO_AUTH; a non-transferable MPT simply rejects secondary transfers. The absence of a flag is enforced as a hard tec/tem rejection, not a warning — so an incomplete configuration surfaces as failed transactions, not silent weakening of your controls.
  • Supply is sfOutstandingAmount, bounded by MaximumAmount. There is no separate "mint" primitive: issuing is a Payment from the issuer that raises outstanding amount, and clawback/redemption lowers it. If you cap supply, cap it at creation — MaximumAmount is immutable and bounded by 2⁶³−1.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
When should a developer choose Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs) over standard issued currencies?

Choose an MPT when you need per-issuance policy and metadata baked into the token itself, and an issued currency when you need maximum liquidity and the deepest DEX/AMM/pathfinding integration. The distinction is structural, not cosmetic:

  • Holder-side reserve and object model. An issued-currency balance lives in a bidirectional RippleState (trust line) that both parties can be charged an owner reserve for and that carries NoRipple/freeze/limit state on each side. An MPT balance lives in a single MPToken object owned by the holder, pointing at one shared MPTokenIssuance. For issuers with large holder sets, the MPT model is simpler to reason about and the policy lives in one place (the issuance) rather than being negotiated per trust line.
  • Policy is first-class on an MPT. Capabilities (CanTransfer, CanClawback, CanLock, RequireAuth, CanEscrow, CanTrade), an optional hard supply cap (MaximumAmount), AssetScale, on-ledger MPTokenMetadata (≤ 1024 bytes), and a DomainID binding are all attributes of the issuance object. With issued currencies the equivalent controls are spread across account flags (AccountSet) and per-trust-line flags (TrustSet).
  • The trade-off is liquidity and maturity. Issued currencies are the older, universally-supported primitive with the richest tooling and market depth. MPTokensV1 is active but the surrounding ecosystem (AMM support via MPTokensV2, dynamic mutation via DynamicMPT) is still maturing. For a stablecoin that must trade everywhere today, issued currency is the safe default; for a regulated security or structured product where controls and compact per-holder state matter more than DEX ubiquity, MPT fits better.

Confirmed against source — MPT capability flags and DomainID/MaximumAmount/ AssetScale/MPTokenMetadata fields in MPTokenIssuanceCreate.cpp; the single-MPToken-per-holder model in MPTokenAuthorize.cpp.

How are decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials integrated into the asset lifecycle?

XRPL exposes three native, composable identity primitives, and they attach to tokens through permissioned domains rather than living inside the token object:

  • DID (ltDID) — one per account, an on-ledger anchor holding a DIDDocument, URI, and/or Data (all optional). It identifies who an account is (e.g. a KYC'd institution) in a W3C-DID-compatible way, but does not itself gate anything.
  • Credential (ltCREDENTIAL) — an attestation by an issuer about a subject: required Subject, Issuer, CredentialType, plus optional Expiration and URI. Created with CredentialCreate and made effective when the subject runs CredentialAccept — a two-party handshake mirroring MPT authorization. This is the verifiable-credential equivalent ("this account has passed accredited-investor KYC").
  • PermissionedDomain (ltPERMISSIONED_DOMAIN) — an AcceptedCredentials allowlist (credential type + issuer pairs). It answers "which credentials grant entry to this compliance perimeter?"

The lifecycle linkage: an issuer creates a domain listing the credential types it trusts, then binds a token to it. An MPT issuance carries a DomainID (which requires tfMPTRequireAuth), and PermissionedDEX restricts order books to domain members. The result is credential-gated access enforced on-ledger: only accounts holding an accepted, unexpired credential can hold or trade the asset — without the issuer manually authorizing each holder.

Confirmed against source — object fields in ledger_entries/{DID,Credential,PermissionedDomain}.h; credential handshake in CredentialCreate.cpp / CredentialAccept.cpp; DomainID-requires-RequireAuth in MPTokenIssuanceCreate.cpp.

What does the end-to-end lifecycle of a Real-World Asset (RWA) look like on-ledger?

A representative regulated-RWA lifecycle, composing the primitives above:

  1. Identity & compliance setup. The issuer establishes its own DID, then stands up a PermissionedDomain whose AcceptedCredentials name the KYC/accreditation credential types (and trusted credential issuers) required to hold the asset.
  2. Investor onboarding. A credential issuer runs CredentialCreate for the investor; the investor CredentialAccepts it. The investor now satisfies the domain without any bespoke per-investor issuer action.
  3. Asset issuance. The issuer runs MPTokenIssuanceCreate with tfMPTRequireAuth + a DomainID, capabilities matching the offering docs (CanTransfer, CanClawback, CanLock), a MaximumAmount cap, and MPTokenMetadata anchoring the legal wrapper (hash of the offering document).
  4. Primary distribution. Domain-member investors opt in (MPTokenAuthorize), then receive units by Payment, raising sfOutstandingAmount.
  5. Secondary market. Members trade on a PermissionedDEX order book scoped to the domain; a configured TransferFee accrues to the issuer on each transfer.
  6. Corporate actions & lifecycle events. Coupons/dividends are paid as separate payments; freezes use MPTokenIssuanceSet (tfMPTLock) per holder; compliance recovery uses Clawback.
  7. Maturity / redemption / retirement. Holders return units to the issuer (lowering sfOutstandingAmount); once fully redeemed the issuer can MPTokenIssuanceDestroy, and expired credentials naturally drop investors from the domain.

Educated guess (not directly encoded in source): the ordering above (identity → domain → credentials → issuance) is a design recommendation, not a protocol-enforced sequence. The protocol enforces the individual dependencies (a DomainID requires RequireAuth; a domain must exist before it is referenced; a holder must opt in before authorization), but composing them into this end-to-end flow is an application-level pattern.

← Back to Chapter 2 — Issuing Value

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Markets and Liquidity
docs.text: This chapter covers the XRP Ledger's native decentralized exchange (DEX) and automated market maker (AMM) — both protocol-level primitives that enable atomic, cross-currency value flows.

docs.title: Architect's Intent
docs.text:
"The goal was a system where you could send any currency to anyone, and the system would find a path. The order book is how you make that possible without a central intermediary deciding the exchange rate." — Jed McCaleb, co-founder, XRPL (2011)

When Jed McCaleb, David Schwartz, and Arthur Britto designed the 2012 genesis ledger, they embedded a central limit order book (CLOB) directly into the protocol — not as a feature to be added later, not as a smart contract to be deployed, but as a consensus-layer primitive that every node enforces identically.

The reason is architectural. The co-founders wanted to solve the cross-currency payment problem: how do you send USD to someone who wants EUR without a central clearing house setting the exchange rate? The answer, in the XRPL's design, is to let the market set the rate, on-ledger, atomically, in the same transaction as the payment itself. An offer placed by a Tokyo trader and a payment initiated in London can interact in the same ledger — with the same deterministic outcome — because the order book lives in the replicated state machine, not in an application server.

This design choice — DEX as consensus primitive, not application contract — has consequences that reverberate through everything in this chapter:

  • Auto-bridging through XRP is possible because the protocol can compose two offers (A/XRP + XRP/B) atomically in a single payment step. No application logic required.
  • AMM pools (added via the AMM amendment in 2024) slot into the same pathfinding layer — a cross-currency payment can consume AMM liquidity, CLOB liquidity, or both, in the same transaction.
  • Oracles (added via PriceOracle amendment, 2024) are also consensus primitives: price data written by authorized publishers becomes a ledger object that any transaction can read, without an off-chain API call.

The thread from Fugger's credit-network insight (ch02) to McCaleb's exchange- at-the-protocol-level bet (this chapter) to the AMM addition is a continuous evolution: each layer makes the XRPL more capable of moving any value between any parties without a central intermediary.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: The XRPL was designed from day one to be an exchange. Unlike other blockchains where DeFi is implemented via third-party smart contracts, the XRPL's liquidity exists at the protocol level. This means: 1. Atomic execution: A payment can swap from one asset to another using liquidity from the DEX and AMM in a single atomic step. 2. Zero counterparty risk in trade: No "wrapped" tokens or bridge-layer risks for native assets. 3. No contract risk: There are no smart contracts to audit; the exchange logic is enforced by the protocol itself.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
1. DEX — The central limit order book: offer lifecycle, crossing rules, fill-or-kill semantics, auto-bridging through XRP, and reserve costs of open offers. Source: OfferCreate.cpp.

  2. AMM — The geometric-mean automated market maker: pool creation, single/double-asset deposit math, LP token mechanics, continuous auction slot, and AMMClawback risk. Source: AMMCreate.cpp, AMMDeposit.cpp, AMMBid.cpp.

  3. Oracles — On-ledger price oracles: PriceOracleSet, get_aggregate_price aggregation, staleness handling, and trust model. Source: OracleSet.cpp. Activation: PriceOracle amendment 2024-11-02.

  4. DeFi — cross-cutting composition guide — Not a peer topic to DEX/AMM/Oracles. This section shows how the three primitives above compose atomically inside a single Payment transaction: pathfinding across mixed liquidity sources, atomic settlement guarantees, and the unified mental model you need for production system design. Read it after sections 1–3.

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: Because liquidity exists at the protocol level rather than in application contracts, it composes atomically with payments. A cross-currency payment can route through DEX hops and AMM pools in the same transaction, with no intermediate settlement steps and no possibility of partial execution — there is no "smart contract to audit," only a fixed set of protocol rules that every validator enforces identically.

docs.title: What you should be able to do after this chapter
docs.text:
• Place and manage offers on the native DEX, and predict when they auto-bridge.
  • Create and manage AMM pools, including single-asset and double-asset flows.
  • Reason about AMM pricing using the geometric-mean invariant and continuous auction mechanism.
  • Use pathfinding to route payments across multiple DEX and AMM liquidity sources in a single transaction.
  • Safely consume on-ledger price oracles for valuation and risk management, including understanding oracle liveness and aggregation assumptions.

docs.title: Testnet/Devnet guidance
docs.text: To experiment with these features: 1. DEX: Active on all networks. Use OfferCreate to place orders. 2. AMM: Active on Mainnet and Testnet. Use AMMCreate to bootstrap a pool. 3. Oracles: Active on Mainnet. Use PriceOracleSet to simulate price feeds on Devnet.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: The XRPL AMM is a protocol-level automated market maker — one pool per asset pair, governed by a geometric-mean invariant enforced by the ledger itself. Unlike application-layer AMMs (Uniswap et al.), there are no smart contracts to audit: the pricing formula, fee structure, and LP token math are part of the consensus rules every validator enforces identically.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
The AMM holds two assets and maintains the invariant:

sqrt(asset1_balance × asset2_balance) ≥ LPTokensBalance

Swaps move along this curve. The continuous auction slot lets one LP bid for the right to trade at a discounted fee for 24 hours — incentivizing active LPs to manage the pool while still earning fees from passive LPs.

docs.title: Pool structure
docs.text:
Each AMM is a protocol-owned account that: - Holds exactly two assets (XRP or any issued currency). - Mints LPToken issued currency on deposit; burns on withdrawal. - Has a TradingFee (0–1% in units of 1/100000; max 1000 = 1%). - Stores an AuctionSlot object for the continuous auction mechanism.

Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/AMMCreate.cpp

docs.title: Pricing formula (source: AMMHelpers.cpp)
docs.text:
For a swap of asset1_in → asset2_out:

f1 = 1 - trading_fee / 100000
asset2_out = asset2_bal - (asset1_bal × asset2_bal) / (asset1_bal + asset1_in × f1)

Single-asset deposit incurs an implicit swap cost because it shifts the pool ratio. Double-asset deposit maintains the ratio and mints LP tokens proportionally.

docs.title: Continuous auction mechanism
docs.text:
Parameter Constant Value Slot window kTotalTimeSlotSecs 86,400 s (24 hours) Decay intervals kAuctionSlotTimeIntervals 20 Discounted fee fraction kAuctionSlotDiscountedFeeFraction 1/10 of pool fee Max authorized accounts kAuctionSlotMaxAuthAccounts 4

The slot holder pays 1/10 of the regular trading fee during their window. They can authorize up to 4 additional accounts to share the discount. After 24 hours (or if outbid), the slot is open for new bids.

Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/AMMBid.cpp

docs.title: Create and deposit into an AMM pool
docs.text:
1. AMMCreate — Alice provides initial liquidity (10 XRP + 100 USD), sets TradingFee = 300 (0.3%). The protocol creates an AMM account and mints LP tokens proportional to sqrt(10_drops × 100_USD).

  2. Verify via amm_info — confirms pool balances, LP token supply, and current slot holder.

  3. Double-asset deposit — Bob provides 5 XRP + 50 USD (same ratio as pool). LP tokens minted: lp_tokens_out = lp_supply × (asset1_in / asset1_bal). Both assets increase; the pool price is unchanged.

  4. Single-asset deposit — Carol provides 10 XRP only (no USD). The pool internally swaps half the XRP for USD to maintain the invariant, incurring the implicit swap cost (trading fee applies to the internal swap).

  5. Swap (via Payment) — Dave submits a Payment with pathfinding; the ledger routes through the AMM pool, applies the pricing formula, updates balances atomically.

docs.title: Auction slot bidding
docs.text:
1. Eve calls AMMBid with BidMin = 50 LPTokens to acquire the slot.
  2. If no current holder or Eve's bid > current slot value, Eve wins the slot.
  3. Eve's next 24 hours of trades execute at 1/10 the pool fee.
  4. Eve authorizes her market-making bot's account via AuthAccounts.
  5. After 24 hours, the slot expires and is available for a new bid.

Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/AMMBid.cpp

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Using the Testnet faucet at https://xrpl.org/resources/dev-tools/xrp-faucets:

  1. Run examples/04-amm-deposit/ — observe the LP token minted and the amm_info response. What is the initial price in XRP per USD?
  2. Perform a single-asset deposit of XRP only. Compare LP tokens received vs. a double-asset deposit of the same value. Which mints more?
  3. Simulate a swap by sending a Payment through the pool. Check the pool balances before and after — how much did the price move?
  4. Bid on the auction slot with a small LP token amount. Verify your account is in the AuctionSlot.AuthAccounts field via amm_info.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Single-asset deposit impermanent loss: Single-asset deposits move the pool price. If the asset price moves against you between deposit and withdrawal, you receive less than you deposited (impermanent loss). Prefer double-asset deposits.
  • Price manipulation via flash trades: Because XRPL has no concept of a flash loan, AMM price manipulation requires capital. Still, large swaps move the price significantly — use SendMax/DeliverMin to bound slippage.
  • Auction slot front-running: Slot bids are visible before ledger close. A competitor can observe your bid and outbid you in the same ledger. Size your bids conservatively; the excess is returned if you overbid.
  • AMMClawback: If the pool contains a clawback-enabled issued currency, the issuer can claw back their asset from the pool, draining it. Verify clawback flags on pool assets before LPing. Source: AMMClawback.cpp.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Ignoring TradingFee units. Fee is stored as basis points × 10 (e.g., 300 = 0.3%), not as a fraction. Off-by-one-order-of-magnitude errors result in pools with 30% fees or 0.003% fees.
  • Withdrawing with wrong flags. AMMWithdraw has 7 distinct flag modes (double-asset, single-asset, LP-token-only, etc.). Using the wrong flag causes an unexpected mix of returned assets.
  • Not checking lp_token in amm_info. LP token supply is the denominator for all share calculations. Always fetch current supply before computing expected mint/burn amounts.
  • Assuming AMM price = DEX price. The AMM price can diverge from the DEX order book. Arbitrageurs close the gap, but during high volatility, spreads widen temporarily.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Verify no Clawback flag on either pool asset before depositing.
  • [ ] Test single-asset deposit math on Testnet; compare LP tokens received to expected formula output.
  • [ ] Set DeliverMin on all swap payments to cap slippage.
  • [ ] Monitor amm_info pool balances at each ledger close if you are an LP.
  • [ ] Model impermanent loss for your target asset pair before providing liquidity.
  • [ ] Test AMMBid on Testnet before bidding with real LP tokens on Mainnet.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• The AMM is a protocol account, not a contract. The issuer of the LP token is the AMM account itself. LP tokens can be transferred, used in trust lines, and even placed in further AMM pools — composability is native.
  • Trading fee compounds for LPs. Each swap retains the fee in the pool, increasing the asset1_bal × asset2_bal product. LP token value grows as trades happen, even without new deposits.
  • Auction slot ROI is non-obvious. The slot value is lp_tokens_bid × asset_price. A high-volume pool may make the discounted fee worth bidding; a low-volume pool may not. Model expected volume before bidding.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How does the AMM interact with the DEX crossing engine? When a Payment path includes both DEX offers and AMM liquidity, which is evaluated first? Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/app/paths/.
  • What happens to the AMM pool if one asset is globally frozen by its issuer? The freeze prevents peer-to-peer transfers but the AMM holds the asset on behalf of the protocol account. Behavior under freeze needs operational verification.

← Back to Chapter 3 — Markets and Liquidity

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: The XRPL's DeFi primitives — the native order book DEX and the AMM — are built into the protocol, not smart contracts. This means they compose atomically with payments and require no external contracts to audit. But it also means liquidity behavior, fee mechanics, and execution guarantees differ fundamentally from EVM-based DeFi. Practitioners must understand these mechanics before building routing, liquidity provision, or treasury management on top of them.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Two complementary liquidity mechanisms, both native to the protocol:

  • DEX (order book) — a central limit order book where offers are on-ledger objects. Offers cross automatically when placed; unfilled orders rest in the book. Auto-bridging routes through XRP when it improves execution price.
  • AMM — a pool using a geometric mean invariant: the LP token supply is anchored to sqrt(asset1 × asset2) (ammLPTokens in AMMHelpers.cpp computes root2(asset1 * asset2), with the on-ledger invariant LPTokenBalance ≤ sqrt(asset1 × asset2)), which behaves like a constant-product market maker for marginal trades. Each AMM is a ledger account (ltAMM) holding two assets (sfAsset/sfAsset2); LP tokens represent proportional ownership. The protocol charges a trading fee (sfTradingFee) set at pool creation and adjustable via a governance vote (AMMVote, up to kVoteMaxSlots = 8 weighted votes). The fee is capped at kTradingFeeThreshold = 1000, i.e. 1% (fee units are 1/100000, so 1 = 0.001%); there is no protocol-mandated default.

Pathfinding combines both: a cross-currency payment may route through DEX order book hops, AMM pools, or both in a single atomic transaction. This liquidity is not consumed in isolation — it is what Foundations → Payments routes through when settling a cross-currency Payment; the atomicity and tecPATH_DRY/tecPATH_PARTIAL failure modes described there are the payment-side view of the mechanics detailed below.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Offers — on-ledger objects specifying an exchange rate and quantity. Passive offers avoid crossing on placement; fill-or-kill offers expire immediately if not filled.
  • AMM pools — one pool per asset pair; a protocol-owned account holds the reserves and mints LP tokens on deposit.
  • Liquidity provision — double-asset deposits maintain pool ratio; single-asset deposits incur an implicit swap cost.
  • Continuous auction mechanism — the AMM's sfAuctionSlot lets one LP win the slot (via AMMBid) and trade at a discounted fee for a 24-hour window (kTotalTimeSlotSecs), incentivizing active management. The slot holder pays the discounted fraction kAuctionSlotDiscountedFeeFraction = 1/10 of the pool fee; the window is divided into kAuctionSlotTimeIntervals = 20 decay intervals, and up to kAuctionSlotMaxAuthAccounts = 4 additional accounts can share the discount.
  • Oracles — on-ledger price oracle objects aggregate off-chain feeds; consumers must account for staleness and aggregation methodology.

docs.title: AMM Swap via Pathfinding
docs.text:
1. Transaction Submission: A user submits a Payment transaction with tfPartialPayment and a specified Paths array (calculated via ripple_path_find).
  2. Path Selection: The ledger's pathfinding engine evaluates the cheapest route:
  3. Route A: XRP/USD DEX Offer (order book).
  4. Route B: XRP/USD AMM Pool (automated liquidity).
  5. Invariant Check: The AMM calculates the swap impact from the constant-product relationship. Illustratively (ignoring fees), the output is asset2_out = asset2_bal - (asset1_bal * asset2_bal) / (asset1_bal + asset1_in); the exact xrpld formulas (AMMHelpers.cpp, Equations 3/4/7/8) fold in the fee multipliers f1 = 1 - tfee and f2 = (1 - tfee/2)/f1.
  6. Execution: If Route B is cheaper, the AMM reserves are updated: asset1 increases, asset2 decreases, and the trading fee (set per pool, e.g. 0.3%) is retained in the pool reserves, effectively increasing the value of all LP tokens.
  7. Finality: The transaction completes atomically; the user receives USD, and the AMM pool state is updated in a single ledger close.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Using the Testnet faucet at https://xrpl.org/resources/dev-tools/xrp-faucets:

  1. Run examples/04-amm-deposit/ — observe the LP token minted after creating the AMM. Then compute the expected token count using the formula sqrt(asset1 × asset2) and compare.
  2. Submit a cross-currency Payment from XRP to your USD issuer without specifying Paths. Does pathfinding route through the AMM automatically?
  3. Set DeliverMin on a payment to reject partial fills. Try with and without tfPartialPayment and observe the result codes.
  4. Use ripple_path_find to see what routes the engine proposes for a USD→EUR swap. Does it suggest DEX hops, AMM hops, or both?
  5. Bid on the auction slot with AMMBid and verify your account appears in the AuctionSlot.AuthAccounts field of the amm_info response.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• AMM prices can be manipulated within a single ledger close; use TWAP or multi-source oracles for any on-chain pricing logic.
  • LP positions are exposed to impermanent loss when asset prices diverge; model this explicitly in treasury strategies.
  • Offers resting in the book are visible to all participants; large orders can be front-run by higher-fee transactions in the same ledger close.
  • Oracle data has a freshness timestamp; never consume a price without validating it against an acceptable staleness threshold.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Ignoring auto-bridging. Routes through XRP can provide better execution than direct pairs; pathfinding must be allowed to explore XRP-bridged routes.
  • Not accounting for slippage in AMM swaps. The geometric-mean invariant means large swaps move the price significantly; set SendMax or a slippage tolerance appropriately.
  • Single-asset AMM deposits without modeling the swap cost. Single-asset deposits implicitly swap half the deposit to rebalance the pool, incurring a fee and price impact.
  • Stale oracle consumption. Using a price without a freshness check can cause mispriced liquidations or incorrect valuations.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Pathfinding is configured to explore both DEX and AMM routes.
  • [ ] Slippage tolerance is set on all market-taking transactions.
  • [ ] Oracle prices are validated against a freshness threshold before use.
  • [ ] LP positions are monitored for impermanent loss against rebalancing thresholds.
  • [ ] AMM trading fees and auction slot status are tracked for LP positions.
  • [ ] Large orders are split or timed to minimize price impact.

This checklist covers markets and liquidity. Before production, also complete the account-security checklist in ch04-hardening/security and the node-operations checklist in ch04-hardening/operations.

  • Trading-fee bound kTradingFeeThreshold (1000 = 1%), fee units (1/100000), and auction-slot constants (kTotalTimeSlotSecs, kAuctionSlotTimeIntervals, kAuctionSlotDiscountedFeeFraction, kAuctionSlotMaxAuthAccounts, kVoteMaxSlots) — include/xrpl/protocol/AMMCore.h.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Protocol-native DeFi is safer but more rigid. You cannot "hot-fix" an AMM bug like you can with a smart contract, but you also don't have to worry about re-entrancy attacks or contract-level vulnerabilities.
  • LP tokens are trust-line IOUs. AMM LP tokens are issued by the AMM account and held as RippleState (trust line) balances; the pool's total is tracked in sfLPTokenBalance on the ltAMM object. (An MPT-based variant is only relevant once MPTokensV2 activates; it is not on Mainnet today.)
  • The trading fee is capped at 1%, with no protocol default. 0.3% is a common convention, not a hardwired value; the protocol only enforces the kTradingFeeThreshold = 1000 (1%) ceiling. The continuous auction slot can significantly change the yield profile for active LPs by discounting that fee to 1/10 for the slot holder.
  • Pathfinding is the "invisible hand." It doesn't matter if liquidity is in the DEX or AMM; the protocol will find it.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
What are the mechanics of the native Decentralized Exchange (DEX) vs. the Automated Market Maker (AMM)?

They are two distinct liquidity structures that pathfinding treats interchangeably, but their execution models differ fundamentally:

  • DEX (central limit order book). Liquidity is discrete: each Offer is an on-ledger object at a fixed exchange rate and quantity. An incoming offer consumes resting offers in price-priority order until it is filled or its limit price is exhausted; anything left rests in the book. Price is whatever counterparties posted — there is no formula. tfPassive avoids crossing on placement; fill-or-kill / immediate-or-cancel variants control partial execution. Auto-bridging synthesizes an XRP hop between two IOU books when that improves the effective rate.
  • AMM (constant-function pool). Liquidity is continuous: a single ltAMM pool of two assets prices every trade off the geometric-mean invariant. There are no counterparties — the pool is the counterparty — and the marginal price moves with every unit traded (slippage is a function of trade size relative to pool depth). LPs earn the sfTradingFee, which stays in the pool and accrues to LP-token value.
  • How they compose. An AMM does not rest orders in the book. Instead, during payment execution the engine synthesizes a virtual offer from the pool (AMMOffer/AMMLiquidity) and lets it compete with real order-book offers hop-by-hop. A single Payment can therefore consume order-book offers and AMM liquidity in the same atomic transaction, always taking the best-quality slice first. See the worked cross-currency example in Foundations → Payments for the payment-side view of this same flow.

Confirmed against source — order-book stepping and auto-bridging in the dex/OfferCreate.cpp transactor and tx/paths book steps; AMM virtual offers in tx/paths/AMMOffer.cpp and AMMLiquidity.cpp; the geometric-mean invariant in ammLPTokens (AMMHelpers.cpp).

How do lending protocols and vaults leverage XRPL's native liquidity?

Through two composable ledger objects that sit above the DEX/AMM rather than inside them — currently code-complete but in the voting stage (SingleAssetVault and LendingProtocol are Supported::Yes / VoteBehavior::DefaultNo, so not yet active on Mainnet):

  • Vault (ltVAULT, XLS-65). A single-asset pool where many depositors aggregate liquidity. Deposits mint shares, tracked not as trust lines but as an MPT (sfShareMPTID points at an MPTokenIssuance) — a concrete reuse of the ch02 token primitive. The object tracks sfAssetsTotal, sfAssetsAvailable (idle vs. deployed capital), sfAssetsMaximum (a cap), sfLossUnrealized, and a sfWithdrawalPolicy.
  • Lending (ltLOAN / ltLOAN_BROKER, XLS-66). A loan broker draws on a vault's available assets to originate loans; repayments (principal + interest, less fees) flow back to the vault, raising share value. The difference between sfAssetsTotal and sfAssetsAvailable is exactly the capital currently lent out.

The "leverage native liquidity" linkage is indirect: vaults are a funding layer whose deposited assets can themselves be DEX/AMM-tradable IOUs, and access is gated by the same credential/permissioned-domain machinery from ch02 (only accounts satisfying a domain may participate). The protocol does not automatically route vault capital into AMM pools; composition is an application-level decision.

Confirmed against source — Vault.h fields (sfShareMPTID, sfAssetsTotal, sfAssetsAvailable, sfAssetsMaximum, sfLossUnrealized, sfWithdrawalPolicy), Loan.h / LoanBroker.h, and the Supported::Yes / DefaultNo status in features.macro.

How does the protocol handle liquidations and price stability?

Educated guess (mostly application-level, not protocol-enforced). The XRPL core protocol has no built-in liquidation engine or price-stability mechanism the way a monolithic lending smart contract might. What the protocol does provide are primitives that applications compose into those behaviours:

  • Price inputs come from ltORACLE objects, which carry a sfPriceDataSeries and a sfLastUpdateTime but no protocol-enforced max-age — staleness policy is entirely the consumer's responsibility. Aggregation across providers is exposed via the get_aggregate_price RPC.
  • AMM spot price is manipulable within a single ledger, so any liquidation trigger reading an AMM mid-price directly is unsafe; robust designs read an oracle (or a TWAP) instead.
  • Liquidation execution, when the lending amendments activate, is expected to be driven by the loan/broker logic (comparing collateral value from an oracle against loan terms and seizing/selling collateral), not by a generic protocol liquidation path. The exact on-ledger enforcement lives in the LendingProtocol transactors, which are not yet active on Mainnet.
  • "Price stability" for stablecoins is handled by issuers (ch02) off-ledger — reserves, redemption, TransferRate, freeze/clawback — not by any ledger-level peg mechanism.

The honest summary: the ledger supplies oracles, atomic settlement, and the AMM/DEX/vault primitives; liquidation and peg maintenance are assembled from those pieces at the application layer.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: The XRPL DEX is a protocol-level central limit order book (CLOB) — not a smart contract, not an application layer. Every offer placed via OfferCreate competes for liquidity in the same book that the pathfinding engine uses for cross-currency payments. Understanding the offer lifecycle and crossing rules is essential for any application that places orders, routes payments, or needs predictable execution.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Think of the XRPL DEX as a ledger-enforced exchange with three properties:

  1. Atomic crossing — when you place an offer, it immediately crosses any existing counter-offers at the same or better price. No two-step settlement.
  2. Auto-bridging — the engine can route XRP→IOU or IOU→IOU through an intermediate XRP step automatically, without requiring a direct IOU/IOU pair.
  3. Time-priority within price — at the same price level, earlier offers execute first (FIFO within each ledger close).

docs.title: Offer lifecycle
docs.text:
OfferCreate submitted
     │
     ▼ preflight checks (tem*)
     │
     ▼ try to cross existing counter-offers (best price first)
     │    ├── fully filled → offer consumed, deleted
     │    ├── partially filled → remainder placed in order book
     │    └── no match → full offer placed (unless fill-or-kill/immediate-or-cancel)
     │
     ▼ offer placed in order book as RippleState/Offer ledger object
          → expires when ledger index > Expiration field (if set)
          → auto-deleted when fully consumed or when another offer crosses it

Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/OfferCreate.cpp

docs.title: Key offer flags
docs.text:
Flag Hex Effect tfPassive 0x00010000 Does not consume offers at the same price on placement tfImmediateOrCancel 0x00020000 Fills as much as possible, cancels the rest tfFillOrKill 0x00040000 Fills completely or fails entirely (tecKILLED) tfSell 0x00080000 Sell exactly TakerGets, accept any TakerPays ≥ market

Source: rippled/include/xrpl/protocol/TxFlags.h

docs.title: Auto-bridging
docs.text:
When trading IOU-A → IOU-B, the engine automatically checks if a two-hop route through XRP (IOU-A→XRP→IOU-B) is cheaper than the direct pair. This reduces the combinatorial explosion of required trust-line pairs and makes XRP the universal liquidity backbone of the DEX.

Conditions for auto-bridging: - One asset must be XRP - OR the direct pair must have less liquidity than the XRP-bridged route

docs.title: Place and partially fill a limit order
docs.text:
1. Alice places OfferCreate: TakerGets = 100 USD, TakerPays = 50 XRP (asking 2 USD per XRP, willing to sell XRP).
  2. Ledger checks existing offers: Bob has TakerGets = 30 XRP, TakerPays = 60 USD (offering 30 XRP for 60 USD = 2 USD/XRP — price matches).
  3. Alice's offer crosses Bob's: 30 XRP trades for 60 USD. Bob's offer is deleted.
  4. Alice's remainder (70 USD, wanting 35 XRP) is placed in the order book.
  5. Result: Alice holds 60 more USD, 30 fewer XRP. Bob holds 30 more XRP, 60 fewer USD.

docs.title: Fill-or-Kill rejection
docs.text:
1. Alice submits OfferCreate with tfFillOrKill for 100 USD.
  2. Only 70 USD of counter-offers exist at the target price.
  3. Engine returns tecKILLED — no state changes, fee charged, sequence advanced.

Source: fixFillOrKill amendment, activated 2024-04-11. rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/OfferCreate.cpp

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Using the Testnet faucet at https://xrpl.org/resources/dev-tools/xrp-faucets:

  1. Place a limit offer with tfPassive for XRP→USD. Then submit a crossing offer and observe both offers consumed atomically.
  2. Submit a tfFillOrKill offer with a quantity larger than available liquidity. Confirm tecKILLED is returned and the sequence is advanced.
  3. Set Expiration to a past ledger close time and observe the offer is rejected.
  4. Place 5 open offers and check account_objects — see 5 Offer objects consuming 1 XRP of your reserve.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Offer sniping: Offers are visible on-ledger. Competing participants can front-run large orders by placing passive offers ahead of yours. Use tfPassive + Expiration for limit orders where timing matters.
  • Stale offers: Offers with no Expiration stay in the book indefinitely. Old offers at stale prices accumulate and consume your reserve (0.2 XRP each). Always set Expiration or cancel stale offers explicitly.
  • Auto-bridge price manipulation: If you are an AMM LP, large DEX auto-bridge flows can affect your AMM pool's balance. Monitor for correlated DEX activity.
  • tfFillOrKill double-cost: tecKILLED charges a fee and advances the sequence even on failure. Account for this in fee budgeting.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting reserve cost. Each outstanding offer object costs 0.2 XRP. An account with 100 open offers needs 20+ XRP locked.
  • Not checking for crossing on tfPassive. Passive offers won't consume existing offers at the same price, but they will be consumed by subsequent offers. They are not "hidden."
  • Ignoring Expiration. An offer expiring in the past is immediately invalid on entry, not silently accepted. Use the current ledger's close time as the floor.
  • Conflating DEX and AMM routing. A Payment may route through both DEX offers and AMM pools. OfferCreate only interacts with the CLOB, not AMM pools.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Set Expiration on all offers that are price-sensitive.
  • [ ] Monitor open offer count per account; auto-cancel stale offers.
  • [ ] Size XRP balance to cover base reserve + (max_open_offers × 0.2 XRP).
  • [ ] Test tfFillOrKill rejection paths — ensure your retry logic handles tecKILLED.
  • [ ] Verify auto-bridging behavior on Testnet for IOU↔IOU pairs you support.
  • [ ] Subscribe to transaction stream on the account to detect offer deletions.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Decentralized Exchange
  • OfferCreate transaction
  • rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/OfferCreate.cpp
  • rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/OfferCancel.cpp
  • fixFillOrKill amendment activated 2024-04-11

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Auto-bridging is silent. The engine routes through XRP automatically without any transaction-level flag. You may receive more or less of an asset than expected if the XRP bridge is cheaper — always use SendMax on payments.
  • Offers are objects, not events. A placed offer consumes reserve and persists until consumed, expired, or cancelled. This changes the economics of high-frequency market making vs. traditional exchanges.
  • tfSell changes the semantics. Without it, you specify exactly what you want to pay and receive. With tfSell, you specify exactly what you give up — the engine maximizes what you receive.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• What is the practical throughput of the DEX (orders per second per ledger close) before crossing overhead impacts ledger close time? The engine processes crossing serially within a transaction.
  • How does the engine choose between DEX and AMM routing when both provide the same effective price? Source: pathfinding in rippled/src/libxrpl/app/paths/.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: XRPL price oracles are on-ledger objects that aggregate off-chain price feeds into a canonical source a smart-contract-equivalent (or any RPC consumer) can query. Unlike off-chain oracle services, an on-ledger oracle is immutable per ledger close, auditable by anyone, and subject to XRPL's finality guarantees. Understanding staleness, aggregation methodology, and trust assumptions is critical before using oracle prices in any financial logic.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
An oracle is a PriceOracle ledger object owned by an account (the oracle provider). Multiple oracle objects for the same asset pair exist independently; consumers use the get_aggregate_price RPC to aggregate across a set of trusted oracles using median, trimmed-mean, or other methods.

Key insight: the XRPL oracle is a data availability layer, not a trust layer. The ledger enforces that the data came from the account that signed the PriceOracleSet transaction, but it does not validate that the price is correct. Consumers must apply their own trust model (e.g., trust N of M known providers).

docs.title: PriceOracle ledger object structure
docs.text:
Field Type Description sfProvider STBlob Human-readable provider name (e.g., "Chainlink") sfAssetClass STBlob Asset class tag (e.g., "currency") sfPriceDataSeries STArray Array of {BaseAsset, QuoteAsset, AssetPrice, Scale} sfLastUpdateTime UINT32 Unix timestamp of last update sfExpiration UINT32 Optional; price is stale after this time

AssetPrice is stored as a UINT64 integer; the actual price is AssetPrice × 10^(-Scale). Example: AssetPrice=17500, Scale=2 → 175.00.

Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/oracle/OracleSet.cpp

docs.title: get_aggregate_price RPC
docs.text:
{
  "command": "get_aggregate_price",
  "base_asset": "XRP",
  "quote_asset": { "currency": "USD", "issuer": "<issuer>" },
  "oracles": [
    { "account": "<provider1>", "oracle_document_id": 1 },
    { "account": "<provider2>", "oracle_document_id": 1 }
  ],
  "trim": 20
}

Response includes: - entire_set.mean, entire_set.std_dev, entire_set.size - trimmed_set.mean, trimmed_set.std_dev, trimmed_set.size - time (median LastUpdateTime across oracles)

The trim parameter (0–25) removes the top and bottom trim% of prices before computing the mean — reducing manipulation via outlier submissions.

docs.title: Publish a price feed (provider role)
docs.text:
1. Oracle provider account submits PriceOracleSet: 
    {
  "TransactionType": "OracleSet",
  "Account": "<provider>",
  "OracleDocumentID": 1,
  "Provider": "MyFeed",
  "AssetClass": "currency",
  "PriceDataSeries": [
    { "PriceData": {
        "BaseAsset": "XRP",
        "QuoteAsset": { "currency": "USD", "issuer": "<issuer>" },
        "AssetPrice": 17500,
        "Scale": 2
    }}
  ],
  "LastUpdateTime": <unix_timestamp>
}
  2. Oracle object is created (or updated) on-ledger.
  3. Provider repeats with each new price; the ledger stores only the latest value for each (Account, OracleDocumentID) pair.

docs.title: Consume a price feed (consumer role)
docs.text:
1. Call get_aggregate_price with the set of trusted oracle accounts.
  2. Inspect trimmed_set.mean for the consensus price.
  3. Check time vs current ledger close time — if |time - now| > threshold, treat the price as stale and reject.
  4. Apply your application's business logic with the validated price.

Source: rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/oracle/OracleSet.cpp Activation: PriceOracle amendment, 2024-11-02.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Using the Testnet faucet at https://xrpl.org/resources/dev-tools/xrp-faucets:

  1. Submit a PriceOracleSet with a synthetic XRP/USD price. Then call get_aggregate_price and verify your price appears in the result.
  2. Submit two oracle providers with different prices. Observe how the mean and std_dev are computed. Then set trim=25 and verify the trimmed result.
  3. Delete one oracle with OracleDelete and re-run get_aggregate_price. How does the result change?
  4. Set Expiration to a past timestamp and observe what happens when consumers call get_aggregate_price after expiry.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Staleness is your responsibility. The ledger does not enforce that prices are fresh. The LastUpdateTime field is set by the provider; if the provider stops updating, the price will be stale indefinitely unless Expiration is set.
  • Trust model is off-chain. The ledger validates that the provider signed the transaction, but not that the provider's price is accurate. Evaluate oracle provider reputation, SLA, and dispute history off-chain.
  • Outlier manipulation. A single oracle provider submitting a wildly wrong price can skew the mean. Use trim (e.g., 20–25%) and require a minimum quorum (e.g., oracles.size >= 5) before accepting the aggregate.
  • OracleDelete removes the object. If a provider deletes their oracle object, your get_aggregate_price call will silently include one fewer oracle. Monitor provider count in responses.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Not checking LastUpdateTime. Consumers that trust the ledger's get_aggregate_price result without checking time against the current ledger close time will use stale prices during provider downtime.
  • Using a single oracle. Relying on one provider makes you vulnerable to that provider's errors, downtime, or malicious behavior. Use a minimum of 3.
  • Ignoring Scale. AssetPrice=17500 with Scale=2 is $175.00, not $17500. Always apply the scale factor before comparing prices.
  • Treating oracle price as exact. The aggregate price has a std_dev. High std_dev signals disagreement across providers — widen your slippage tolerance or pause automated execution.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Monitor LastUpdateTime on each oracle; alert if > freshness threshold.
  • [ ] Require a minimum quorum of oracles (e.g., ≥ 3) before executing.
  • [ ] Use trim=20 or higher to reduce outlier impact.
  • [ ] Monitor trimmed_set.size — if it drops below quorum, pause.
  • [ ] Implement circuit-breaker: if std_dev / mean > 5%, reject the aggregate.
  • [ ] Test with PriceOracle amendment on Testnet before Mainnet deployment.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Price Oracles concept
  • OracleSet transaction
  • get_aggregate_price RPC
  • rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/oracle/OracleSet.cpp
  • rippled/src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/oracle/OracleDelete.cpp
  • PriceOracle amendment activated 2024-11-02

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• On-ledger oracles solve the finality problem. Off-chain oracle requests race against ledger closes. An on-ledger oracle price is fixed for the entire ledger close — every transaction in that ledger sees the same price. No race conditions.
  • The provider account IS the oracle's trust anchor. If the provider account is compromised, its price submissions are indistinguishable from legitimate ones. Monitor the provider's signing key health.
  • get_aggregate_price is server-side computation. The aggregation is computed by the node, not consensus. Different nodes may return slightly different results if they have different oracle objects cached. Use a trusted, self-operated node for financial decisions.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Can oracle providers be permissioned? Currently any account can create an oracle object. An application-level allowlist of trusted provider accounts is needed to prevent oracle injection attacks.
  • What is the update frequency limit? PriceOracleSet costs a standard fee and is subject to normal rate limiting. For high-frequency feeds, evaluate whether XRPL on-ledger oracles provide sufficient freshness.
