docs.title: Chapter 4 — Hardening
docs.text: Two complementary disciplines, kept separate because they address different failure modes: account security (key compromise → funds loss) and node operations (software lag, disk exhaustion → availability loss). Added here is the custody integration layer for institutional and exchange-grade signing.

docs.title: Architect's Intent
docs.text:
"We deliberately designed the system so that no single entity — not Ripple, not any validator, not the developers — can unilaterally reverse a transaction or rescue a compromised key. The finality that makes XRPL good for payments is the same finality that makes security non-negotiable." — David Schwartz (JoelKatz)

The original architects made two choices that define the threat model for every XRPL production deployment:

1. No admin override. There is no sudo. There is no "Ripple can help recover your funds" escape hatch. The co-founders deliberately excluded any mechanism that would allow a central party — including themselves — to reverse a validated transaction or unlock a locked account. This was not an oversight; it was the same design decision that makes the ledger trustworthy as a settlement network. A financial counterparty cannot trust a ledger whose history can be rewritten by a company.

2. Amendments are irreversible. When validators reach 80 % supermajority approval and the two-week window closes, a feature activates on every node simultaneously — and there is no rollback. Arthur Britto's transaction-set design and David Schwartz's consensus protocol were built for convergence, not for undecidability. That same convergence property means the network cannot "agree to undo" a change once consensus has been reached.

The practical consequence: security in XRPL is a pre-condition, not a layer you add after launch. Vinnie Falco's NuDB (ledger state storage) and the rippled C++ team's focus on invariant checking (InvariantCheck.h) mean the protocol itself tries to prevent application-layer errors from corrupting consensus state — but they cannot protect an application that misconfigures its own signing authority.

This chapter is where the founders' design philosophy meets your operational responsibility. Every control here — multi-signing, regular keys, amendment monitoring, codec pinning — exists because the protocol's irreversibility demands that you get it right before you go live.

docs.title: Why this chapter matters
docs.text: On the XRPL, almost every catastrophic failure is irreversible. A key lost behind lsfDisableMaster cannot be recovered; an amendment that activates on an unprepared node cannot be rolled back; and a codec mismatch in an HSM can permanently strand funds. Hardening is not a layer added at the end; it is the set of controls that makes the rest of the playbook safe to run in production.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Section Scope Security Master key disablement, multi-signing quorums, regular keys, and operational account topologies. Operations Amendment monitoring, online deletion, health checks, and node-level infrastructure hardening. Custody 3-tier signing stacks, server_definitions codec pinning, and the offline transaction construction workflow.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
1. Security — Start by securing the account itself. Learn why and how to disable master keys and structure quorums.
  2. Operations — Move to the node level. Learn how to keep the infrastructure healthy and responsive to network governance (amendments).
  3. Custody — The bridge between security policy and operational execution. Essential for anyone building custom signing infrastructure or HSM integrations.

docs.title: What you should be able to do after this chapter
docs.text:
• Secure an issuer or treasury account such that no single key compromise is catastrophic.
  • Configure xrpld for production with appropriate online-deletion and read-path redundancy.
  • Implement a codec-pinned signing flow that detects amendment-driven changes before they cause transaction failures.
  • Conduct a key ceremony and maintain an auditable trail of signing authority.
  • Monitor the network for pending amendments and execute node upgrades before activation.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text:
On the XRPL there is no undo. A transaction that reaches a validated ledger is final. For custodians — exchanges, institutional wallets, treasury systems — this means correctness must be guaranteed before a key signs anything.

The core risk is codec drift: an offline signer (HSM, vault, air-gapped machine) that serializes a transaction using an outdated field definition produces bytes the network cannot verify. The signature will fail or, in a worse scenario, validate a different byte string than intended.

The server_definitions RPC method is the protocol-level solution. It exposes the complete serialization codec as a single, hash-pinned JSON payload. Matching that hash across environments proves the codec is byte-identical and offline signing is safe.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Two environments. One codec. The definitions_hash is the handshake.

┌─────────────────────────────┐       ┌───────────────────────────────┐
│  ONLINE ENVIRONMENT         │       │  AIR-GAPPED / HSM             │
│                             │       │                               │
│  Transaction builder        │──────▶│  Cached server_definitions    │
│  (constructs JSON fields)   │ hash  │  (field order, type codes,    │
│                             │ check │   signing-field flags)        │
│  server_definitions check   │       │                               │
│  (verifies hash matches)    │       │  Private key                  │
│                             │       │  (never leaves this env)      │
└─────────────────────────────┘       └───────────────────────────────┘
          │                                         │
          │         signed tx_blob                  │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                    submit RPC
                          │
                    xrpld node

If the hashes match: the offline signer will produce byte-identical serialization to what the network expects. Sign.

If the hashes diverge: an amendment has shipped new field definitions. Block signing. Alert operator. Refresh the cached codec before continuing.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
3-tier signing stack:

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Transaction Builder<br/>(online)
    participant G as Codec Gate<br/>(online boundary)
    participant S as Offline Signer<br/>(air-gapped / HSM)
    participant N as XRPL Node

    B->>N: server_definitions
    N-->>B: {FIELDS, TYPES, hash}
    B->>B: Build unsigned tx JSON<br/>(fee, sequence, LastLedgerSeq)

    B->>G: Forward tx JSON + expected hash
    G->>N: server_definitions (verify)
    N-->>G: {hash}

    alt Hash matches
        G->>S: tx JSON + cached definitions
        S->>S: Serialize with cached codec<br/>Sign → tx_blob
        S-->>G: tx_blob
        G->>N: submit tx_blob
        N-->>G: preliminary result
    else Hash mismatch
        G->>G: HALT — amendment detected<br/>Alert operator<br/>Refresh codec before retry
    end
  1. Transaction builder (online) — constructs the transaction JSON from business logic (amount, destination, fee from server_info, sequence from account_info, LastLedgerSequence from current ledger).
  2. Codec gate (online, boundary layer) — calls server_definitions with the cached hash. Match → forward to signer. Mismatch → halt and alert.
  3. Offline signer (air-gapped / HSM) — receives the transaction JSON, serializes using cached definitions, signs the hash, returns tx_blob.

The private key never enters tier 1. The definitions JSON is not secret — it is publicly derivable from any xrpld node of the same version.

docs.title: server_definitions deep dive
docs.text: Handler: rippled/src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/server_info/ServerDefinitions.cpp Role: USER (no admin credentials required)

docs.title: Response structure
docs.text: Section Contents TYPES SerializedTypeID → name mapping (UInt32, Amount, AccountID, Blob, STObject, STArray, …) FIELDS Array of [name, {nth, isVLEncoded, isSerialized, isSigningField, type}] — the binary codec backbone TRANSACTION_TYPES Payment: 0, EscrowCreate: 1, AMMCreate: 80, … TRANSACTION_FORMATS Per-type required/optional field lists (the template for each tx) LEDGER_ENTRY_TYPES ltACCOUNT_ROOT, ltRIPPLE_STATE, ltAMM, ltMPTOKEN, … LEDGER_ENTRY_FORMATS Per-type required/optional field lists for ledger objects TRANSACTION_RESULTS Full TER taxonomy (tesSUCCESS: 0, tecUNFUNDED_PAYMENT: 101, …) TRANSACTION_FLAGS Per-type flag bitmasks (tfPartialPayment: 0x00020000, …) LEDGER_ENTRY_FLAGS Per-type ledger state flag bitmasks (lsfDisableMaster, …) ACCOUNT_SET_FLAGS asf* integer values for AccountSet operations hash SHA512Half(canonical_json_of_all_sections_above) — the codec fingerprint

docs.title: Hash computation (source-verified)
docs.text:
// ServerDefinitions.cpp:361–366
std::string const out = json::FastWriter().write(defs_);
defsHash_ = xrpl::sha512Half(xrpl::Slice{out.data(), out.size()});
defs_[jss::hash] = to_string(defsHash_);

The hash is computed once at server startup from the canonical JSON serialization of all sections. It is stable for the lifetime of the process and changes only when the xrpld version ships a new codec (typically via amendment activation).

docs.title: Bandwidth optimization
docs.text:
The handler accepts an optional hash parameter:

{ "command": "server_definitions", "hash": "<your-cached-hash>" }
  • Hash matches → response is { "hash": "<hash>" } only (~60 bytes). Client already has the current codec; no re-download needed.
  • Hash missing or mismatch → full response (~100 KB JSON).

Use this in the codec gate on every signing session: cheap confirmation that the codec has not changed, with automatic full refresh on divergence.

docs.title: Setup (once per xrpld version)
docs.text:
1. Call server_definitions (no hash param)
2. Receive full codec JSON
3. Compute: expected_hash = SHA512Half(canonical_json)
4. Assert: expected_hash == response.hash  ← verify no MITM/truncation
5. Store: (codec_json, hash) → HSM firmware / signing library config
6. Tag: firmware_version = xrpld_version_string

docs.title: Per-session codec gate (online, before each signing batch)
docs.text:
1. Call server_definitions with { hash: cached_hash }
2. If response contains only "hash" field:
     → codec unchanged; proceed to signing
3. If response contains full definitions:
     → hash changed (amendment activated)
     → HALT: do not sign with stale codec
     → ALERT: operator must review new definitions and upgrade signing env
     → After upgrade: repeat Setup step

docs.title: Signing (offline / HSM)
docs.text:
1. Receive transaction JSON from online builder
2. Validate all fields exist in cached TRANSACTION_FORMATS for this tx type
3. Sort fields by fieldCode = (type_id << 16) | field_index
4. Exclude fields where isSigningField = false (TxnSignature, Signers array)
5. Serialize each field per its type and isVLEncoded flag
6. Hash: signing_hash = SHA512Half(0x53545800 || serialized_bytes)
   (prefix 0x53545800 = "STX\0" — the transaction signing prefix)
7. Sign signing_hash with private key (RFC 6979 deterministic for secp256k1)
8. Encode signature as DER; enforce low-S (canonical signature)
9. Insert TxnSignature into tx, re-serialize full blob (now including sig field)
10. Return tx_blob (hex)

Source refs: - Field metadata: FIELDS section of server_definitions - Signing prefix: rippled/include/xrpl/protocol/HashPrefix.h (transactionID) - Canonical low-S: rippled/src/libxrpl/protocol/SecretKey.cpp

docs.title: Amendment lifecycle for custody
docs.text:
When an amendment activates, xrpld may add or reorder fields in the codec. The server_definitions hash changes at that moment.

Risk without pinning: An HSM running old definitions serializes a transaction without a new required field (or with it in the wrong position). The live network deserializes different bytes than the HSM hashed → signature verification fails → transaction rejected with temINVALID.

Safe upgrade path:

1. Monitor: amendment reaches 80% support (alert from operations runbook)
2. Pre-upgrade: fetch new server_definitions from a Testnet/Devnet node
   running the new version → test signing against it
3. Activation: amendment goes live on Mainnet (hash changes on live nodes)
4. Codec gate detects mismatch → signing halted automatically
5. Deploy: update HSM firmware / signing library with new definitions
6. Resume: codec gate confirms new hash → signing resumes

Testnet typically activates amendments before Mainnet. Use it to rehearse the codec upgrade before the Mainnet hash changes.

See also: Operations → Amendment monitoring.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Using the Testnet faucet at https://xrpl.org/resources/dev-tools/xrp-faucets:

  1. Run examples/05-offline-signing/ — trace each tier. What does the server_definitions hash look like? How long is it (bytes)?
  2. Deliberately corrupt the transaction blob before submission (flip one hex character). What error does the node return? Is it a tem* or something else?
  3. Simulate a codec mismatch by hardcoding a wrong pinnedHash in the offline-sign script. Does the gate correctly refuse to sign?
  4. Compare server_definitions hashes between two different Testnet nodes. Are they identical? What does it mean if they differ?
  5. Sign a transaction with a future Sequence (current + 10). Submit it. What happens? Can you submit the gap transactions to make it validate later?

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Codec JSON is not a secret. Any xrpld node of the same version returns identical definitions. Protect the private key, not the definitions.
  • Codec injection. If the online codec gate is compromised, an attacker could serve a modified definitions payload that maps fields to different byte positions — causing the HSM to sign bytes the network interprets differently. Mitigate: verify the hash locally against a trusted node and a pinned known-good hash from the signing library vendor.
  • Library pinning. Client libraries (xrpl.js, xrpl-py) bundle their own copy of server_definitions. Pin the library version alongside the xrpld version. A library upgrade may ship updated definitions — verify the embedded hash matches the live network before deploying.
  • Multi-sig and codec. Each co-signer in an M-of-N setup must use the same codec. Staggered HSM upgrades can cause co-signers to produce signatures over different byte representations of the same transaction. Upgrade all co-signers atomically, or collect all signatures before switching any node.
  • Key material isolation. The private key must never transit the online environment. The definitions JSON (not secret) flows online → offline. The tx_blob (signed, public) flows offline → online. Nothing else crosses.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Signing without a codec gate. Using a hard-coded or bundled codec without verifying against the live network. Silent until an amendment ships; then all signatures fail.
  • Comparing library version instead of hash. A library patch release can ship updated definitions. Always compare hashes, not version strings.
  • Forgetting the signing prefix. The bytes signed are SHA512Half(0x53545800 || serialized_tx), not SHA512Half(serialized_tx). Signing the wrong preimage produces a valid-looking but unverifiable signature.
  • Including TxnSignature in the signing payload. isSigningField = false for TxnSignature. Including it produces a circular dependency. The field is inserted after signing, not before.
  • Staggered co-signer upgrades. In multi-sig setups, upgrading one HSM before others causes codec mismatch between co-signers. Signatures over different byte representations do not combine — the transaction is rejected.
  • Not testing on Devnet/Testnet first. Amendments activate on Testnet before Mainnet. The codec upgrade drill should always run on Testnet first.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] server_definitions hash verified against live node before every signing session; mismatch halts signing and pages on-call.
  • [ ] Cached definitions stored with the xrpld version tag they were fetched from.
  • [ ] Signing library (xrpl.js / xrpl-py) version pinned; embedded definitions hash confirmed to match live network hash.
  • [ ] Amendment monitoring alert fires when any pending amendment reaches ≥ 70% support for one week (gives one week before activation).
  • [ ] Codec upgrade runbook written and rehearsed on Devnet/Testnet.
  • [ ] Multi-sig co-signers have a coordinated upgrade plan; no staggered HSM firmware deployments across a signing quorum.
  • [ ] Signing prefix (0x53545800) and low-S enforcement verified in signing library test suite.
  • [ ] TxnSignature and Signers excluded from signing payload (confirmed via isSigningField = false in definitions).
  • [ ] Submitted tx_blob round-tripped: decode and compare field-by-field against original transaction JSON before broadcasting.
  • [ ] Key material never transits the online environment; only tx_blob (public) crosses the boundary from offline to online.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• The hash is the handshake, not the payload. The definitions JSON is large (~100 KB) but changes rarely. The hash check is cheap (one RPC, tiny response when cached). Build the codec gate around the hash check, not a full re-download every session.
  • isSigningField is the serialization boundary between construction and signing. Understanding which fields are excluded (signature, multi-sig array) clarifies why offline signers need the full field metadata, not just the field names.
  • Testnet is the amendment rehearsal environment. The two-week majority window on Mainnet almost always follows an earlier Testnet activation. The codec upgrade drill should be a standard part of the Testnet runbook, not an emergency response to Mainnet activation.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Will a future server_info response embed the definitions_hash inline, eliminating the need for a separate server_definitions round-trip in the codec gate?
  • How should a custody system handle an xrpld node that is running a version ahead of the HSM's pinned codec (e.g., a node upgraded before the amendment activated, serving updated definitions before the network hash changes)?

← Back to Chapter 4 — Hardening

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: Account security keeps your keys safe; node operations keep your service running. An xrpld node that falls behind the protocol, runs out of disk, or is blindsided by an amendment activation becomes an availability risk that no amount of key management can fix. Production systems need both disciplines.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Think of a running xrpld node as a protocol participant that must satisfy three invariants simultaneously:

  1. Software currency — the node understands every amendment the network has activated. A node that doesn't is amendment-blocked and stops processing.
  2. Storage bound — ledger and transaction history grows without limit unless online deletion is configured. Unbounded growth ends in a forced outage.
  3. Read-path redundancy — a single node is a single point of failure. Any application that trusts one node exclusively inherits its availability budget.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Amendment lifecycle. A ledger-rule change is proposed by validators and tracked in-ledger via pseudo-transactions. It activates only after ≥ 80% validator approval sustained for two consecutive weeks. Activation is irreversible — there is no disable/rollback path. A server that does not understand an enabled amendment cannot operate on that ledger: it becomes amendment-blocked and halts validation.
  • SHAMapStore / online delete. xrpld stores ledger objects and transaction history in a key-value store (NuDB or RocksDB). Without pruning, this grows indefinitely. The online-delete mechanism uses two rotating databases (writable
  • recent-archival); on each rotation the older archive is dropped atomically. Configured in rippled.cfg under [node_db]:
  • online_delete — number of ledgers between deletion cycles.
  • advisory_delete — if 1, deletion only runs when triggered via the can_delete RPC; useful for coordinating pruning across a cluster.
  • Node topology. Production read paths should use at least two nodes behind a load balancer or with automatic failover. Validator nodes (if any) should be peered through a stock (non-validator) relay node to avoid exposing the validator IP.

docs.title: Surviving an amendment activation
docs.text:
The failure mode this runbook prevents: an amendment your xrpld build does not understand reaches its activation threshold, the network enables it, and your node becomes amendment-blocked and stops processing. Because activation is irreversible, the only remedy is to upgrade before the deadline.

  1. Monitor the vote. Poll the feature RPC on a node you operate. With no feature parameter it returns the full amendment table under features; each amendment the network has seen reach majority carries a majority field — a timestamp of when it first held majority. That timestamp plus the two-week window (kDefaultAmendmentMajorityTime = weeks{2}) is the earliest possible activation time. Alert when any amendment your current build does not support gains a majority timestamp.
  2. Confirm you don't support it. An amendment with a majority timestamp that is not in your build's supported set is the one that will block you. Cross-check the amendment ID against your xrpld version's release notes.
  3. Upgrade before the deadline. Install the xrpld release that supports the pending amendment, on Testnet first, then on each production node. You have until majority + 2 weeks — but the majority can be lost and regained, which resets the clock, so treat the first majority timestamp as the hard deadline and upgrade well ahead of it.
  4. Verify not amendment-blocked. After upgrading, call server_info. A healthy node omits the amendment_blocked field entirely; the node only sets amendment_blocked: true when it is actually blocked. Also confirm complete_ledgers is advancing and the node is full/proposing as expected. Only then consider the upgrade complete.

Why timing is the whole game: the 80% threshold (kAmendmentMajorityCalcThreshold = 80/100) and the two-week hold are the only warning you get, and there is no rollback once an amendment enables. A node that misses the window returns stale validated data silently until it is upgraded — so the monitoring in step 1 is not optional instrumentation, it is the control that keeps the service available.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• An amendment-blocked node returns stale ledger data silently; downstream services may not detect the staleness until reconciliation fails.
  • Online delete with advisory_delete = 1 requires an operator-triggered RPC; forgetting to trigger it means the older archive is never pruned — verify the delete cycle is automated or monitored.
  • Exposing a validator's public IP directly allows targeted DoS; relay through a stock node and keep the validator's peer list private.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running a stale xrpld and ignoring amendment votes. An amendment that reaches its two-week threshold will activate and amendment-block the node, with no warning beyond the vote tracking data.
  • Disabling online delete (or leaving it unconfigured). Disk fills silently until the node halts and the service goes dark.
  • Depending on a single self-hosted node without failover. Any planned or unplanned restart takes the dependent application offline with it.
  • Not testing the upgrade path on Testnet first. xrpld upgrades that coincide with amendment activations can have ordering requirements; validate on Testnet before production.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] xrpld version is current; subscribe to release notifications.
  • [ ] Amendment voting status is monitored; alert fires ≥ 3 days before any amendment reaches its two-week activation threshold.
  • [ ] Online delete (online_delete) is configured in [node_db]; if advisory_delete = 1, the RPC trigger is automated and monitored.
  • [ ] Disk usage alerting is active with headroom ≥ 2× one deletion cycle.
  • [ ] At least two nodes are in the application read path with automatic failover; no single node is a hard dependency.
  • [ ] Validator (if any) is peered only through stock relay nodes; validator IP is not publicly exposed.
  • [ ] xrpld upgrade procedure is documented and has been tested on Testnet.
  • [ ] Node restart runbook exists; RTO target is defined and has been drilled.

This is the node-operations baseline for every deployment. It complements the domain checklists in ch01 payments, ch02 issuer-controls / stablecoins / tokenization, and ch03 defi, plus the security checklist.

  • Activation gate (*majorityTime + majorityTime_) <= closeTime and the configurable, 15-minute-minimum majority window — src/xrpld/app/misc/detail/AmendmentTable.cpp, src/xrpld/core/detail/Config.cpp.
  • feature RPC output (per-amendment majority timestamp; full features table) — src/xrpld/rpc/handlers/server_info/Feature.cpp.
  • amendment_blocked signal in server_info (set only when blocked) — src/xrpld/app/misc/NetworkOPs.cpp.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Amendment activation is a deadline, not an event you react to. The only warning is the majority timestamp exposed by the feature RPC plus the two-week hold. Because activation is irreversible and a blocked node fails silently, monitoring the vote is the load-bearing control — everything else in the runbook is downstream of catching the majority early.
  • The two-week window is a default, not a constant. amendmentMajorityTime is configurable (down to a 15-minute floor) and defaults to weeks{2}. On mainnet it is two weeks, but test networks may differ — never hard-code the deadline; read it from the network you are actually operating on.
  • A healthy node says nothing about being blocked. server_info only emits amendment_blocked when the node is blocked; the absence of the field is the success signal. Alerting must treat "field present and true" as the failure, not expect a "false".
  • Storage and amendments are the two silent killers. Both online-delete misconfiguration and a missed amendment fail quietly — the node keeps answering with stale or soon-to-halt state — which is why both belong in the same operational discipline rather than being treated as unrelated concerns.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
How far ahead of the activation deadline should an upgrade be scheduled?

Educated guess (operational best practice, not protocol-enforced): treat the first majority timestamp as the deadline and aim to upgrade within a few days of it, not near the two-week edge. The majority can be lost and regained — which resets the clock — so the true activation time can only slip later, never earlier; upgrading early is therefore always safe. Testing on Testnet first (where the amendment typically activates ahead of mainnet) gives a rehearsal of the exact upgrade before it matters in production.

Can online deletion and a missed amendment interact to cause data loss?

Confirmed against source (mechanics) + educated guess (operational risk): online delete rotates two databases and drops the older archive atomically, so pruning itself is safe. The risk is procedural: an amendment-blocked node that is also still pruning can discard history it will need after the upgrade to resync cleanly. The conservative posture is to pause advisory_delete-driven pruning (stop triggering can_delete) once a node is known to be blocked, until it is upgraded and caught up.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: On the XRPL there is no "undo." A signed transaction that reaches a validated ledger is final — lost keys mean lost funds, and misconfigured accounts can permanently lock assets. Security is not a layer added on top of the design; it is baked into the account and signing architecture from day one.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Think in layers of signing authority:

  1. Master key — unconditional authority over the account. Treat it like a root CA private key: generate it offline, use it once to configure the account, then disable it.
  2. Regular key — a delegated signing key. Rotate without touching the master key. Revoke without losing the account.
  3. Signer list (multi-signing) — M-of-N authorization. Required for any account where a single key compromise must not be catastrophic.

Every operational account should have the master key disabled and use either a regular key, multi-signing, or both.

Key type selection. Choose between secp256k1 (standard) and Ed25519 (modern) based on your hardware/HSM requirements. See Mental Models for the underlying math.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph TD
    MK["Master Key<br/>(generated offline)"]
    RK["Regular Key<br/>(hot / HSM)"]
    SL["Signer List<br/>(multi-sig quorum)"]
    COLD["Cold Account<br/>(issuer / admin)"]
    HOT["Hot Account<br/>(operational)"]
    MON["Monitoring Account<br/>(read-only observer)"]

    MK -->|"disabled after setup<br/>(lsfDisableMaster)"| COLD
    RK -->|"day-to-day signing"| HOT
    SL -->|"multi-sig backup<br/>(SetRegularKey, AccountSet)"| COLD
    COLD -->|"issues IOU, sets flags"| HOT
    MON -->|"subscribe transaction stream"| HOT
    MON -->|"subscribe transaction stream"| COLD
  • Issuing / cold accounts — air-gapped, master key disabled, multi- signing only. Signs the minimum necessary: configuration, issuance, emergency freeze.
  • Hot / operational accounts — regular key or HSM-backed signing; multi-signing for high-value thresholds. Signs day-to-day transactions.
  • Monitoring account — subscribes to the account's transaction stream; triggers alerting and incident response workflows.
  • Key ceremony — documented, auditable procedure for generating and distributing master and signer keys.

Signing environments and codec safety. When an HSM or air-gapped machine signs transactions, it must serialize fields in exactly the same order and encoding the live network expects. Pin the serialization codec using server_definitions and verify the definitions_hash before every signing session — a hash mismatch means an amendment has shipped new field definitions and the offline signer must refresh before proceeding. See Custody for the full workflow.

Node-level hardening (amendments, online delete, topology) is covered in the companion Operations section.

docs.title: Rotating a compromised regular key
docs.text:
This runbook assumes the recommended posture: the account's master key is disabled (lsfDisableMaster) and day-to-day signing uses a regular key, with a signer list as the independent backstop. That backstop is what makes rotation safe — the protocol refuses to strand an account.

  1. Detect. Monitoring (see the account transaction stream in Architecture) flags anomalous activity signed by the current regular key. Treat the regular key as compromised and freeze outbound automation.
  2. Rotate via multi-sign. Because the master key is disabled, you cannot sign with it. Instead, submit a SetRegularKey transaction naming a freshly generated key in sfRegularKey, and authorize it with the signer list (M-of-N), not the compromised key. Two protocol rules matter here:
  3. The new regular key cannot equal the account address itself — SetRegularKey rejects that with temBAD_REGKEY (preflight).
  4. The first SetRegularKey an account submits for itself can be fee-free (the lsfPasswordSpent one-shot), but a multi-signed rotation is a normal fee-bearing transaction — budget the fee.
  5. Verify. Read the AccountRoot back and confirm sfRegularKey is the new key. Send a low-value test transaction signed by the new regular key and confirm it validates; attempt one signed by the old key and confirm it now fails authorization. Only then re-enable automation.
  6. Revoke (implicit) / de-provision. Assigning a new sfRegularKey in step 2 replaces the old one — there is only ever one regular key, so the compromised key is revoked the moment the rotation validates. Destroy the old key material and rotate any secrets that referenced it.

Why the account can never be stranded: if you ever try to remove the regular key (a SetRegularKey with no sfRegularKey field) while the master key is disabled and no signer list exists, the transaction returns tecNO_ALTERNATIVE_KEY — the ledger will not leave an account with no usable signing method. Likewise, disabling the master key in the first place (asfDisableMaster) requires that a regular key or signer list already exist, and must itself be signed by the master key (tecNEED_MASTER_KEY / tecNO_ALTERNATIVE_KEY). Keep the signer list independent of the regular key's infrastructure so a single compromise never takes out both.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• DepositAuth requires the account to explicitly authorize incoming payments; prevents unsolicited asset delivery.
  • DisallowIncoming flags block incoming trust lines, offers, and NFT offers — use on accounts that should not receive unsolicited objects.
  • Tickets allow pre-authorizing transactions at a known sequence; useful for queued multi-party signing workflows.
  • Fee escalation under load can cause legitimate transactions to expire; monitor fee levels and adjust transaction costs dynamically.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Leaving the master key active on operational accounts. A single key compromise yields full account control.
  • Insufficient signer quorum. A 1-of-3 signer list provides less security than it appears if signers share infrastructure.
  • No LastLedgerSequence on signed transactions. Transactions without an expiry can be applied to the ledger long after signing.
  • Hot wallet holds excessive XRP. Minimize funds on hot accounts; sweep regularly to cold storage.
  • No incident response runbook. The ledger is live 24/7; a compromised key at 3 AM requires a practiced response, not improvisation.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Master key disabled on all operational accounts.
  • [ ] Multi-signing configured on issuing and high-value accounts.
  • [ ] Regular key rotation procedure is documented and tested.
  • [ ] DepositAuth enabled on accounts that should not receive unsolicited payments.
  • [ ] All submitted transactions include a valid LastLedgerSequence.
  • [ ] Hot wallet balances are minimized and swept on schedule.
  • [ ] Real-time monitoring and alerting is active on all operational accounts.
  • [ ] Incident response runbook exists, is versioned, and has been drilled.

This is the account-security baseline for every deployment. It complements the domain checklists in ch01 payments, ch02 issuer-controls / stablecoins / tokenization, and ch03 defi, plus the operations checklist.

  • Disable-master guard (asfDisableMaster needs master signature + pre-existing regular key or signer list; tecNEED_MASTER_KEY / tecNO_ALTERNATIVE_KEY) and asfNoFreeze master-key requirement — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/account/AccountSet.cpp.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• The protocol refuses to strand an account. Every path that would leave an account with no usable signing method is blocked: removing the regular key while the master is disabled and no signer list exists returns tecNO_ALTERNATIVE_KEY, and disabling the master key requires an alternative to already be in place. Key rotation is therefore safe by construction — but only if you set up the backstop (regular key and an independent signer list) before you disable the master.
  • Rotation is replacement, not addition. An account has exactly one regular key; assigning a new one via SetRegularKey atomically revokes the old one the moment the transaction validates. There is no window where two regular keys are valid, and no separate "revoke" transaction is needed.
  • Some actions are master-key-only, forever. asfNoFreeze (and disabling the master itself) must be signed by the master key. If you have already disabled the master, you can never set NoFreeze — so irreversible posture decisions have to be made during the initial key ceremony, not retrofitted.
  • The first regular-key set can be free, once. The lsfPasswordSpent one-shot lets a newly funded account self-assign a regular key without a fee, but it arms only once; every subsequent (and every multi-signed) rotation is a normal fee-bearing transaction.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
When should an account use a regular key versus a signer list versus both?

A regular key is a single delegated signer — operationally simple, ideal for automated hot-path signing where one HSM or service holds the key. A signer list is M-of-N — it removes any single point of compromise but adds coordination cost per transaction. The recommended production posture uses both: the signer list is the high-assurance backstop (and the thing that makes disabling the master safe), while the regular key handles routine signing. Crucially, keep their infrastructure independent, so compromising the regular key never also yields a signer-list quorum. Confirmed against source — both are accepted alternatives to the master key in the disable-master guard (AccountSet.cpp) and the SetRegularKey.cpp removal check.

What is the safe ordering of the initial key ceremony?

Educated guess (operational best practice, not protocol-enforced): (1) fund the account; (2) install the signer list (SignerListSet); (3) install the regular key (SetRegularKey); (4) set any master-key-only irreversible flags you need (asfNoFreeze, etc.); (5) last, disable the master key (asfDisableMaster). The protocol enforces the individual dependencies (you cannot disable the master without an alternative, and NoFreeze needs the master), but the sequence that avoids ever being locked out is an application-level discipline.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Operations — Apply the key hierarchy you designed here to a production runbook: amendment monitoring, ledger retention, and node-health checks.
  • Custody — Deep-dive into the signing stack: how offline signers, HSMs, and multi-party approval workflows implement the key hierarchy in practice.
  • Chapter 5 — Reference Architectures — See how this security model integrates into a complete production system.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — Reference Architectures
docs.text:
Prerequisite: all prior chapters.

Shows how the primitives from every prior chapter compose into real production systems. Each architecture covers account topology, transaction flows, failure and recovery paths, reconciliation, and monitoring.

docs.title: Architect's Intent
docs.text:
"The ledger is a platform. The interesting part is what you build on top of it — and whether what you build actually reflects how the ledger works, or just assumes it works like something else you already know." — David Schwartz (JoelKatz)

The original architects did not build the XRPL to be a database, a message queue, or an Ethereum alternative. They built it to be a settlement layer — a shared, neutral record of who owns what and what obligations exist between parties — that any application can read and write to with the same level of trust as any other participant.

That goal shaped a specific composition model:

  • Payments, exchange, and issuance are peers, not layers. A single Payment transaction can move value from USD to EUR across multiple DEX hops and an AMM pool, paying from a trust-line balance, and settle atomically. This is not an application-level composition; it is one operation on the replicated state machine.

  • Account topology replaces contract architecture. On a contract-based chain, security boundaries are enforced by smart-contract logic. On the XRPL, they are enforced by who controls which keys and which accounts. The issuer account, the hot wallet, the cold wallet, the signer list — these are your architecture, not your code.

  • The system boundary is where the complexity lives. Jed McCaleb's exchange vision, Ryan Fugger's credit-network insight, and David Schwartz's deterministic finality all converge on the same problem for production engineers: the XRPL side is often simpler than the off-ledger side. Reconciling on-ledger finality with an off-ledger database, handling fiat- rail delays against atomic on-ledger settlement, and keeping account topologies auditable as systems grow — that is where production systems fail.

The five architectures in this chapter are structured to make those system boundaries explicit, so you encounter them in a controlled environment before encountering them in production.

docs.title: Why this chapter comes last
docs.text: By this point you have the full vocabulary: payment primitives (ch01), value issuance and compliance controls (ch02), DEX/AMM liquidity mechanics (ch03), key management and operational hardening (ch04). The reference architectures make no sense without that context — they are the integration layer, not a shortcut past it.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Section What you will be able to do Reference Architectures Design a complete cross-border payment provider, stablecoin issuer, RWA tokenization platform, exchange/custody integration, or DeFi treasury — with documented failure modes, operational runbooks, and a production-ready checklist.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text: 1. Reference Architectures — work through each of the five architectures in order; they build in complexity from the simplest (cross-border payment) to the most compositional (DeFi treasury).

docs.title: What you should be able to do after this chapter
docs.text:
• Design an account topology for any of the five reference use cases, naming each account's role, signing posture, and reserve requirements.
  • Trace a full transaction flow — from business event through on-ledger primitives to validated finality — for each architecture.
  • Identify the failure modes specific to each architecture and the recovery path for each.
  • Specify a reconciliation loop that keeps off-ledger state consistent with the validated ledger.
  • Apply the codec-pinning (server_definitions) workflow when the architecture includes an offline signer or HSM (see ch04 Custody).

The non-obvious insight this chapter teaches: The hardest problems in XRPL production systems are not protocol problems — they are system boundary problems: reconciling on-ledger finality with off-ledger databases, handling partial failures across fiat rails, and keeping account topologies auditable as systems grow. The reference architectures make these boundaries explicit.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: Individual XRPL primitives are powerful in isolation; their value compounds when composed correctly into a complete system. Reference architectures make the composition explicit — account topologies, data flows, failure modes, and operational runbooks that production systems require. Studying them prevents architects from discovering edge cases in production.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Every XRPL application can be decomposed into three concerns:

  1. Account topology — which accounts exist, what roles they play, and what signing authority each carries.
  2. Transaction flows — the sequence of on-ledger operations that implement a business function, and how they fail and recover.
  3. Off-ledger integration — how the application connects to traditional systems (databases, fiat rails, compliance tools) while keeping the validated ledger as the source of truth.

docs.title: Account topology at a glance
docs.text:
The diagram below shows the canonical separation of concerns that every production XRPL system should express. The exact shape changes per architecture, but the cold/hot/operational split is universal.

graph TD
    subgraph Offline ["🔒 Offline / Air-gapped"]
        Cold["Cold Issuer Account\n(master key only)\nSets policy flags;\nnever signs routine ops"]
    end

    subgraph Online ["🌐 Online / Operational"]
        Hot["Hot / Distribution Account\n(regular key or SignerList)\nDay-to-day sends & authorization"]
        Ops["Operational Account\n(regular key, master disabled)\nSubmits payments;\nuses DestinationTag for routing"]
    end

    subgraph Users ["👥 Counterparties / Customers"]
        Holder["Holder Accounts\n(trust line to issuer)"]
        Sender["External Senders"]
        Recv["Beneficiaries"]
    end

    Cold -- "TrustSet authorize / Clawback\n(signed offline)" --> Holder
    Cold -. "delegates signing\n(RegularKey / SignerList)" .-> Hot
    Hot -- "Payment (issue / redeem)" --> Holder
    Ops -- "cross-currency Payment" --> Recv
    Sender --> Ops

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Five reference architectures follow. Each one names its account topology, the primitives it composes (with the xrpld source that defines them), and a runbook for the operations that matter. Paths are relative to the vendored rippled/ tree; the software is xrpld in prose.

docs.title: 1. Cross-border payment provider
docs.text:
Move value from a sender in one currency to a beneficiary in another, settling on-ledger via cross-currency payments.

Account topology. A funded operational account (day-to-day signing via a regular key, master disabled) submits payments; per-customer routing uses DestinationTag rather than one account per customer.

Primitives. - Cross-currency Payment — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/payment/Payment.cpp. Pathfinding routes across DEX order books and AMM pools (see ch03 DeFi). - tfPartialPayment (0x00020000, include/xrpl/protocol/TxFlags.h:105) — let the delivered amount fall short rather than fail on a thin path; always read the metadata delivered_amount (include/xrpl/protocol/jss.h:216), never the sent Amount. - LastLedgerSequence on every submission for deterministic expiry; retry logic per ch01 Payments.

Runbook. Ingest fiat → construct the cross-currency Payment with a bounded SendMax and a LastLedgerSequence a few ledgers out → submit and poll the validated ledger → on success read delivered_amount for the payout leg → on tecPATH_DRY/tecPATH_PARTIAL alert and re-quote. Reconcile fiat in/out against validated deliveries on a schedule.

docs.title: 2. Stablecoin issuer platform
docs.text:
Issue a fiat-backed IOU with reserve attestation and regulatory controls.

Account topology. A cold issuing account (master key, kept offline) sets issuer policy; a hot distribution account (regular key / signer list) does day-to-day sends. This mirrors ch02 Stablecoins.

Primitives. - Issuer flags via AccountSet — asfRequireAuth, asfDefaultRipple, asfNoFreeze, asfGlobalFreeze, asfAllowTrustLineClawback (include/xrpl/protocol/TxFlags.h; guards in src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/account/AccountSet.cpp). asfRequireAuth and asfAllowTrustLineClawback require zero owner objects first (tecOWNERS, include/xrpl/protocol/TER.h). - TrustSet / RippleState for balances; TransferRate for the transfer fee. - Clawback — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/Clawback.cpp. The sfAmount issuer field is the holder's account, not the issuer — the single most error-prone detail in the whole flow.

Runbook. Ceremony: on the cold account set asfRequireAuth (before any trust lines) and, if required, asfAllowTrustLineClawback and/or asfNoFreeze; disable the master only after a regular key/signer list exists (see ch04 Security). Steady state: authorize holder trust lines → issue from hot account → reconcile on-ledger supply against reserves → freeze/claw back per policy.

docs.title: 3. RWA tokenization platform
docs.text:
Represent a real-world asset as a permissioned token with identity-gated access and a defined lifecycle.

Account topology. An issuer account owns the MPT issuance; a domain owner account owns a permissioned domain that gates who may hold or trade.

Primitives. - MPT lifecycle — MPTokenIssuanceCreate (capability flags tfMPTRequireAuth, tfMPTCanTransfer, tfMPTCanLock, tfMPTCanClawback, tfMPTCanEscrow, tfMPTCanTrade), MPTokenAuthorize (auth handshake; tecNO_AUTH / tecNO_PERMISSION), MPTokenIssuanceSet (lock/unlock; DynamicMPT conditional mutability), MPTokenIssuanceDestroy (tecHAS_OBLIGATIONS while sfOutstandingAmount/sfLockedAmount ≠ 0; tecNO_PERMISSION if not issuer) — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/. See ch02 Tokenization. - Identity primitives — ltDID, ltCREDENTIAL, ltPERMISSIONED_DOMAIN (include/xrpl/protocol/detail/ledger_entries.macro); access is gated by binding the issuance's DomainID (which requires tfMPTRequireAuth), not by putting identity inside the token.

Runbook. Establish issuer identity (DIDSet) → create the permissioned domain listing accepted credentials → issuers/verifiers issue credentials (CredentialCreate → CredentialAccept) → MPTokenIssuanceCreate with DomainID → holders opt in and are authorized → distribute → (secondary trading scoped to the domain) → at maturity redeem to zero, then MPTokenIssuanceDestroy. The ordering is an application pattern; the protocol enforces only the individual gates.

docs.title: 4. Exchange / custody integration
docs.text:
Detect deposits, segregate hot/cold funds, and process withdrawals safely.

Account topology. A deposit account per venue (shared, keyed by DestinationTag), a hot withdrawal account (minimal balance, swept), and a cold reserve account (multi-sig, offline).

Primitives. - asfDepositAuth (include/xrpl/protocol/TxFlags.h:431) and the asfDisallowIncoming* family to constrain who/what can pay an account. - Hot/cold separation via regular keys and signer lists (src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/account/SignerListSet.cpp) — see ch04 Security. - TicketCreate (src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/system/TicketCreate.cpp) to pre-allocate sequence slots for out-of-order / parallel withdrawal signing. Tickets decouple sequence assignment from signing order, which is essential when the cold signer is offline and multiple withdrawals must be queued.

Withdrawal signing flow.

Every withdrawal passes through three stages before broadcast:

1. Transaction builder (online)
   └─ Construct tx JSON: Amount, Destination, DestinationTag, Fee (from
      server_info), Sequence or Ticket, LastLedgerSequence

2. Codec gate (online, boundary)
   └─ Call: server_definitions { hash: <cached_hash> }
      Match  → forward tx JSON to signer
      Mismatch → HALT: amendment shipped, refresh codec before proceeding
      See [ch04 Custody](../../ch04-hardening/custody/README.md#codec-pinning-workflow)

3. Signer (hot key / cold signer-list quorum, offline)
   └─ Serialize fields in fieldCode order using cached server_definitions
   └─ Sign SHA512Half(0x53545800 || serialized_bytes) with private key
   └─ Return signed tx_blob

4. Submit (online)
   └─ submit RPC with tx_blob
   └─ Poll validated ledger for tx hash; credit only on tesSUCCESS/tec in
      validated ledger

Below the withdrawal threshold: hot account signs via regular key (online HSM). Above the threshold: cold account signer-list quorum required (M-of-N, each co-signer runs the same codec gate independently before signing).

Runbook. Credit deposits only after they appear in a validated ledger and match an expected DestinationTag; sweep the hot account to cold on a threshold; sign withdrawals from the hot account (regular key) or, above a limit, require the cold signer-list quorum; reconcile balances against the internal ledger continuously.

docs.title: 5. DeFi-powered treasury
docs.text:
Deploy idle treasury assets into on-ledger liquidity with oracle-driven, rules-based rebalancing.

Account topology. A treasury account (multi-sig) holds positions; automation signs via a scoped regular key with tight monitoring.

Primitives. - AMM — AMMCreate/AMMDeposit/AMMWithdraw/AMMBid/AMMVote (src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/). Invariant sqrt(asset1 * asset2) >= LPTokensBalance (src/libxrpl/ledger/helpers/AMMHelpers.cpp:47). Trading-fee ceiling kTradingFeeThreshold = 1000 (1%) in units of 1/100000 (kAuctionSlotFeeScaleFactor = 100000), auction slot kTotalTimeSlotSecs = 86400 split into kAuctionSlotTimeIntervals = 20, kVoteMaxSlots = 8 (include/xrpl/protocol/AMMCore.h). See ch03 DeFi. - PriceOracle — OracleSet (src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/oracle/OracleSet.cpp) for freshness-checked prices driving rebalancing decisions. - OfferCreate (src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/OfferCreate.cpp) for order-book execution alongside AMM.

Runbook. Read oracle price and check freshness → compute target allocation → rebalance via AMMDeposit/AMMWithdraw or OfferCreate with slippage bounds → monitor LP position for impermanent loss against thresholds → record every action against the validated ledger for audit.

docs.title: End-to-end cross-border payment (USD → EUR)
docs.text:
This traces the cross-border architecture (§1) from a customer's fiat deposit to the beneficiary payout, showing where each on-ledger primitive and each failure path fits.

  1. Fiat deposit (off-ledger). The customer wires USD to the provider's bank. The provider records an internal credit but treats nothing as settled until the on-ledger leg validates.
  2. Construct the payment. Build a cross-currency Payment (src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/payment/Payment.cpp) from the operational account: Destination = the payout account, a DestinationTag identifying the beneficiary, a bounded SendMax in the source asset, the target Amount in the destination asset, and a LastLedgerSequence a few ledgers ahead for deterministic expiry. Set tfPartialPayment (0x00020000, include/xrpl/protocol/TxFlags.h:105) only if a short delivery is acceptable and priced accordingly.
  3. Submit and observe. Pathfinding routes across DEX order books and AMM pools (see ch03 DeFi). Submit, then poll the validated ledger — not the current one — for the transaction result.
  4. Read what was actually delivered. On success, read the metadata field delivered_amount (include/xrpl/protocol/jss.h:216), never the requested Amount. With tfPartialPayment, the two can differ; crediting the requested amount instead of the delivered amount is the classic exploit.
  5. Payout (off-ledger). Release EUR to the beneficiary only after the on-ledger delivery is validated and delivered_amount is confirmed.
  6. Failure paths. tecPATH_DRY / tecPATH_PARTIAL mean liquidity was insufficient — alert, surface a human-readable error, and re-quote rather than blindly retrying. If LastLedgerSequence passes with no result, the transaction expired safely and can be rebuilt at a fresh sequence (idempotent by hash — see ch01 Payments).
  7. Reconcile. On a schedule, reconcile fiat in/out against validated delivered_amount totals; any gap is an alert, not a rounding note.

Why the validated ledger is the pivot: every "settled" decision in this flow hangs on a validated result and the metadata delivered amount. Trusting the submitted amount, the current (unvalidated) ledger, or an off-ledger assumption is where cross-border integrations lose money.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
• Each architecture includes a threat model: which accounts can be compromised, what the blast radius is, and how to recover.
  • Monitoring and alerting must cover both on-ledger events (account activity, balance changes) and off-ledger state (reconciliation gaps, reserve shortfalls).
  • All operational accounts follow the security model in Security.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Missing reconciliation. Treating on-ledger state as always consistent with off-ledger databases without a reconciliation process leads to silent discrepancies that compound over time.
  • No monitoring on operational accounts. The ledger is live 24/7; unmonitored accounts are undefended accounts.
  • Single-account topologies. Combining issuer, hot wallet, and operational roles in one account maximizes blast radius.
  • Untested recovery procedures. Failure recovery paths that have never been executed will fail when they are needed most.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Account topology diagram is documented and reflects live state.
  • [ ] Each account's role, signing authority, and reserve requirements are documented.
  • [ ] Transaction flows include explicit failure handling and retry logic.
  • [ ] Reconciliation runs on a defined schedule with alerting on gaps.
  • [ ] On-ledger monitoring covers all operational accounts.
  • [ ] Recovery procedures are documented and have been drilled.
  • [ ] Off-ledger systems treat the validated ledger as the source of truth.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• XRPL Use Cases
  • Cross-Border Payments

xrpld source referenced in this section (paths relative to the vendored rippled/ tree — the on-disk directory retains the historical name):

  • Cross-currency Payment, tfPartialPayment, delivered_amount — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/payment/Payment.cpp, include/xrpl/protocol/TxFlags.h, include/xrpl/protocol/jss.h.
  • Issuer flags and clawback (sfAmount issuer = holder), tecOWNERS — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/account/AccountSet.cpp, src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/Clawback.cpp, include/xrpl/protocol/TER.h.
  • MPT lifecycle (tecHAS_OBLIGATIONS, tecNO_AUTH, tecNO_PERMISSION) and identity objects (ltDID, ltCREDENTIAL, ltPERMISSIONED_DOMAIN) — src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/, include/xrpl/protocol/detail/ledger_entries.macro.
  • Deposit/withdrawal controls and tickets — asfDepositAuth (include/xrpl/protocol/TxFlags.h), src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/system/TicketCreate.cpp, src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/account/SignerListSet.cpp.
  • AMM invariant and constants, oracle, offers — src/libxrpl/ledger/helpers/AMMHelpers.cpp, include/xrpl/protocol/AMMCore.h, src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/oracle/OracleSet.cpp, src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/dex/.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Reference architectures are compositions, not new primitives. Every one of the five reuses transactors and flags documented in ch01–ch04; the value is in the account topology and ordering, not in any single on-ledger feature.
  • The validated ledger is the only source of truth, in all five. Deposit crediting, payout release, reserve reconciliation, and treasury audit all hang on a validated result and, for payments, the metadata delivered_amount. The recurring failure mode is trusting a submitted amount or an unvalidated ledger.
  • Account topology is a security decision. Splitting issuer/hot/cold and cold/hot/deposit roles bounds blast radius; the protocol's disable-master and signer-list guards (ch04) are what make those splits safe to operate.
  • The protocol enforces gates, not sequences. Order-of-operations in the RWA and stablecoin runbooks (identity → domain → issuance, or ceremony ordering) is an application-level discipline; the ledger enforces only the individual preconditions (tecOWNERS, tecNO_ALTERNATIVE_KEY, tecHAS_OBLIGATIONS).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
When should a design use separate accounts versus DestinationTags on one account?

Educated guess (operational trade-off, not protocol-enforced): use a single account with DestinationTags when the sub-entities share a trust and compliance boundary (e.g. many customers of one custodian) — it minimizes reserve cost and key management. Use separate accounts when roles differ in signing authority or blast radius (issuer vs. hot vs. cold), where the point is isolation, not accounting. The protocol supports both; the deciding factor is who must be able to sign and what a compromise would cost.

How much of a production system's correctness can the ledger guarantee?

Confirmed against source (on-ledger half) + educated guess (off-ledger half): the ledger guarantees the on-ledger invariants each transactor enforces — authorization, obligations, key availability, AMM balance. It cannot guarantee that off-ledger fiat, reserves, or databases agree with on-ledger state; that is what reconciliation exists to catch. Every one of the five architectures therefore pairs an on-ledger flow with an off-ledger reconciliation loop, and the boundary between them is where production bugs concentrate.

← Back to Chapter 5 — Reference Architectures

docs.title: Chapter 6 — Features and Amendments
docs.text:
Every capability on the XRP Ledger — from payment channels to NFTs, AMM pools to confidential transfers — arrives as an amendment. Understanding the amendment pipeline tells you what the network can do today, what is coming next, and what operational risk each change poses to your system.

Read this chapter after Chapter 4 (Hardening → Operations). The amendment lifecycle mechanics are covered there; this chapter focuses on the features themselves.

docs.title: Architect's Intent
docs.text:
"The amendment system was designed to allow the network to evolve without disruptive hard forks. The validators themselves — not any single company — decide when a change goes live. That's the whole point." — David Schwartz (JoelKatz), paraphrased from the original amendment RFC

When Schwartz, McCaleb, and Britto shipped rippled 0.31.0 in 2016, they faced a problem every decentralized network eventually hits: how do you change the rules without breaking the network or trusting a central authority to call the shot?

Bitcoin's answer at the time was a contentious hard fork. The XRPL's answer was to make protocol evolution a first-class, on-ledger process:

  • Validators vote by embedding amendment preferences in the validations they already sign every ledger — no separate election, no out-of-band coordination.
  • A supermajority (≥ 80%) must hold for two consecutive weeks before anything activates — a deliberate social buffer that gives every operator time to upgrade.
  • Activation is irreversible — the ledger's own append-only history enforces it. A flawed amendment is not "turned off"; it is superseded by a corrected successor (exactly what happened with Batch → BatchV1_1 and PermissionDelegation → PermissionDelegationV1_1).
  • A node that cannot process an enabled amendment fails loud (visible as amendment_blocked in server_info) rather than silently forking.

The design philosophy is the same one that runs through the whole ledger: make illegal states unrepresentable or immediately detectable. A stale node fails safe. An unactivated feature returns temDISABLED before it can claim a fee. A flawed amendment is retired, not deleted. Every mechanism favors a loud halt over a silent inconsistency.

This chapter is the operational expression of that philosophy: know exactly what the network supports, what it is about to support, and what to do when the answer changes.

docs.title: Why this chapter comes before Chapter 5
docs.text: Reference architectures (ch05) must be grounded in what the network actually supports today vs. what is coming. Building an architecture on an unactivated amendment is a design risk. This chapter provides the status reference that ch05 depends on.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Section Scope Feature Reference Version compatibility matrix (xrpld 1.10–3.3); active, voting, and in-development features grouped by domain; use-case guide for each feature group; obsolete amendment notes.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
1. Start here — read the chapter overview for the amendment lifecycle mental model (why features are permanent once activated, what Supported::No means, what VoteBehavior::DefaultNo implies for your validator).
  2. Feature Reference — use as a reference when building or planning: check whether the feature you need is active, voting, or still in development, and which minimum xrpld version to target.
  3. Cross-reference Operations — for the amendment monitoring runbook: how to detect upcoming activations and upgrade your node before becoming amendment-blocked.

⚠️ Devnet ≠ Mainnet. Devnet runs with many amendments force-enabled via feature force_enable in the rippled.cfg. Code that works on Devnet may silently rely on amendments that are still voting (or not yet votable) on Mainnet. Always verify feature status against server_info on the target network before shipping. A feature active on Devnet that returns temDISABLED on Mainnet will cause silent, hard-to-debug submission failures in production.

docs.title: What you should be able to do after this chapter
docs.text:
• State the current mainnet status of any feature covered in this chapter (active, voting, in-development, or obsolete).
  • Identify the minimum xrpld version required to use a given feature in your application.
  • Explain why Batch and PermissionDelegation are listed as obsolete and which amendments replaced them.
  • Select the correct amendment set to enable on a private test network for a specific use case.
  • Build an upgrade and activation monitoring plan for features currently open for voting that your application depends on.

← Back to Playbook Overview

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text: XRPL features are permanent once activated — no rollback, no opt-out. A transaction type or ledger entry type introduced by an unactivated amendment returns temDISABLED. An architecture built on an amendment that later stalls in voting will not ship on schedule. This reference gives you the current activation status, minimum xrpld version, and the practical use cases for every significant feature through xrpld 3.3.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
The amendment lifecycle has four stages, derived from the source:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> InDevelopment : merged into xrpld\n(Supported::No)

    InDevelopment --> OpenForVoting : Supported::Yes\n(API frozen; validators can vote)

    OpenForVoting --> MajorityHeld : ≥ 80% of UNL\nvotes yes on a flag ledger\n(DefaultNo: opt-in)\n(DefaultYes: auto-voted)

    MajorityHeld --> Active : majority held\ncontinuously for 2 weeks →\nEnableAmendment pseudo-tx\nat next flag ledger

    MajorityHeld --> OpenForVoting : majority lost\nbefore 2 weeks\n(clock resets)

    Active --> Retired : ≥ 2 years active →\ngating code removed\nfrom xrpld source\n(still fully live on Mainnet)

    OpenForVoting --> Obsolete : superseded by a\ncorrected amendment\n(e.g. Batch → BatchV1_1)

    note right of InDevelopment
        temDISABLED on all networks.
        Only on private devchains
        with force_enable.
    end note

    note right of Active
        Permanent. Irreversible.
        Cannot be turned off.
    end note

    note right of Retired
        "Retired" ≠ deactivated.
        Still enforced on Mainnet;
        the gating toggle was deleted.
    end note

"Retired" does not mean deactivated — it means the opposite. A retired amendment is still permanently enabled on Mainnet. It has simply been active long enough (≥ 2 years) that it is now a mandatory part of the protocol, so xrpld deleted the old "if this amendment is enabled" toggle code and moved the identifier to its deprecated XRPL_RETIRE_FEATURE list in features.macro. A retired amendment can never be turned off. Retirement is a source-code cleanup milestone, not a deactivation. This is why the tables below show entries like Escrow as ✅ Active (retired): fully live on Mainnet, and so entrenched that its gating code no longer exists.

Obsolete = supported but permanently flagged as never-to-be-voted-for. This happens when an amendment is replaced by a corrected version.

docs.title: The problem amendments were built to solve
docs.text:
Every blockchain eventually needs to change its rules. The conventional answer is a hard fork: operators coordinate off-chain to run new software by a flag date, and nodes that miss the date end up on a diverging chain. For a decentralized value-settlement network that is a serious hazard — a botched or contested fork can split the ledger, and "the rules changed out from under me" is exactly the failure a settlement system cannot tolerate.

The XRP Ledger's answer, introduced in rippled 0.31.0 (2016), was to make protocol evolution a first-class, on-ledger process rather than an off-chain social coordination problem. The design goal, in the original framing, was "sensible evolution": let the network adopt new features without disruptive hard forks, with the validators themselves — not any single company — deciding when a change goes live, and with an explicit safety mechanism for nodes that fall behind. This is why the amendment system predates most of the features this chapter documents: it is the substrate that made all of them shippable.

docs.title: From idea to on-ledger switch
docs.text:
The insight that makes the system work is that a rule change does not need a new chain — it only needs a coordinated flag day that the ledger itself records and enforces. The mechanism has three moving parts, all visible in xrpld source:

  1. The vote rides on validations. Each validator publishes its amendment preferences in the sfAmendments field of the validations it already signs every ledger (src/xrpld/app/misc/detail/AmendmentTable.cpp — see doVoting()). No separate election is needed; governance piggybacks on consensus.
  2. The network writes its own transactions. When an amendment's support crosses the threshold, the network injects an EnableAmendment pseudo-transaction — transaction type ttAMENDMENT (100), include/xrpl/protocol/detail/transactions.macro — that no account submits. It is applied by the Change transactor (src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/system/Change.cpp, applyAmendment()).
  3. The ledger holds the canonical state. applyAmendment() maintains the Amendments singleton object (keylet::amendments()): a running sfMajorities array (each entry an amendment plus the sfCloseTime when it first reached majority — the start of the clock) and the sfAmendments list of what is permanently enabled. The tfGotMajority flag adds an entry and starts the timer; tfLostMajority removes it and resets the timer; an EnableAmendment with no flag pushes the amendment into sfAmendments and enables it for good.

The activation rule sits on top of that state: an amendment enables only after it has held ≥ 80% support for two consecutive weeks (kAmendmentMajorityCalcThreshold = 80/100 and kDefaultAmendmentMajorityTime = weeks{2} in include/xrpl/protocol/SystemParameters.h; the gate (*majorityTime + majorityTime_) <= closeTime in AmendmentTable.cpp). Because losing majority resets the sfCloseTime, the two-week clock is a sustained threshold, not a one-time poll — a design choice that favors stability over speed. See ch04 Operations for the operator-facing side of these same constants.

docs.title: The safety valve: amendment-blocking
docs.text: The other half of "no disruptive hard forks" is what happens to a node that is behind. When applyAmendment() enables an amendment the local build does not understand, it calls setAmendmentBlocked() (Change.cpp) and the node stops processing rather than applying rules it cannot validate correctly. A stale node fails safe and loud (visible as server_info.amendment_blocked) instead of silently diverging onto its own fork. This is the mechanism that lets the network upgrade itself without splitting.

docs.title: Milestones and lessons
docs.text:
• FeeEscalation — the first activated amendment (2016-05-05). Fittingly, the amendment system's debut change hardened the network under load (transaction-cost escalation), proving the pipeline on an operational fix before feature work.
  • MultiSign — governance enabling security. Multi-signing shipped as one of the earliest amendments, establishing the pattern that even account-security primitives arrive through the same vote.
  • Feature waves. Escrow and payment channels, then Flow (the rewritten payment engine), later the AMM, and most recently permissioned tokens and DEX — each entered through the identical pipeline, which is why this chapter can describe them uniformly as active / voting / in-development.
  • Obsoletion is part of the design, not a failure of it. Batch and PermissionDelegation were superseded by corrected versions (BatchV1_1, PermissionDelegationV1_1); the originals are marked permanently un-votable rather than deleted. The lesson: because activation is irreversible, a flawed amendment is retired by shipping a fixed successor, not by "turning it off" — reinforcing why the two-week sustained threshold and validator opt-in exist in the first place.

docs.title: How amendments affect your code
docs.text:
• New transaction type — submitting before activation → temDISABLED.
  • New ledger entry type — ledger_entry queries return nothing or errors.
  • New RPC method — returns unknown command on nodes below the minimum version.
  • Flag changes — new flags on existing transactions are silently ignored or error depending on whether the amendment is active.

Always check server_info.amendment_blocked on any production node. A value of true means the node is running software that does not support an enabled amendment — it is no longer tracking the live ledger.

docs.title: Version compatibility matrix
docs.text:
Status key: ✅ Active — enabled on Mainnet | 🗳️ Voting — open, not yet activated 🔧 Dev — Supported::No; not votable | ⚠️ Obsolete — removed/replaced

✅ Active (retired) — enabled on Mainnet and active for 2+ years, so its amendment-gating code has been removed from xrpld (identifier moved to the XRPL_RETIRE_FEATURE list). It is still fully active and can never be disabled — "retired" refers only to the source-code cleanup, not to the amendment's status on the ledger. Do not read (retired) as "off" or "deprecated feature."

Sources: features.macro (xrpld 3.3 branch), xrpscan.com/amendments (live Mainnet status), xrpl.org/resources/known-amendments, API-CHANGELOG.md.
